title: DexPort: A Hand-Held Skill Interface for Dexterous Hand Data Collection
authors: Amber Xie,Jiawei Fu,Xiaofeng Guo,Carmelo Sferrazza,Guanya Shi,Haozhi Qi
comment: Website:this https URL
abstract:
Collecting high-quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning
dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it
requires a complete robot setup and
places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human
demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and
retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this
paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface for high-DoF
robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment,
avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and
measured joint states. Our key
observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous
tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand-held interface to specify
the robot’s wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger
motion. This removes the need to control
each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and
in-hand manipulation. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations across several real-world
tasks in laboratory and in-the-wild settings without a robot arm. We then use behavior
cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and
hand commands, without skill labels.
We evaluate on four tasks: pick-and-place with diverse objects, screwing with
in-hand tool use, drawer stowing that requires simultaneous grasping and pulling,
and bimanual barcode scanning. Using recorded robot commands instead of measured
joint states improves average final-task success from 11% to 64% across the
three tasks evaluated by success rate. Co-training with in-the-wild data improves
average pick-and-place success from 36% to 78% across the three evaluation
conditions. Videos are available at https://amberxie88.github.io/dexport/.
introduction:
Multi-fingered hands allow robots to use different grasps, manipulate tools, and
reorient objects in hand. Learning these behaviors from demonstrations requires
data that capture detailed finger motion and contact-rich interactions.
Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot
setup. Collecting in-hand manipulation demonstrations through teleoperation is
particularly challenging because the operator must coordinate many finger
joints [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. On the other hand, human hand
demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and
retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot
actions [6, 7, 8]. We therefore need a method that scales beyond
a fixed robot setup while preserving executable hand actions.

To address this issue for parallel-jaw grippers, the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) [9] uses a portable, hand-held
interface to collect demonstrations naturally and at scale. However, extending this paradigm to multi-fingered hands has not been
trivial. Early efforts, including DexUMI [10] and DEXOP [11],
can collect dexterous and contact-rich behaviors using wearable hand exoskeletons.
However, designing a high-DoF exoskeleton involves a difficult trade-off between
dexterity and wearability: supporting more independent finger motions increases
both mechanical complexity and the operator’s control burden. In addition, these systems
record exoskeleton configurations rather than the commands and resulting states
of the deployed robot hand. RealDexUMI [12] preserves this
information by collecting executable commands with the physical robot hand, but
demonstrates the approach on a hand with only six active DoFs. It remains unclear
how to preserve these benefits for a hand with many independently controlled
joints without making the interface cumbersome.

Inspired by these works, we address three requirements for a portable interface
for dexterous hands. Table I compares existing systems against these
requirements.
First, the interface should use the same end effector as the deployed robot
(Same Emb.), so that hand motions need no retargeting and no embodiment
gap is introduced. Second, it should record the commands sent to the hand
(Action Data) rather than relying only on actions inferred from future
measured states. This distinction matters during contact, when the commanded
target and measured joint state may differ. Third, it should expose enough
controllable degrees of freedom (DoF) to support tasks that require
multi-fingered dexterity; otherwise, a simpler gripper would be sufficient.
Reusing the deployment hand satisfies the first two requirements, but creating
an intuitive and comfortable interface for high-DoF control is challenging,
especially when the operator must control each joint directly.

In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface built
around these requirements. Our key design principle is to collect demonstrations with the same
hand hardware used at deployment while controlling it through a small set of skills.
Because the collection hand shares the deployment hand’s hardware and control
interface, each demonstration records native commanded joint targets and
resulting states.
The operator moves the device to specify the robot’s wrist motion and selects or
adjusts skills to control the hand. Parameterized skills produce power, pinch, and two-finger
grasps, while a learned closed-loop skill generates the finger gaiting needed
for in-hand rotation. This skill-level interface leaves task decisions to the
operator while the robot hand produces the coordinated finger motion.

We evaluate DexPort on four tasks that require different forms of dexterity:
selecting grasps for objects of different shapes, opening a drawer while holding
an object in the same hand, rotating a tool in hand, and coordinating two hands
to scan a barcode. We collect demonstrations both in the lab and in
unstructured environments, without a robot arm or external tracking
infrastructure. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies
directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels.
Our policies complete all four tasks and outperform a state-as-action baseline
trained without commanded hand actions on each task. Across the three tasks scored by
success rate, final-task success averages 64% versus 11%. Co-training with in-the-wild demonstrations
further improves pick-and-place in every condition, including unseen objects and
scenes with distractors. DexPort also collects demonstrations at roughly
1.4×1.4\times the rate of glove teleoperation.

To summarize, our contributions are as follows:

A portable and ergonomic data-collection interface that uses the same
hand hardware and control space as the deployed robot. It avoids a hand embodiment
gap and records native commanded actions and measured states.

A skill-level control scheme that makes a high-DoF hand practical to
operate during portable data collection. A compact set of parameterized and
learned skills replaces joint-by-joint control while preserving the ability
to perform dexterous tasks.

An evaluation across four real-world tasks, including data collection in
unstructured environments and visuomotor policies trained directly on the
recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels.

1. A portable and ergonomic data-collection interface that uses the same
hand hardware and control space as the deployed robot. It avoids a hand embodiment
gap and records native commanded actions and measured states.

2. A skill-level control scheme that makes a high-DoF hand practical to
operate during portable data collection. A compact set of parameterized and
learned skills replaces joint-by-joint control while preserving the ability
to perform dexterous tasks.

3. An evaluation across four real-world tasks, including data collection in
unstructured environments and visuomotor policies trained directly on the
recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels.

title: ViT-H: Generative Video-To-Humanoid Control with Motion Tracking Feedback
authors: Zimo He,Tianyi Bian,Zizhong Yang,Hongjie Li,Nan Jiang,Jieming Cui,Baoxiong Jia,Yizhou Wang,Siyuan Huang,Yixin Zhu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: The first four authors contributed equally. Project website:this https URL
abstract:
Learning humanoid control from monocular human videos offers a scalable way to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors.
Yet, existing reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines
are limited in system-level scalability by separately optimized intermediate stages and cannot directly optimize reference motion executability using downstream tracking feedback.
We present ViT-H, a video-to-humanoid control framework following a generation-and-tracking paradigm.
ViT-H directly generates humanoid reference motions from videos with a diffusion model, bypassing human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and uses motion-tracking outcomes to post-train the generator with direct preference optimization.
We further introduce an autoregressive variant that enables real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency.
Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms state-of-the-art reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines in both motion quality and executability.
We further show that ViT-H scales favorably with model size and with both pre-training and post-training data scale, while motion-tracking feedback consistently improves executability across different motion trackers. Project page: https://awfuact.github.io/vit-h/.
introduction:
Monocular human videos record whole-body behaviors at a scale and diversity that motion capture datasets (Mahmood et al., 2019) cannot match, making them an attractive source of skills for humanoid robots. Recent works have leveraged human videos to learn expressive whole-body skills (He et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025; Sleiman et al., 2026), environment-aware behaviors that interact with surrounding geometry (Allshire et al., 2025), and interactive skills involving objects and humans (Wang et al., 2026b). Most existing systems realize this capability through a reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipeline, which first reconstructs human motion from video, then retargets it to the humanoid embodiment, and finally tracks the resulting reference motion. This modular separation is increasingly practical as recent advances in general whole-body tracking enable a shared tracker to execute diverse reference motions (Luo et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026). However, the upstream reconstruction-and-retargeting stages remain an indirect route from video to humanoid motion, where errors can accumulate to produce inconsistent, distorted, or dynamically infeasible references, making downstream tracking more difficult.

Prior work has sought to improve reference motion quality by strengthening individual stages of this pipeline, either by enforcing physical plausibility in reconstructed human motions (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2025) or by improving motion retargeting (Araujo et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026a; Cao et al., 2026). However, such stage-local remedies expose two structural limitations of the pipeline. First, its system-level scalability remains bounded by the remaining stages. Human motion reconstruction is not optimized for the morphology and dynamics of the target humanoid, while retargeting can only operate on reconstructed motions after upstream errors have propagated and discarded visual evidence can no longer be revisited. Second, executability is difficult to optimize end-to-end. Tracking results are observed only after reconstruction and retargeting, making it difficult to use execution outcomes to directly improve the complete video-to-humanoid mapping. Consequently, plausible reference motions at intermediate stages may still be difficult for the control policy to track.

To this end, we introduce ViT-H, a generative Video-To-Humanoid control framework following a generation-and-tracking paradigm. At the core of ViT-H are (i) a motion generator that maps monocular videos directly into the target humanoid motion space, eliminating the intermediate bottleneck of human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and (ii) whole-body control policies that not only track the generated reference motions but also evaluate their executability, providing motion-tracking feedback for post-training the reference motion generator, thereby closing the loop between generation and control (Figure 2).

Concretely, our motion generator is a video-conditioned humanoid motion diffusion model (Ho et al., 2020) first pre-trained on video-motion pairs and motion-only data. The whole-body control policies are fine-tuned from a pre-existing general motion tracker, yielding a deployable tracking policy and a privileged variant with additional global observations. We evaluate motions sampled from the generator with both tracking policies and use the resulting tracking outcomes to construct preference pairs for  dpo (dpo) (Rafailov et al., 2023; Wallace et al., 2024), explicitly incorporating executability into the humanoid motion generator. Because preference pair construction needs no ground-truth motion, post-training extends to unannotated internet videos. Additionally, we further extend ViT-H with an autoregressive variant of the motion generator that produces motions in temporal segments, enabling online control from streaming video and real-time video teleoperation of a physical Unitree G1 from a single RGB camera (Figure 1).

Our contributions are fourfold. First, we introduce ViT-H, a generative video-to-humanoid control framework that directly generates executable humanoid motions from monocular videos without human motion reconstruction and retargeting. Second, we introduce dpo post-training with motion-tracking feedback, which explicitly incorporates executability into reference motion generation while requiring no motion annotations. Third, extensive experiments demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms state-of-the-art reconstruction-retargeting-tracking baselines in motion quality and executability. Fourth, we demonstrate that ViT-H scales favorably with model capacity and both pre-training and post-training data size, while its post-training gains generalize to three held-out general motion trackers (Qi et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a).

title: RynnUnify: Towards Unified Embodied Brain
authors: Minghao Zhu,Bohan Hou,Kun Xiang,Zixuan Wang,Yinzhou Tang,Yifei Yang,Zhikai Wang,Tianyi Zhang,Kehan Li,Haoyu Zhao,Siteng Huang,Leigang Qu,Sicong Leng,Dongchi Huang,Mingxiu Chen,Shijian Lu,Yue Wang,Xiaodan Liang,Zhenyu Zeng,Deli Zhao,Chengju Liu,Jianfei Yang,Xin Li
abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video–language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.
introduction:
Developing general robot brains damo2026rynnbrain, li2026rynnbrain11capablegeneralizable requires models that understand the physical world, anticipate interaction outcomes, and translate task intentions into action. Across interdependent operations, a robot must identify subgoals, predict scene changes, and determine how they affect subsequent decisions. These demands motivate unified embodied models that coordinate understanding, world prediction, and action generation cosmos3, liang2026rxbrain.

Existing unified multimodal models (UMMs) have made encouraging progress in jointly modeling understanding and generation cosmos3, liang2026rxbrain, deng2025bagel. Their coordination requires strong embodied understanding to ground task intentions, reason about physical interactions, and interpret predicted outcomes. Sustaining this interaction over long horizons remains challenging as scene changes and prediction errors accumulate, while static visual predictions can overlook intermediate dynamics. Addressing these challenges requires interleaved reasoning hou2026interlv that connects embodied understanding with temporally coherent video prediction.

To this end, we introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model built upon the Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture liang2025mixtureoftransformers of Cosmos3 cosmos3, comprising an 8B autoregressive reasoner and an 8B diffusion generator. Centered on interleaved video-language reasoning, RynnUnify combines strong embodied understanding with video prediction to support understanding-guided long-horizon visual planning: the reasoner guides successive video predictions, whose outcomes provide context for subsequent subtask planning. To explore generation-enhanced embodied understanding, we further post-train an additional 8B agent from RynnUnify’s reasoner through reinforcement learning with final-answer feedback. The agent dynamically chooses between direct answering and invoking the frozen RynnUnify model to generate videos, which it then interprets to answer questions about unobserved future states and interaction outcomes. To bring the UMM’s understanding and world-prediction capabilities to robot control, we also extend the full RynnUnify model to a World-Action Model (WAM) through latent planning and joint video-action training.

We perform extensive pretraining on general multimodal understanding, spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and affordance grounding, complemented by subtask planning, world-modeling descriptions, and question answering with intermediate video context. This supervision strengthens foundational embodied understanding while preparing the reasoner to formulate task-relevant visual predictions and interpret their outcomes. Generation training covers long-horizon egocentric activities, robot manipulation, and embodied reasoning videos. We introduce scene memory and self-forcing huang2025selfforcing to improve visual consistency and robustness during long-horizon generation.

Dedicated benchmarks remain lacking for assessing sustained visual planning and the contribution of video prediction to future-state reasoning. We therefore introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU. Rynn-VP evaluates whether visual plans remain consistent with the task and preceding operations over long horizons. Rynn-GEU focuses on action consequences, physical changes, and spatial relationships after motion or viewpoint changes, whose answers concern states not directly observable in the input. Its direct setting tests whether models can infer these states without explicit video generation, while its generation-assisted setting tests whether predicted videos improve answers to the same questions.

Extensive evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art embodied understanding among the evaluated UMMs on public benchmarks, together with strong video generation performance. RynnUnify also demonstrates sustained planning on Rynn-VP and strong direct anticipatory reasoning on Rynn-GEU, with further GEU improvements through its agentic extension. For robot control, the WAM extension achieves a 51.5% success rate on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 robocasa365 tasks. Experiments on Astribot S1 further demonstrate effective multi-step manipulation involving body reorientation, precise object handling, and history-dependent execution.

Figure 1 summarizes RynnUnify’s capabilities and representative evaluation results.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce RynnUnify, a unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with interleaved video-language reasoning for long-horizon visual planning.

We post-train an agent from RynnUnify’s reasoner to explore generation-enhanced embodied understanding, demonstrating the utility of video predictions for reasoning about unobserved future states.

We extend the full RynnUnify UMM to a WAM through latent planning and joint video-action training, and validate its capabilities in simulated and real-robot manipulation.

We introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory embodied reasoning, complemented by extensive evaluations on public benchmarks that establish RynnUnify’s state-of-the-art embodied understanding among the compared UMMs.

1. We introduce RynnUnify, a unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with interleaved video-language reasoning for long-horizon visual planning.

2. We post-train an agent from RynnUnify’s reasoner to explore generation-enhanced embodied understanding, demonstrating the utility of video predictions for reasoning about unobserved future states.

3. We extend the full RynnUnify UMM to a WAM through latent planning and joint video-action training, and validate its capabilities in simulated and real-robot manipulation.

4. We introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory embodied reasoning, complemented by extensive evaluations on public benchmarks that establish RynnUnify’s state-of-the-art embodied understanding among the compared UMMs.

title: Robotic Optical Coherence Tomography-Guided Geometric Modeling of Soft Tissue: 3D Representations for Data-Driven Closed-Loop Shape Control
authors: Chaoyu Zhang,Guangshen Ma,Mark Draelos
abstract:
In medical robotics, data-driven soft-tissue shape control requires deforming tissue toward desired morphologies through sequential physical interactions.
This challenge is particularly important in microscale manipulation, where localized deformation is difficult to observe, represent, and control, while physics-based models can be computationally expensive and difficult to adapt to realistic environments.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides high-resolution volumetric perception of tissue deformation, but target-conditioned control requires effective representations of both observed and desired tissue states.
In this work, we introduce an OCT-guided data-driven framework for tissue shape control, learned from user-guided demonstrations and executed with closed-loop OCT feedback.
We study full-volume, tissue-masked sparse-volume, and voxelized point-cloud representations, with or without residual conditioning, using deterministic (Explicit) and generative diffusion (Diffusion) policies.
Across 12 configurations and 576 phantom rollouts on 3-DoF depth and 6-DoF directional tasks, OCT-derived 3D representations support both Explicit and Diffusion policies, with performance depending on representation and residual conditioning.
Residual conditioning reduces directional Shape RMSE from 0.748 to 0.555 mm for full-volume Diffusion, while voxelized point-cloud Explicit with residuals achieves 0.534 mm for depth and 0.443 mm for directional control, with comparable accuracy at intermediate unseen targets and consistent performance across deployments.
We further evaluate the framework in 60 ex vivo porcine rollouts, extending to biological tissue with final geometric errors comparable to human demonstrations.
These results establish volumetric OCT as current and goal representations for learned closed-loop tissue shape control across deterministic and generative action models.
introduction:
In medical robotics, microscale tissue manipulation requires precise control of deformable tissue through physical interaction, where tissue configuration can directly affect task execution (Thach et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023).
For example, robotic palpation relies on controlled tool-tissue interaction to induce and regulate local deformation toward a desired morphological state.
The control objective is therefore not simply a tool pose, but a target tissue morphology achieved through sequential interactions and successive observation of tissue response.
Goal-conditioned deformable manipulation has demonstrated this principle using image contours and point clouds (Navarro-Alarcon & Liu, 2018; Thach et al., 2022; Thach et al., 2024).
Extending this paradigm to volumetric medical imaging is particularly relevant to microscale manipulation, where 3D image volumes preserve spatial and structural information (Zhou et al., 2026) and allow desired tissue morphologies to be represented directly in the imaging space using both intensity-based and geometric representations.

At the microscale, morphology-based control requires high-resolution volumetric observations that capture both surface geometry and depth-dependent tissue structure.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides such observations, resolving local surface morphology and subsurface structure within a 3D imaging volume (Huang et al., 1991; Ma et al., 2025).
This volumetric perception has enabled robotic OCT systems for learned interaction, insertion control, and deformation-aware instrument navigation (Keller et al., 2020; Edwards et al., 2022; Arikan et al., 2025).
Based on these capabilities, we develop OCT-guided soft-tissue shape control, a learning-based framework (Fig. 1) that uses OCT feedback to guide tool motion toward a target tissue morphology represented in the same imaging space.
This closed-loop formulation enables the robot to adapt its actions to observed deformation, providing a foundation for image-guided tissue shaping in microscale interventions.

Realizing closed-loop OCT-guided shape control requires jointly addressing target construction, OCT representation, and action prediction.
Prior work has used geometric and learned goal shapes for deformable-object manipulation (Thach et al., 2022; Thach et al., 2026), while OCT-derived point clouds have been explored for registration and reconstruction (Liu et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025).
Building upon these directions, we introduce an OCT-guided robotic framework that constructs parameterized target morphologies from measured tissue states and learns to deform tissue toward these targets from user demonstrations.
We investigate full OCT volumes, tissue-masked intensity volumes, and voxelized point clouds for representing current and target states, and compare deterministic Explicit and Diffusion action models (Chi et al., 2023; Ze et al., 2024), with and without representation-specific current–target residual conditioning.
These policies predict incremental 6-DoF tooltip motions, while successive OCT scans provide closed-loop feedback toward the desired tissue morphology.

In this work, we evaluate 12 policy configurations on physical robotic shape control tasks spanning depth and directional deformations, including intermediate targets unseen during training, and further demonstrate the framework on ex vivo porcine tissue with varying surface geometries.
Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using volumetric OCT observations for closed-loop shape control with both Explicit and Diffusion policies, while voxelized point cloud representations provide accurate and repeatable control through compact geometric encoding.
In addition, current-to-target residual conditioning further improves performance across most configurations and strengthens target-dependent responses, particularly for full volume representations.
Overall, this work establishes a systematic framework for studying how volumetric and geometric OCT representations support learned closed-loop tissue shape control, connecting high-resolution medical imaging with deterministic Explicit and generative Diffusion action policies for deformable tissue manipulation.

title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
authors: Thomas Landeg,Thierry Tambe
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once
their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such
failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at
inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for
frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on
outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA’s existing internal representations to
estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a
threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm’s recently achieved motion, and hands
control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds
only 0.48–0.88% to the policy’s parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs
spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and π\pi0.5, which use flow-matching action
experts, and the autoregressive π\pi0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step
tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy’s
failure rate by 19–48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites,
where control success is already 85–99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations
tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.
introduction:
Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have spurred the development of
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Black et al., 2025a; Pertsch et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025).
These models typically use pretrained VLMs as a backbone, leveraging their visual and language representations to condition the generation of robot actions.
Yet even large VLAs trained on diverse, multi-embodiment robotics datasets remain brittle outside their training distribution: modest changes to camera viewpoint, robot initialization, or scene composition can sharply reduce success rates (Fei et al., 2026).
This challenge is particularly relevant for compact VLAs such as SmolVLA, whose VLM backbone benefits from broad vision-language pretraining, but whose robotics training consists of fewer than 30,000 episodes of community-contributed demonstrations collected primarily on a single robot embodiment (Shukor et al., 2025).

Out-of-distribution states are not only something a VLA encounters; they are also something it can create. Robot imitation datasets are built primarily from successful demonstrations and contain comparatively little data showing how to recover once something has gone wrong (Dai et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025). For instance, when a VLA drops an object, knocks something over, or otherwise makes a mistake, it can therefore place itself in a state poorly represented in its training data.
Simply allowing more execution time leaves most failures unresolved: on LIBERO-Long,
doubling the episode step budget increases success by only 2.3–3.7 percentage points across
the three evaluated VLAs (Appendix A.3).

One remedy is to give the policy the data it is missing: collect demonstrations of failures and their recoveries, then train on them (Dai et al., 2025).
But collecting recovery data is expensive, and the cost may need to be paid again for every new embodiment and task. Instead, we ask whether part of the distribution shift can be reversed directly. After a mistake, both the scene and the robot may have changed: objects may have been displaced, while the arm has moved into an unfamiliar configuration. Changes to the scene are difficult to undo, since restoring a displaced object is itself a manipulation problem. The arm configuration, however, is under our control. This suggests a simple recovery strategy: retrace the arm’s motion along the path that led to failure, in the hope of returning toward an earlier configuration from which the unchanged policy can successfully retry.

In this work, we introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs (Figure 1). Similar to SAFE (Gu et al., 2025), a small failure prediction head reads features the policy has already computed and estimates the probability that the current episode will end in failure; when that probability exceeds a threshold, a controller retraces the arm’s recent motion and returns control to the policy. The only supervision Backtrack needs is whether autonomous rollouts of the frozen policy succeed or fail: no teleoperated recovery demonstrations, no policy retraining, and no second model at inference. The head adds just 0.48–0.88% to the policy’s parameters.

We evaluate Backtrack on three policies with two different action-generation mechanisms: SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) and π\pi0.5 (Black et al., 2025a) use flow-matching action experts, while π\pi0-FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025) generates discrete action tokens autoregressively.
On LIBERO-Long (Liu et al., 2023a), the suite on which all three policies fail most often,
Backtrack reduces failure rates by 19% to 48%; averaged over all four LIBERO suites, the
reduction is 20–26%.
On MetaWorld (Yu et al., 2020), where we evaluate SmolVLA on a second benchmark
with a different embodiment, all twelve controller configurations we test improve on the
unassisted policy.

title: HoloBoxing: A Simple Recipe for Humanoid Boxing with 7 Minutes of Single-GPU Training
authors: Xihan Ma,Bo Zhang,Boxiong Li,Yuhan Bao,Ziyue Liu,Yucheng Wang
abstract: HoloBoxing presents a simple recipe for learning humanoid boxing by building on a pretrained whole-body controller. The recipe separates reusable motor skills from task decisions: a compact planner requests future body-point targets, while the frozen controller handles joint-level execution. A learned decoder maps 32-dimensional actions to structured target windows, and measured-state imitation initializes the planner before reinforcement learning. Task learning then refines interaction behavior while reusing the decoder and controller, avoiding the need to relearn whole-body control. This combination keeps task optimization focused on a compact upper policy and supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven exploration. Starting from that available controller, the recipe accounts for about seven minutes of additional training, including reused representation fitting and a single-GPU task run. This excludes controller pretraining, data preparation, evaluation, and search. Simulated boxing experiments and component controls evaluate the resulting behavior and the roles of imitation initialization and the target representation.
introduction:
A motion controller can reproduce a punch without deciding when or where to use it.
Humanoid boxing adds an opponent, changing contact, and the need to remain upright after an exchange.
Learning all of these behaviors from joint commands couples motor execution with task decisions.
HoloBoxing instead asks how far a simple, short training recipe can go when whole-body motor capability is already available.

Reusable whole-body controllers make task adaptation above existing motor capability a practical starting point.
The recipe separates what must be learned for boxing from what can be reused.
A pretrained HoloMotion v2 controller executes movement requests and remains frozen.
A learned target decoder represents short windows of future body-point poses with a 32-dimensional action.
A compact feedback planner selects these actions from measured robot state and opponent positions.
Task learning therefore adapts movement requests while retaining the underlying execution capability.

We initialize this planner through measured-state imitation before refining it with reinforcement learning.
The fixed controller first tracks reference motions to collect actual robot observations and future-target labels.
Supervised learning turns those pairs into an initial feedback policy.
Standing warmup and interaction against a fixed standing opponent then adjust behavior through rewards.
The decoder and lower controller are reused throughout, as illustrated in Figure 1.

These choices make the training problem smaller in three concrete ways.
Controller reuse removes joint-level motor learning from task adaptation.
The target representation reduces the planner’s action dimension from 225 coordinates to 32 latent variables.
Imitation supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven exploration.
Together, they define the simple recipe whose training cost and resulting behavior we evaluate.

The primary recipe accounts for 7.0 minutes, combining a new single-RTX-4090 run with previously recorded target-representation fitting. A 21.4-minute long version provides a higher-budget comparison.
Simulation experiments assess whether this short adaptation produces interactive boxing, while matched-budget controls remove imitation initialization or the target decoder.
We also test observation choices and representation quality to explain the interfaces used by the recipe.
Detailed timings and competitive outcomes appear in the experiments; assumptions and remaining validation needs are discussed separately.

title: When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation
authors: Vigneshwaran Subbaraju,Obaidullah Zaland,Monowar Bhuyan
comment: Accepted for presentation at SPAIS workshop in CoRL 2026
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot’s closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot actions [23]. Local robot policies can learn from human intervention and online correction [8, 2]; UniSteer specifically adapts a VLA using human takeover actions [10]. In parallel, FedVLA and ForgeVLA show ways to learn from distributed VLA task data without centralizing raw interaction records [12, 22]. A recent study of federated VLA fine-tuning reports that cross-site heterogeneity is more pronounced on physical robots than in its simulations [4]. These strands motivate a prospective setting: robots learn locally from human corrections, then selectively share resulting adaptations. The cited federated systems do not establish the safety of federating multimodal corrections.

Such feedback is heterogeneous in ways that task labels do not capture. People may signal a similar intended change by speech, gesture, guided motion, or teleoperation, with different urgency and precision. Consider two sites where a human helps a robot insert a panel. At one site, an operator standing beside the fixture points to a narrow gap and says bring it through here; the pointing gesture performed near the intended path clearly resolves an ambiguous verbal reference. At another site, an operator farther from the fixture gives a detailed verbal description or draws the desired trajectory on a camera image. The reliability of pointing changes with distance, while a drawn 2D route alone may leave depth, contact force, and handover timing unspecified [18, 11]. Each correction may improve its local policy, but their learned effects are not interchangeable. At a receiving site with a rotated fixture, different gripper, or different human hand position, a shared update could reduce clearance or release a jointly held panel too early. A learned motion may also behave differently with another gripper, compliance controller, or action decoder. Federated optimization can encounter client distribution shift and conflicting updates; in embodied systems, a regression can increase contact force, delay a yield, or leave a shared load unsupported. A successful average trajectory offers little evidence about a rare, hazardous interaction. Updates can also reveal private training information even when raw observations remain local [21].

Our question. What and how may robots learn from diverse, multimodal human corrections across sites, and when may that learning safely change another robot’s behavior? Consider a person and robot jointly inserting a panel. A spoken wait, a raised hand, and physical guidance might all signal a needed hold, but they may refer to different hazards or changes in task goal. The source robot can learn useful timing; a receiving robot with a different grip and fixture could release too early. We argue that corrective experience should travel only with a justified scope, receiving-site safety assessment, and an explicit privacy risk assessment. We develop three positions and an evaluation agenda rather than a new algorithm or empirical result.

title: Predictive Long-Horizon Progress Modeling with Action-Aware Quantification
authors: Tianchi Xu,Yalin Zheng,Yangxin Zhu,Ruonan Ren,Zheng Fu,Yunlong Wang,Yuanxin Zhong
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Process reward models (PRMs) evaluate intermediate execution states from visual observations, supplying dense feedback for robotic data curation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning [33, 42].
Consider a robot instructed to stack blocks in sequence: a completed placement advances the task, an attempted grasp earns temporary partial credit, and a dislodged block triggers revocation of its earlier placement credit.
Faithful process supervision must track these state changes across hesitation, progress regression, and recovery.
Recent methods draw on vision–language model (VLM)-based reward learning to bring task semantics to visual evaluation, and on video world models to supervise temporal dynamics through future prediction [27, 36].

Current PRMs learn relative progress through trajectory comparisons [21], interpolate across manually annotated task stages [7], or assign VLM-generated subtask budgets [14].
Relative comparisons establish trajectory ordering while leaving cross-task progress magnitude unspecified, and elapsed-time interpolation varies with execution speed for the same achieved state [7].
Long-horizon feedback must also quantify what a partial attempt contributes and which credit is revoked when a later action destroys an earlier achievement.
Scaling process evaluation thus requires both a unified absolute progress specification and a critic that tracks non-monotonic execution across subtasks.

To overcome these challenges, we propose action-aware quantification. We first define a subtask as a sequence of operations on the same manipulated object.
We then allocate a fixed local budget using the weights of executed actions and the necessary remaining actions. Action boundaries locate the curve breakpoints, and retained weighted action credit determines local progress within this budget.
Forward effects receive full credit, engaged-only attempts receive temporary half credit, and subsequent revocations remove the credit of the referenced earlier occurrence.
Finally, global progress tracks retained contributions across subtasks, including credit revoked by later destructive actions.
VLM pre-annotation and human verification establish structured action records, from which rule-based post-processing computes dense progress for training and evaluation.
We assemble a training dataset of 253,276 episodes spanning 800+ hours of robot and human video, together with LOOM (a LOng-hOrizon Manipulation progress benchmark), comprising 300 cross-embodiment trajectories evaluated at 19,618 human-calibrated frames.
The benchmark follows successive subtasks in long-horizon execution, covering different rates of advancement, hesitation, regression, recovery, and incomplete execution.

Building on this foundation, we introduce NimCritic (A Nimble Critic via Joint Video–Progress Learning), a dual-diffusion-transformer world reward model with separately supervised progress and completion outputs.
We term the model nimble because it uses predictive video learning during training and scores subtasks in parallel at inference [41], and a critic because it evaluates task advancement and goal satisfaction.
Joint Video–Progress Learning models how the observed state evolves while tying those transitions to advancement toward the specified subtask goal, complemented by Historical Progress Perturbation to regularize sequential history conditioning and contrastive Video–Progress Alignment to strengthen cross-modal correspondence.
On the established Video Progress Benchmark (VPB), NimCritic achieves 0.77 overall PRC-F1 and 0.82 TSA (surpassing GVL with GPT-6-Sol by about 65%).
On LOOM, it leads all external baselines across all four metrics in the overall and multi-task groups (0.86 and 0.95 PRC-F1), and on RoboArena it retrieves human-selected successful rollouts with 96.72% overall recall and 98.09% hit rate.

We summarize our main contributions as follows:

We formulate action-aware quantification, which converts object-level action effects into dense progress through weighted credits, explicit revocation, and composition across complete and incomplete subtasks.

We construct an 800+ hour action-aware training dataset through VLM pre-annotation and human verification, and LOOM, a 300-trajectory benchmark with 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames for testing long-horizon progress through hesitation, regression, recovery, and incomplete execution.

We propose NimCritic, which combines predictive video learning with progress and completion supervision, using Historical Progress Perturbation and Video–Progress Alignment to support sequential estimates and connect visual features to task progress.

We demonstrate the highest overall PRC-F1 and TSA on VPB and LOOM, together with 96.72% successful-rollout recall on RoboArena, and analyze the roles of egocentric human videos, non-expert trajectories, and predictive supervision.

1. We formulate action-aware quantification, which converts object-level action effects into dense progress through weighted credits, explicit revocation, and composition across complete and incomplete subtasks.

2. We construct an 800+ hour action-aware training dataset through VLM pre-annotation and human verification, and LOOM, a 300-trajectory benchmark with 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames for testing long-horizon progress through hesitation, regression, recovery, and incomplete execution.

3. We propose NimCritic, which combines predictive video learning with progress and completion supervision, using Historical Progress Perturbation and Video–Progress Alignment to support sequential estimates and connect visual features to task progress.

4. We demonstrate the highest overall PRC-F1 and TSA on VPB and LOOM, together with 96.72% successful-rollout recall on RoboArena, and analyze the roles of egocentric human videos, non-expert trajectories, and predictive supervision.

title: Adaptive World-Models for Anomaly Recognition (AWARE): A Framework for Robot Dynamics Prediction and Introspection
authors: Luke Beddow,George Mavroghenis,Rodrigo Chacon Quesada,Kamil Dreczkowski,Cong Sun,Jiankai Wang,Oscar Kwong-Fai Pang,Antoine Cully
abstract: Unrecognized anomalies in critical infrastructure can rapidly cascade into catastrophic physical or operational failures. Current anomaly detection approaches often rely on direct access to the monitored system by utilizing onboard sensors, such as motor encoders, to detect anomalous states. However, legacy hardware often lacks these sensors, or strict security protocols may prohibit access altogether. We therefore present Adaptive World-model for Anomaly REcognition (AWARE), a world model framework that is capable of anomaly detection using only external camera monitoring via system dynamics estimation and state prediction. Evaluated across 240240 real-world robotic crane trajectories, including payload collisions and motor degradations, AWARE demonstrates a 26%26\% improvement in anomaly classification over our strongest baseline under noisy, camera-only state estimation. Furthermore, the inferred dynamics parameter can be decoded to identify the source of faults, localizing the degrading motor with 88%88\% accuracy.
introduction:
Critical infrastructure, such as ports, power plants, and factories, heavily relies on robotic platforms to perform tasks [31]. Disruption to these systems, such as through unauthorized operation or cyberattacks, can be physically dangerous to nearby workers, and cause significant economic disruption. Consequently, monitoring these systems for anomalous behavior is crucial to ensure safe and continuous nominal operation.

Traditional learning-based anomaly detection approaches focus either on spatial reconstruction methods for detecting unexpected features in high-dimensional state data (e.g. via variational auto-encoders), or temporal sequence methods for forecasting and measuring divergence from predicted states (e.g. via dynamics models)  [7, 11]. However, these methods require precise estimation of the current robot state, typically via access to onboard sensors, such as motor encoders [28]. Many infrastructure applications prevent this low-level access due to lacking the required sensors or because of strict security protocols. Such applications, necessitate a physical ’air-gap’ between the state estimation system and the observed hardware, such as through an external camera. This form of external passive state estimation injects noise throughout the entire anomaly detection pipeline and prevents sufficient system identification, drastically degrading the performance of learned models.

Foundation model-based approaches, (e.g. LLMs, VLMs) offer a promising alternative  [2, 36] . Instead of relying on precise state data, they leverage a more general semantic understanding of the scene (i.e. directly from vision or text descriptions) to detect anomalies. However this comes with a clear trade-off: sacrificing a precise understanding of temporal dynamics for semantic generalizability, which may prohibit detection of subtle, mechanics-based anomalies.

To bridge this gap, we introduce Adaptive World-Models for Anomaly Recognition (AWARE): a framework for anomaly detection under high-uncertainty camera-only state estimation. AWARE jointly trains a latent dynamics estimator and world model. The estimator provides a latent representation of the robot’s intrinsic parameters, such as motor gain or mass, while the world model uses this representation, along with an intended action, to produce an accurate prediction of the next robot state under the assumed dynamics. AWARE directly addresses the three prior challenges of passive monitoring by introducing noise resilience via a novel dual-signal architecture, relaxing system identification requirements through domain randomization and world model dynamics conditioning, and providing explainable anomaly detection by identifying the fault source. Figure 1 shows the AWARE system overview.

The key contributions of this work are:

AWARE framework. An adaptive world model conditioned on a latent dynamics estimator designed for anomaly detection under high noise state estimation. AWARE is trained fully in simulation using domain randomization, without requiring perfect system identification or explicit priors on anomaly types.

Robust detection and identification. We demonstrate that a novel dual-signal architecture of world model prediction error and latent dynamics deviation improves the detection of in and out-of-distribution anomalies on a challenging real world platform. AWARE shows a modest, but statistically significant, 3%3\% improvement over the next best baseline under low-noise state estimation, and a significant 26%26\% performance increase while identifying the source of in-distribution anomalies in 88%88\% of cases under high-noise state estimation.

Rigorous real-world experimental analysis. We evaluate AWARE over 240240 real world robotic crane trajectories driven by 55 different human operators. We perform a detailed analysis and ablation of the AWARE components and compare with a comprehensive selection of baselines including simulators, world models, foundation models, dynamics estimators and established anomaly detection approaches.

title: Conditional Neural Processes for Self-Supervised Goal Discovery in Action Imitation
authors: Marco Gabriele Fedozzi,Yukie Nagai,Francesco Rea,Alessandra Sciutti
comment: Presented at the poster session of the Workshop on World Models and Predictive Coding in Cognitive Robotics @ IROS2023 (this https URL)
abstract: Inspired by infants’ ability to learn novel tasks by imitating others, in this work we evaluate to what extent Conditional Neural Processes can autonomously learn representations of actions that are informative about their underlying goal. We show that the addition of an attention mechanism in the hidden space fosters the emergence of robust goal representations early on in the observation of an action sequence, making it a promising model for a robotic self-supervised general learner.
introduction:
The Mirror Neuron System (MNS) has a central role in our ability to predict the evolution of observed actions [1], being therefore associated with the inference of others’ mental states (Theory of Mind [2]). The predictive ability of the MNS appears to work at multiple layers of abstraction, ranging from the evolution of the motor plan to its underlying goal [3].
The emergence of this forecasting ability during infancy is accredited to a ”passive” observation of others and an ”active” association of self-actions with the generated sensory feedback [4, 5]. Both modes are ultimately connected to infants’ ability to imitate others, providing a shortcut to associate drives, goals, and motions, without explicit rewards [6].
This association requires the formation of distinct (but connected) representations of different actions in the absence of direct supervision.
This capability inspires cognitive robotics’ solutions, as a good self-supervised representation learning can ease later learning of novel tasks11
1
            
            
          E.g. refer to BERT [7] and its robustness to multiple fine-tuned tasks..
This work evaluates to which extent Deep Modality Blending Networks (DMBN) [8], a multimodal generative robotic control model inspired by the MNS, manifest those emergent properties.

title: Robust Offset-Free Lane-Keeping Control Framework for Vision-Only Automated Vehicles
authors: Der-Hau Lee
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Achieving accurate, real-time lane-keeping control during high-speed cornering on large-curvature roads while ensuring robust vehicle stability is a critical challenge in autonomous driving. To address this challenge, this study developed a robust offset-free model predictive control (OF-MPC) framework for vision-based autonomous vehicle lane-keeping. The regulation problem in this framework is solved using several algorithms. Numerical simulation results indicated that the interpolation-tube-based constrained iterative linear quadratic regulator (itube-CILQR) algorithm outperformed solvers based on the standard Interior Point Optimizer (IPOPT) and Operator Splitting Quadratic Program (OSQP), achieving a mean computation time of less than 5 ms. The itube-CILQR algorithm was then used for vehicle control in vision-based lane-keeping experiments in a simulation environment to quantify the perceptual uncertainty of a visual perception model (multitask UNet). This quantification was performed using the OF-MPC framework for traffic scenes that were not encountered during model training. Overall, the developed OF-MPC framework and the proposed method for characterizing the perceptual uncertainty of a visual perception system in unseen environments can contribute to the future development of advanced autonomous driving systems.
introduction:
Offset-free model predictive control (OF-MPC) is an advanced control strategy for solving the steady-state error problem in the presence of internal disturbances (plant–model mismatch) or external disturbances (measurement noise), which cannot be accurately modeled in standard MPC [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. An OF-MPC system typically consists of three components, namely a state estimator, target selector, and regulator. By augmenting the system state with an integrating disturbance, OF-MPC can eliminate the discrepancies between the steady states of system models and achieve offset-free control performance. OF-MPC was originally developed for industrial process control, and its control mechanisms were then incorporated into economic MPC, which aims to optimize economic objectives, such as maximizing profit, rather than primarily track predefined setpoints [6, 7]. Although numerous studies have employed OF-MPC in automated industrial processes, limited studies have used it in automated automotive applications.

In [8], an OF-MPC framework was developed for linear systems to address common model mismatches and disturbances in the lateral control of autonomous vehicles, including tire stiffness mismatches, steering angle offsets, and lateral slope disturbances, all of which contribute to steady-state tracking errors and degrade vehicle dynamic performance. The framework integrates these mismatches and disturbances into a single disturbance term, which is estimated using the Kalman filter; the term is then incorporated into an optimization process to eliminate lateral steady-state tracking errors. The study revealed that this framework could efficiently complete calculations in less than 7 ms. On the basis of this framework, [9] developed an OF-MPC framework for the longitudinal and lateral control of autonomous vehicles to achieve offset-free trajectory tracking. In this framework, the friction circle is incorporated into motion constraints to prevent vehicle tires from losing adhesion. In addition, nonlinear constraints derived from the friction circle are transformed into linear constraints through polygon approximation. This framework exhibited an average computation time of approximately 5 ms in simulations and real-world experiments with a vehicle speed of 25.2 km/h. In [10], an OF-MPC scheme incorporating a moving-horizon estimation (MHE) approach was developed to compensate for the heading bias resulting from localization uncertainty in lateral motion planning for autonomous buses; the measurable variables were yaw rate, heading error, and lateral position error, whereas the disturbance variables were heading-error bias, road-curvature bias, and control-input bias. Thus, the disturbance vector had the same number of dimensions (three) as the measurement vector did. This scheme required average computational times of 1.26 and 3.22 ms for solving the MPC and MHE problems, respectively, in lateral motion planning during vehicle tests with a maximum speed of 40 km/h. An OF-MPC framework was proposed in [11] to address model mismatches, parameter variations, and unexpected disturbances in integrated brake system control for autonomous vehicles. The proposed framework incorporates the total disturbance as a measurable disturbance input. The performance of the framework was assessed through simulations and experiments, and its suitability for braking systems was verified on a microchip; the framework exhibited an average computation time of 70 μ\mus. In [12], an offset-free economic MPC framework was developed to minimize the tracking error and control effort of an autonomous electric vehicle while accounting for economic criteria. The offset-free mechanism of this framework compensates for disturbances and prediction errors resulting from self-triggered control operations. Real-world experiments revealed that the developed framework effectively tracked the reference trajectory of an autonomous electric vehicle operating at a speed of 2 m/s, requiring less than 0.05 s to generate each control update. In summary, the preceding discussion suggests that OF-MPC is a promising approach for controlling vehicles in resource-limited automotive applications owing to its low computational burden and real-time computation performance.

Lane-keeping control is a type of lateral vehicle control, although the corresponding MPC problem typically involves constrained nonlinear optimization because of road curvature [13]. Solving this problem becomes particularly challenging in high-speed cornering scenarios on roads with tight curves, when limited on-board computational resources may hinder the generation of real-time problem solutions and timely control actions, thereby compromising driving safety. To mitigate this problem, we previously proposed a tube-based robust control strategy for vision-guided autonomous vehicles [14]. Specifically, a computationally efficient interpolation-tube-based constrained iterative linear quadratic regulator (itube-CILQR) algorithm was developed and incorporated into the vision perception system proposed in [15] for autonomous vehicle lane keeping. The feasibility of this algorithm was validated through numerical simulations and vision-based experiments conducted in The Open Racing Car Simulator (TORCS) [16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. Nevertheless, certain limitations were observed in [14]. First, the itube-CILQR algorithm does not incorporate output feedback, which is crucial in autonomous driving applications. Second, this algorithm does not address lateral steady-state tracking errors, resulting in lateral position deviations from the optimal vehicle trajectory along curvy road sections. Third, the perceptual uncertainty of the adopted visual perception system [15] was not quantified in previously unseen scenarios. Quantifying perceptual uncertainty in unseen environments is crucial for developing high-performance visual perception and autonomous driving systems.

To address the aforementioned limitations, the present study developed a robust OF-MPC framework, incorporated it into the visual perception system [15], and then assessed the perceptual uncertainty of this system in unseen environments. By modeling the nonlinear road curvature term as an integrating disturbance, the OF-MPC framework efficiently solves the lane-keeping control problem in high-speed cornering scenarios on curvy roads. It achieves near-zero steady-state tracking errors while maintaining robust, stable, and real-time performance. The main contributions of this study are outlined as follows:

We developed a robust offset-free lane-keeping control framework for autonomous driving that requires only visual information as input data. The regulation problem in the offset-free control framework is solved using the itube-CILQR control algorithm, which ensures the robustness of real-time lane-keeping control without steady-state errors for autonomous vehicles navigating tight curves.

We validated the performance of the proposed control framework through numerical simulations and vision-based experiments. The vision-based experiments were conducted in TORCS in high-speed cornering scenarios on roads with large curvature. Moreover, we quantified the perceptual uncertainty of the adopted visual perception framework through vision-based experiments in unseen driving scenes.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the adopted lane-keeping dynamics model. Section III describes the developed OF-MPC framework for lane keeping. Section IV introduces the itube-CILQR algorithm. Section V presents the experimental results. Finally, Section VI provides the conclusion.

title: Monte Carlo-Based Indoor UAV Localization in Dynamic Environments Using Only Four Onboard Range Sensors
authors: Mohammad Reza Ranjbar Divkoti,A. Pedro Aguiar
abstract: Indoor UAV localization with minimal onboard sensing remains challenging, particularly in dynamic environments. We propose augmented filtered Monte Carlo localization (AF-MCL) for 2D localization using only four single-point range sensors and measured heading. AF-MCL rejects range measurements inconsistent with the known static map and adaptively injects particles to recover from localization divergence and kidnapping. Beam classification is performed only at the previous position estimate, making its ray-casting cost independent of the particle count. The particle distribution additionally provides an online measure of localization uncertainty. Real-world experiments in a 2.10 ×\times~1.63 m environment yield mean position errors of 6.4–7.7 cm under static and dynamic conditions. Simulations in 6 ×\times 6 m and 10 ×\times 10 m environments yield 4.5–5.2 cm mean errors; under dynamic obstacles, standard MCL reaches 12.3 cm and reliable MCL 7.7 cm. The results show that robust indoor localization under dynamic obstacles is achievable with only four single-point range measurements and heading.
introduction:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly
deployed for inspection, inventory monitoring, environmental sensing,
and search-and-rescue missions. Their operation indoors requires
accurate and low-latency localization despite confined geometry,
clutter, and the absence of a reliable global positioning
signal [1, 2, 3, 4].

Existing indoor localization solutions typically trade sensing and
computational complexity for accuracy. UWB-based methods require
external infrastructure and remain sensitive to multipath and
non-line-of-sight conditions [5, 6, 7], while vision- and LiDAR-based approaches provide rich
environmental information at higher sensing and computational
cost [8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. Visual-inertial methods reduce
dependence on external infrastructure but accumulate drift, motivating
fusion with additional sensing modalities [4, 13, 14]. These limitations motivate
localization using the sparse, lightweight range sensing available on
small UAV platforms.

A closely related approach is [15], which performs
onboard Monte Carlo localization on a nano-UAV using a pair of 64-zone
time-of-flight (ToF) sensors and a parallel ultra-low-power processor.
Although computationally efficient, each multizone sensor provides
substantially more spatial information than a single-point range
measurement, and the method is evaluated in static environments. The
problem considered here is therefore more sensing-constrained: can
reliable indoor localization be achieved from only four single-point
range measurements and heading when individual measurements may also
be corrupted by unknown moving obstacles?

We address this problem using four single-point range sensors oriented
front, back, left, and right. The UAV position is estimated relative
to a known initial position in a known static map, using the four range
measurements and measured heading θ\theta. Unknown dynamic obstacles
may enter the sensor beams and generate ranges inconsistent with the
static map, as illustrated in Fig. 1. No external
localization infrastructure is used.

To address this setting, we propose AF-MCL. AF-MCL identifies and rejects range measurements
inconsistent with the static map before particle weighting, and
adaptively injects particles when filter divergence is detected.
Crucially, beam classification is evaluated only at the previous
position estimate rather than independently at every particle,
eliminating particle-count dependence from the classification
ray-casting stage. The particle distribution additionally provides an
online measure of localization uncertainty.

The contribution is threefold. First, we demonstrate 2D indoor UAV
localization using only four single-point ranges and measured heading
under both static and dynamic obstacles. Second, AF-MCL combines
dynamic-beam filtering with adaptive particle injection for robustness
to corrupted measurements and localization failures, while requiring
only one classification ray cast per sensor, independent of the
particle count. Third, simulation and real-world experiments evaluate
the contributions of filtering and augmentation, recovery from
kidnapping, computational scaling, retained-beam geometry, and
localization performance. Mean errors of 4.5–5.2 cm are obtained in
the simulated 6×66\times 6 m and 10×1010\times 10 m environments, while
real-world flights in a 2.10×1.632.10\times 1.63 m environment yield
6.4–7.7 cm mean error.

title: Natural-Language to Nav2: Operational Policies for Costmap-Based Navigation
authors: Jiyeong Chae,Hyunkyo Seo,Heonjae Lee,Kyung-Joon Park
comment: including supplementary material. Jiyeong Chae and Hyunkyo Seo contributed equally. Project page:this https URL
abstract: Autonomous mobile robots support material transport in warehouses and industrial facilities, where navigation must adapt to changing operating conditions. Sensor observations reveal physical obstacles, but do not by themselves specify temporary access rules, route preferences, or exceptions known to operators. This paper presents a natural-language policy interface that brings this knowledge into ROS 2 Nav2. A local large language model converts instructions into JSON policies specifying destinations, spatial constraints, and temporal or event conditions. Deterministic checks govern mission acceptance, and three costmap adapters project accepted policies into the existing navigation stack without changing its planner or controller. On 150 researcher-authored English commands, four local models produce 107–142 correct accepted policies, compared with 44 for a rule-based parser, with 3–20 incorrect acceptances per model. Fault injection records rejection of eight endpoint/JSON faults and 29 validator-stage faults. Navigation experiments use correct task policies to evaluate keepouts, zone costs, person-dependent regions, and event-conditioned passage in simulation and on a TurtleBot3. For Tasks 1–3, mean travel times are 18.4–24.5% lower in simulation and 23.1–35.0% lower on the physical testbed than with the baseline lacking those policies. A native KeepoutFilter comparison and two-robot demonstrations examine basic keepout behavior and shared policy projection. The interface connects operator instructions to explicit navigation policies while retaining Nav2’s planning and control components.
introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) support material transport in warehouses and industrial facilities [1, 2]. Their navigation must account for changing workspace conditions as well as the destination of each delivery [3]. Some of these conditions are operating rules: an aisle may be reserved for loading, a corridor may be closed for a shift, or an emergency may permit an otherwise restricted passage. Sensors can detect an obstruction, but its expected duration and permitted exceptions require additional information. Operators need a way to make this knowledge available to the robot when planning a mission.

ROS 2 Nav2 provides planners and controllers for mobile navigation [4]. Layered costmaps combine spatial information [5], and native keepout filters can receive updated masks during operation [6]. These mechanisms provide a means to apply constraints once they have been expressed in a form the navigation stack can use. An instruction such as “avoid Zone A for the next thirty minutes” also requires the system to identify the zone, retain the restriction, and determine when it expires. The problem addressed here is to connect such instructions to Nav2 with explicit rules for policy acceptance, mission replacement, and restriction lifetime.

We introduce a natural-language policy interface that represents destinations together with constraints on reaching them. A locally hosted large language model (LLM) translates each instruction into a structured policy. The bridge checks the complete candidate against the schema and execution context before accepting it. Accepted state supplies waypoint goals and inputs to three costmap adapters for keepouts, zone costs, and object-avoidance regions (Figure 1). The same policy-derived updates can be sent to independent robot instances.

The LLM operates when a policy is submitted, outside the navigation control loop. NavFn computes the global path and DWB controls local motion. The intermediate policy makes the requested destinations, constraints, and conditions available for inspection. Structural acceptance and semantic correctness remain distinct: a candidate may satisfy the interface contract while naming a waypoint the operator did not request. The evaluation measures both.

The work makes three contributions. (1) A policy schema represents destinations together with spatial constraints and temporal or event conditions, providing a common interface between language interpretation and navigation. (2) Transactional acceptance checks the complete candidate against the schema and execution context before replacing the mission snapshot; rejection preserves the preceding mission, while retained restrictions are managed separately. (3) Nav2 projection translates accepted state into waypoint goals and keepout, soft-cost, and object-avoidance inputs for the existing navigation stack, including shared policy updates to independent robot instances.

The evaluation follows this architecture. A 150-command benchmark measures conversion accuracy and accepted errors, and fault injection examines rejection and state preservation. Simulation and physical trials examine route selection under task policies, including a separate comparison of event-conditioned passage permissions.
