title: OWLS: Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields for Zero-Shot Rover Navigation
authors: Chahyon Ku,Erica Tevere,Georgios Georgakis,Rudra Mukherjee,Bernadette Bucher
comment: . 6 figures
abstract:
Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) enable this physical reasoning over terrain outside any fixed label set.
We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), which plans directly over the dense feature map of a VLM.
Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores every pixel of a single camera image; OWLS projects these scores onto the ground, adapts them to the platform with two morphological operations, and uses the result as the speed field of a minimum-time planner, so terrain appearance and obstacle clearance shape one trajectory.
OWLS needs no task-specific training, no terrain annotation, no persistent map, and no exteroceptive sensor beyond the camera.
We evaluate it on a physical rover indoors and off-road, on simulated Mars and Moon rovers over 200 procedurally generated terrains, and on real planetary imagery.
introduction:
Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Whether a robot can cross a stretch of terrain depends on information such as the size of obstacles relative to its footprint and clearance, load bearing, and slip, which a camera cannot measure directly.
Planetary rovers must reason about these physical properties under severe conditions. Rovers drive without GPS, and communication delays force long stretches of onboard autonomy [1].

Existing systems model physical traversability in several ways.
Hand-designed geometric heuristics, such as step-height or slope limits, require substantial per-platform engineering [2].
Learned terrain models [3, 4, 5] predict a fixed set of classes from annotated data, and each class still needs a hand-assigned planning cost, so neither the classes nor the costs cover terrain the dataset did not anticipate.
Self-supervised estimators learn traversability from the robot’s own driving [6, 7], which presumes experience on the target terrain.
Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) remove the fixed label set, but navigation systems built on them take free space from depth or LiDAR and use the VLM to select a goal, rank candidate paths, or annotate that geometric map [8, 9, 10, 11, 12].
None of these existing approaches plan over the VLM’s dense output itself, although that output already scores every pixel against a description of drivable terrain.

We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), a local navigation method that plans directly over the dense feature map of an open-vocabulary VLM (Fig. 1).
Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores each pixel of the camera image, and OWLS turns this score map into a trajectory in three steps.
Ground projection places each score at a metric position in the robot frame.
Two morphological operations then encode the platform, since a semantic score does not say whether a particular robot can drive over a rock or how far it must keep from one: a dilation removes low-scoring regions small enough to drive over, and an erosion surrounds the rest with a clearance buffer scaled to the vehicle.
Finally, rather than thresholding the result into occupancy, OWLS uses it as the speed at which the robot moves through each cell and plans the minimum-time trajectory to the goal, which a waypoint controller tracks.
Obstacle clearance and the VLM’s judgment of the terrain thus enter a single optimization.
OWLS uses the VLM without fine-tuning and needs no terrain annotation, and adapting to a new rover needs at most two radii set from the rover’s dimensions.
It keeps no persistent map, replanning from each new image with a single camera and wheel odometry.

Contributions.
(i) We show how to plan directly over the dense feature map of an open-vocabulary VLM, using ground-projected VLM scores as the speed field of a minimum-time planner, which yields local navigation over previously unseen terrain from a single camera with no task-specific training and no persistent map.
(ii) We introduce an interpretable embodiment adaptation of the VLM map by two morphological operations with radii set from rover geometry, which carries the same VLM and prompt across three rovers of distinct size and camera placement without retraining.
(iii) We evaluate from terrestrial to planetary settings: on a physical rover, on a simulated rover on 200 procedurally generated Mars and Moon terrains with prompt and morphology ablations, and qualitatively on real planetary imagery.

title: UAV-SwarmAgent: Scalable Multi-UAV Reconnaissance and Task Allocation via Code Generation and Vision-Language Reasoning
authors: Oleg Sautenkov,Yasheerah Yaqoot,Muhammad Ahsan Mustafa,Grigorii Kalinin,Chih-Yung Wen,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract:
Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints
and watching every drone. We present UAV-SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent
system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence
and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV
routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a
vision-language model, splits them among NN UAVs by balancing route length,
and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard
decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3
foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of
255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to
5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law,
T⁡(N)=332+174/NT(N)=332+174/N s: the second UAV delivers half of the
attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52×\times. We discuss
what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an
operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.
introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are routinely used for time-critical
reconnaissance such as wildfire assessment, search and rescue, and
environmental monitoring (Su et al., 2023; Lyu et al., 2023). Adding drones
shortens the mission, but it also multiplies the work of the person in charge:
each UAV needs waypoints, and each video stream needs attention. Research on
supervisory control has long shown that the number of robots one operator can
handle is limited by how long a robot can be neglected relative to how long it
takes to service it (Olsen and Goodrich, 2004; Crandall et al., 2005), and that
workload and situation awareness degrade as teams
grow (Chen and Barnes, 2014; Kolling et al., 2016).

Large language and vision-language models offer a different division of labour.
They can read a satellite image, follow an underspecified request, and write
programs that call tools (Yao et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024).
Recent aerial systems use them to navigate from language
instructions (Liu et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024)
or to generate a single-drone mission from a
map (Sautenkov et al., 2025b; Sautenkov et al., 2025c). What is missing
for human-swarm interaction is the step from one instruction to a
multi-drone mission whose duration the operator can anticipate.

This late-breaking report presents UAV-SwarmAgent, a system in which the operator
writes one sentence (“I need to check the houses; one of them might be
on fire”) and receives the locations of detected incidents with the
supporting camera frames (Figure 1). Our contributions are:

a two-tier agent architecture in which a ground-station agent plans by
writing code and delegates incident verification to one agent per UAV;

a simulation study of 255 missions over 4 incident
types and 3 foundation models, with mission-level success and
frame-level false alarms reported separately;

a paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs that yields a
simple law for mission time, which an operator can use to decide how
many drones to send.

1. a two-tier agent architecture in which a ground-station agent plans by
writing code and delegates incident verification to one agent per UAV;

2. a simulation study of 255 missions over 4 incident
types and 3 foundation models, with mission-level success and
frame-level false alarms reported separately;

3. a paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs that yields a
simple law for mission time, which an operator can use to decide how
many drones to send.

title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
authors: I-tak Ieong,Hao Tang
abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room–anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0–10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9–2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6–1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
introduction:
Navigation in an unfamiliar environment benefits from both recognizing visible objects and anticipating where a target might be found. Foundation-model agents provide open-vocabulary semantic cues [26, 17], but ambiguous observations and incomplete spatial memory can still lead to unproductive search. A useful prior should guide exploration without being mistaken for a verified map of the environment.

We study two design challenges: retaining observations across viewpoints and using prior room–object relations to assess candidate directions. VLM detections can be incorrect, while common indoor associations need not hold in every scene. Structural checks may therefore help reject some misleading interpretations but can also suppress valid, atypical observations.

HGWM addresses these challenges through a predict-then-ground design. An LLM first generates a hierarchical goal graph describing plausible rooms, anchors, and connections. During navigation, RGB-D observations populate a persistent spatial-semantic graph. Coarse visual-semantic scoring and fine prior-conditioned matching then inform action selection. Here, grounding means relating a hypothesis to sensor-derived evidence, not proving that either graph is correct.

A category such as bed specifies no room instance, route, or viewpoint. A room–anchor hypothesis supplies plausible search contexts before the target appears, while memory records encountered evidence. Their compatibility gives relational context a defined role in ranking where to look next.

Our contributions are threefold:

A symbolic predictive navigation state coupling a hierarchical goal prior with persistent spatial-semantic graph memory.

A two-stage decision rule that separates prior-conditioned visual scoring from explicit, direction-specific matching of observed and hypothesized relations.

Evaluation on HM3D and MP3D, including four additional component ablations on HM3D v0.2, analysis of success and path efficiency, and qualitative navigation examples.

Relative to the reported WMNav results, HGWM improves SR by 4.5 percentage points (pp) on HM3D v0.1 and 1.4 pp on MP3D; SPL improves by 0.3 pp and 0.7 pp, respectively. These are point-estimate comparisons, not evidence of statistical significance. The qualitative trajectories motivate studying repeated exploration, but no aggregate loop-frequency metric is reported.

1. A symbolic predictive navigation state coupling a hierarchical goal prior with persistent spatial-semantic graph memory.

2. A two-stage decision rule that separates prior-conditioned visual scoring from explicit, direction-specific matching of observed and hypothesized relations.

3. Evaluation on HM3D and MP3D, including four additional component ablations on HM3D v0.2, analysis of success and path efficiency, and qualitative navigation examples.

title: Facultative Swarming: A Capability, Not a Category, for Multi-Robot Systems
authors: Ning Zhou,Edmund R. Hunt
abstract: Collective robotics is split by a long-standing but increasingly artificial boundary between centralised multi-robot systems that prioritise optimality and decentralised swarms that prioritise robustness and adaptivity. We propose a unified control framework, shifting from ‘obligate’ swarms—systems constrained to pure self-organisation—to facultatively swarming systems: hybrid architectures that operate as centrally planned systems under permissive conditions yet degrade gracefully into decentralised swarming under environmental stress. By reframing swarming as a dynamic capability, rather than a rigid system category, we outline a pathway towards collective robotic systems that benefit from centralised optimality when conditions permit and from the flexibility of self-organisation when they do not.

title: From Freehand Demonstrations to Autonomous Robotic Ultrasound: An Anatomy-Anchored Learning Framework
authors: Yuan Bi,Fangxu Han,Ye Su,Yiping Zhou,Zhongliang Jiang,Nassir Navab
abstract: Ultrasound imaging is highly operator-dependent, motivating robotic systems that can reproduce expert scanning skills consistently. However, these skills involve coordinated interpretation of anatomical landmarks, ultrasound images, and probe-tissue interactions that are difficult to encode in manually designed control strategies. Imitation learning offers a promising alternative, but its observation and action representations should reflect the anatomically structured nature of scanning. We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework that integrates anatomy-guided probe placement with learned ultrasound navigation. The placement module identifies a task-specific anatomical starting point from external visual observations and establishes an initial probe pose as the reference frame for subsequent scanning. A flow-based policy combines anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera observations, and contact forces to generate scanning motions, while a termination head predicts task completion. This formulation avoids continuous reliance on third-person vision and reduces dependence on the robot-patient configuration. A handheld acquisition platform enables multimodal demonstrations to be collected during natural freehand scanning without a robot. On 16 previously unseen participants, task success rates reach 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% for kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, respectively. Compared with a fine-tuned π0\pi_{0} model, success on the abdominal tasks improves by 10-42 percentage points, with reduced time-to-target, peak contact force, and trajectory jerk. Ablation studies support the complementary contributions of anatomical anchoring, egocentric vision, and force feedback. End-to-end trials with automatic probe placement achieve 90-100% success, and the policies transfer without retraining to a second robot with 83-100% success on the selected tasks. Code and videos are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Anatomy_anchored_SFP-5B0E/
introduction:
Ultrasound is one of the most widely used medical imaging modalities owing to its real-time imaging capability, non-invasive nature, portability, and relatively low cost [1]. It plays an important role in a broad range of diagnostic and interventional procedures. However, conventional ultrasound scanning remains highly operator-dependent. This dependence on individual skill can lead to considerable variability in image quality and examination outcomes, limiting the standardization and accessibility of ultrasound imaging [2]. Robotic ultrasound offers a promising solution to these challenges by enabling precise, repeatable, and consistent probe manipulation [3]. Nevertheless, autonomous ultrasound scanning is difficult to achieve using manually designed control strategies alone. Many scanning skills rely on subtle adjustments learned through extensive clinical experience. Such expert behaviors are often difficult to formulate explicitly as predefined trajectories or control laws [4]. Robot learning, and imitation learning in particular, therefore provides a promising framework for acquiring ultrasound scanning skills directly from expert demonstrations and transferring them to autonomous robotic systems.

Imitation learning enables robots to acquire control policies directly from expert demonstrations by learning a mapping from sensory observations to robot actions [5]. Early approaches commonly formulated this problem as behavior cloning [6], in which a policy is trained to reproduce the actions demonstrated under corresponding observations. More recently, generative visuomotor policies have substantially improved the ability to model complex and multimodal robot behaviors, such as Diffusion Policy [7] or Flow-based policies [8, 9]. In parallel, vision-language-action models have incorporated pretrained vision-language representations and large-scale robot datasets to improve semantic reasoning and generalization across manipulation tasks [10, 11].

Despite these advances in policy architectures, most imitation-learning frameworks are still designed around the characteristics of general robotic manipulation. Their observations commonly include one or more third-person or wrist-mounted camera views together with robot states, such as joint configurations or end-effector poses [12], while force or tactile measurements may additionally be used for contact-rich tasks [13]. Such observations are well suited to manipulation, where the identities, positions, and spatial arrangements of objects can vary substantially across demonstrations and deployment environments. External vision provides the global scene context required to interpret these variations, while robot states are often represented in a global or robot-base coordinate frame to relate the end effector to the surrounding workspace [14].

Imitation-learning methods for robotic ultrasound, however, adopt different observation configurations. Some retain the multimodal design of general manipulation by combining third-person and wrist-mounted camera views with ultrasound images and robot states [15], whereas others rely primarily on ultrasound images and probe pose [16]. Despite this diversity, the necessity and task-specific role of these modalities have not been systematically examined. This motivates us to revisit the observation design for robotic ultrasound and identify the sensory inputs and pose representations that best reflect the structure of the scanning task.

Unlike general manipulation, robotic ultrasound is an anatomy-conditioned and locally constrained interaction once the probe has been initialized at the target anatomical region. At this stage, continuous third-person observations may provide limited additional information for probe navigation. They also introduce dependence on the workspace configuration. These setup-specific dependencies complicate demonstration collection and can limit generalization across environments and robotic platforms. We therefore argue that external vision is better used for anatomical localization and initial probe placement, rather than as a continuous observation during scanning.

However, removing third-person vision does not imply that ultrasound images alone provide a sufficient representation of the scanning process. Unlike conventional RGB videos, ultrasound images do not directly depict the motion of the probe relative to the patient. Each frame represents a two-dimensional cross-section of three-dimensional anatomy, and out-of-plane probe motion cannot be reliably tracked based only on ultrasound images. Ultrasound feedback alone therefore provides an incomplete and potentially ambiguous representation of probe motion and spatial context.

These observations motivate an anatomy-anchored egocentric formulation for robot learning in ultrasound. We decompose autonomous ultrasound scanning into two phases: an anatomy-guided, rule-based probe initialization phase and a learned probe navigation phase. During initialization, anatomical feature detection is used to place the probe at a scan-specific starting pose. Once stable contact has been established, the learned policy takes over and performs local probe navigation using four complementary modalities: ultrasound images, a probe-mounted wrist-camera view, contact force, and probe pose relative to an anatomical anchor. The ultrasound image provides direct information about the internal anatomy, while the wrist camera captures the local interaction between the probe and the scanning region, including probe motion relative to the patient surface. Force measurements characterize the contact condition, which strongly affects both image quality and tissue deformation.

Because ultrasound scanning is organized around anatomical structures and scan-specific starting locations, the global pose of the probe in the robot-base frame is of limited relevance to the underlying scanning skill. Although anatomy varies across patients, the relative organization of anatomical structures is consistent, and clinical scans are typically initialized from identifiable landmarks or predefined body regions. We therefore use the initial probe pose, established relative to a detected anatomical feature, as the reference frame for the subsequent scan. Expressing probe motion relative to this anatomically anchored initial frame removes variations caused by robot placement, patient positioning, and workspace configuration while preserving information about local scan progression.

This probe-centric observation design also enables demonstrations to be collected independently of the robotic platform. We develop a dedicated handheld demonstration platform that synchronously records ultrasound images, wrist-camera views, probe pose, and contact force while an expert performs natural manual scanning. This eliminates the need to collect demonstrations by remotely controlling the robot or physically guiding its arm. As a result, demonstrations can be acquired more flexibly and efficiently without being constrained by robot availability, workspace limitations, or a specific robotic embodiment.

The contributions are summarized as follow:

We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework for robotic ultrasound that separates scanning into anatomy-guided probe placement and learned navigation. A Streaming Flow Policy generates probe motion relative to an anatomical anchor frame from ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact force, while a dedicated termination head decides when the target view has been reached.

A Streaming Flow Policy generates probe motion relative to an anatomical anchor frame from ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact force, while a dedicated termination head decides when the target view has been reached.

We develop a handheld multimodal acquisition platform that synchronously records ultrasound images, wrist-camera views, probe pose, and contact force during natural freehand scanning. Together with the anchor-relative formulation, it allows demonstrations to be collected without a robot and the learned policies to be deployed on different robotic platforms.

We validate the framework on 16 previously unseen participants across kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, achieving 8888-96%96\% task success and outperforming a fine-tuned π0\pi_{0} model by 1010-4242 percentage points on the abdominal tasks. Ablations show the complementary roles of wrist-camera observation, force feedback, and anchor-relative poses, and additional experiments demonstrate end-to-end scanning with automatic probe placement and its ability to transfer to a second robot without retraining.

title: CoCarry: Contact-Support-Structured Retargeting for Dual-Humanoid Cooperative Carrying
authors: Ziyu Lin,Shihang Du,Tianhang Wang,Xiaodong Liu,Runze Zhang,Zongyou Yu,Haodong Zhang,Alois Knoll,Guang Chen
abstract:
Recent advances in large-scale human motion data, motion retargeting, and
motion imitation have enabled increasingly capable whole-body control for
individual humanoids. Cooperative carrying is more challenging because
successful coordination requires not only plausible individual motions, but
also consistent cross-agent and agent–object relations, including shared
grasp, relative configuration, and whole-body support. We introduce
CoCarry, a cooperative-carrying dataset containing 220 synchronized
two-person sequences across 21 task schemes, five shared-object geometries,
four terrain types, and approximately 61 minutes of motion. We further propose
Contact–Support-Structured Retargeting, which starts from nominal
individual motions and jointly refines both humanoids around the same
prescribed object trajectory. Cooperation-aware object-local hand anchors
preserve compatible four-hand grasp relations, while complementary upper
object-interaction and lower support structures retain object-relative
geometry and coordinated support. Across all 220 CoCarry sequences retargeted
to two A3 humanoids, our method achieves 0.9995 contact preservation, reduces
penetration duration by 67.0% and 71.0% relative to GMR and OmniRetarget,
respectively, and maintains a 100% retargeting success rate. On CORE4D with
Unitree G1 humanoids, it achieves 0.9906 contact preservation with zero
measured sliding. We further validate the generated references through
physics simulation and multiple real-world cooperative carrying experiments
on two physical A3 humanoids, demonstrating their usability for downstream
dual-humanoid control.
introduction:
Recent advances in large-scale human motion data, motion retargeting, and
motion imitation have substantially improved whole-body control for individual
humanoids [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Extending these
capabilities to cooperative tasks is more challenging because two participants
must preserve not only their individual motions, but also cross-agent and
agent–object relations. In cooperative carrying, shared grasp, relative
configuration, and whole-body support must remain mutually consistent
throughout the task.

Existing human–human and human–object–human datasets provide important
resources for multi-person interaction and collaborative manipulation
[7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Our work is
complementary to these efforts and focuses specifically on
dual-humanoid cooperative carrying. We introduce CoCarry,
a dataset of 220 synchronized two-person carrying sequences with shared-object
trajectories, covering diverse task schemes, object geometries, and terrain
conditions. Each sequence preserves both participants and the shared object on
a common timeline together with time-varying hand–object interaction priors.
Figure  summarizes the dataset, proposed retargeting
framework, and downstream execution.

A key challenge is converting these synchronized human motions into
dual-humanoid references. Existing methods provide strong foundations for
general and interaction-aware retargeting
[14, 15, 16], but independently retargeting the two
participants does not explicitly enforce relations required by the shared
task. Two individually plausible motions may still produce incompatible hand
placements, distorted relative configurations, penetration, or inconsistent
support. Thus, good individual retargeting does not necessarily imply
good cooperative retargeting.

We therefore propose Contact–Support-Structured Retargeting, which
starts from nominal individual motions and jointly refines both humanoids under
cooperative constraints. Cooperation-aware object-local hand anchors preserve
shared grasp relations, while complementary upper object-interaction and lower
support structures preserve object-relative interaction and ground-referenced
support. Both humanoids are optimized jointly around the same prescribed
object trajectory.

We evaluate the method on all 220 CoCarry sequences with two A3 humanoids,
on a matched CORE4D subset with two Unitree G1 humanoids, and through physics
simulation and real-world cooperative carrying experiments on two physical
A3 humanoids. These evaluations assess retargeting quality, cross-dataset and
cross-embodiment generalization, and downstream physical usability.

Our contributions are:

CoCarry, a cooperative-carrying dataset with synchronized
two-person motion, shared-object trajectories, and time-varying
hand–object interaction priors.

Contact–Support-Structured Retargeting, a joint
dual-humanoid retargeting method for preserving cooperative grasp and
whole-body support.

Comprehensive validation across A3 and G1 humanoids,
multiple datasets, simulation, and real-world cooperative execution.

1. CoCarry, a cooperative-carrying dataset with synchronized
two-person motion, shared-object trajectories, and time-varying
hand–object interaction priors.

2. Contact–Support-Structured Retargeting, a joint
dual-humanoid retargeting method for preserving cooperative grasp and
whole-body support.

3. Comprehensive validation across A3 and G1 humanoids,
multiple datasets, simulation, and real-world cooperative execution.

title: $R^2E:$ A Role-driven Reward Evolutionary Framework for Automated Reward Function Design
authors: Shouhao Chang,Xuan Liu,Hongye Zhu,Xinning Chen,Shigeng Zhang
abstract:
Designing effective reward functions is a critical challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which traditionally requires costly manual trial-and-error.
While Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise in reward design, undifferentiated sampling and limited use of historical feedback often lead to insufficient exploration of the reward space and optimization instability.
To address these challenges, we propose R2E, a Role-driven Reward Evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization.
R2E employs multiple LLM roles with complementary objectives: an Explorer that promotes novelty to expand the search space, a Guardian that performs conservative refinements to improve training stability, and an Evolver that recombines high-performing rewards via crossover and mutation to integrate effective structures.
A dynamic scheduling strategy coordinates these roles, progressively shifting the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation.
To mitigate optimization instability and provide a medium for cross-role collaboration, R2E incorporates a Global Elite Pool that retains the best-performing rewards to guide subsequent generations, thereby enabling coordinated interaction among roles and ensuring a reliable and consistent refinement process.
Extensive experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
Code is available at https://github.com/ChangYuandao/R2E.
introduction:
Reward function design is a fundamental component in Reinforcement Learning, directly shaping agent behaviors and training stability [26, 21], especially in complex robotic control tasks [15, 25].
Although the field of robotic control has witnessed significant progress [14, 3, 6], achieving high-performance behaviors often necessitates intricate reward shaping.
However, manual reward engineering remains heavily dependent on domain expertise [5], which significantly limits its scalability across diverse tasks.
To address these challenges, Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) [22, 31] and Preference-based Reinforcement Learning (PbRL) [27, 9] have emerged as alternatives to reduce expert reliance.
Nevertheless, they typically incur prohibitive data costs in physical environments [4] and yield black-box representations that lack the structural transparency essential for safety and debugging [23].

Recent advances in LLM have demonstrated strong capabilities in code synthesis and logical reasoning [2, 7], enabling new approaches to reward function design [29, 28].
Building on these capabilities, prior work has proposed iterative frameworks that alternate between reward generation, policy training, and refinement based on feedback [17].
By leveraging environmental feedback, these instruction-driven frameworks enable automated reward discovery, demonstrating substantial potential for scaling to complex, real-world RL applications [18].

Despite these advances, existing LLM-based reward generation frameworks exemplified by Eureka are still constrained by two key limitations, as illustrated in Fig. 1(Left).
First, reward candidates are typically produced through undifferentiated sampling under a monolithic prompting paradigm, where diversity arises mainly from stochasticity rather than a structured search process, making it difficult to explicitly balance exploration and exploitation.
Second, most iterative frameworks rely solely on the best reward and feedback from the immediate preceding iteration, lacking a persistent mechanism to preserve and reuse historically high-performing rewards.
As a result, due to the stochasticity in LLM generation, the candidates produced in the next iteration may be inferior to those from the previous iteration, leading to unstable optimization and potential performance regression.

To this end, we propose R2E, a role-driven reward evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization, as illustrated in Fig. 1(Right).
R2E structures the reward search process into three complementary roles: the Explorer, the Guardian, and the Evolver.
Through a dynamic scheduling strategy, the framework adaptively adjusts the sampling allocation of each role across iterations, enabling a gradual transition from broad exploration to stable refinement.
Furthermore, R2E incorporates a Global Elite Pool as a persistent retention mechanism to store globally best-performing reward functions.
This pool provides high-quality references for subsequent iterations, enabling best-so-far rewards retention and mitigating optimization instability in iterative LLM-based optimization.

The primary contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We propose R2E, a structured reward evolutionary framework that leverages explicit role specialization and a dynamic scheduling strategy to guide reward function design, enabling a progressive shift from broad exploration to focused exploitation.

We propose R2E, a structured reward evolutionary framework that leverages explicit role specialization and a dynamic scheduling strategy to guide reward function design, enabling a progressive shift from broad exploration to focused exploitation.

To facilitate cross-role collaboration, we introduce a Global Elite Pool. By actively retaining the highest-performing reward functions, it mitigates optimization instability and provides a stable foundation for roles to collectively refine designs.

We demonstrate that R2E consistently outperforms baselines across 14 tasks from IsaacGym and Bi-DexHands by effectively discovering high-performing reward functions for locomotion and manipulation.

2. To facilitate cross-role collaboration, we introduce a Global Elite Pool. By actively retaining the highest-performing reward functions, it mitigates optimization instability and provides a stable foundation for roles to collectively refine designs.

title: Graphs of Trajectory Bundles for Nonlinear Motion Planning
authors: Joris Verhagen,Jon Arrizabalaga,Jana Tumova,Zachary Manchester
abstract:
We present the Graphs of Trajectory Bundles (GTB) method for motion planning of systems with nonlinear and black-box dynamics, combining sampling-based motion planning with trajectory optimization and graph search.
Based on a graph-of-convex-sets decomposition of the workspace, GTB iteratively constructs a graph of trajectory bundles that captures the local dynamics of the system at any vertex.
By solving a shortest-path problem on this graph, we find maximally dynamically feasible iterates that satisfy the system’s dynamics in the limit and any constraints such as collision avoidance or additional safety or specification constraints by construction of the underlying graph.
As a result, GTB can handle highly nonlinear, unstable, and even black-box dynamics with complex collision and specification constraints, making it a powerful tool for motion planning of complex systems. code
Keywords: graphs of convex sets, derivative-free optimization
introduction:
We are interested in solving the general motion planning problem of the form

Concretely, we formulate Eq. 1 as a graph of trajectory bundles through which we iteratively seek the path of minimal accumulated dynamic infeasibility, i.e., the shortest path in dynamics space from start to goal, while iteratively resampling and refining the dynamics approximation.

This work makes the following specific contributions:

Graphs of Trajectory Bundles: We propose a novel formulation of the problem in Eq. 1 as a graph-planning problem over sampled trajectory bundles.

Sequential Convex Solution Approach: We solve the Graphs-of-Trajectory-Bundles problem with a sequential convex programming approach on a graph of sampled trajectories.

The problem in Eq. 1 is incredibly general and has been studied extensively in many shapes and forms.
Arguably its most fundamental challenge relates to nonconvexities, making it difficult to find optimal or even feasible solutions.

Popular approaches that maintain a global perspective over the solution space include graph-based planning methods such as Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM) [3] or A*.
These methods search for a path over a graph of feasible states.
By constructing vertices of feasible states and edges of feasible transitions, these methods can find globally optimal solutions, limited by the resolution of the graph.
Recently, the Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) method [1] has been proposed to solve Eq. 1 for differentially flat dynamics. GCS generalizes discrete graph search to problems where vertices and edges can be convex sets and convex costs, respectively.
Extensions have been proposed to enable non-convex constraints of Bézier trajectory optimization [4] and piecewise affine approximations of nonlinear edge costs [5], hybrid contact modes for manipulation [6], and forward search for contact-implicit decision-making [7].
Yet none tackle explicit nonlinear or black-box dynamics.

Trajectory optimization methods, such as nonlinear programming [8] and sequential convex programming [9, 10], have been widely used to find locally optimal solutions to Eq. 1.
These methods rely on gradient-based optimization of a differentiable model; they are sensitive to initial conditions, may converge to local minima, and do not apply when ff is non-smooth or available only through simulation.

Derivative-free optimization [11, 12] and sampling-based trajectory optimization can optimize trajectories without requiring gradient information or explicit dynamics.
The most popular example in robotics is likely Model Predictive Path Integral control (MPPI) [13].
These methods naturally deal with nonlinear dynamics and, with advances in simulators and parallelization, can scale to high-dimensional problems [14] and multi-modal reasoning [15].
Single-shooting methods are, however, unsuitable for long-horizon planning and cannot deal with explicit state constraints [13].
Additionally, for planning in complex geometry, the tail-wagging-the-dog problem can lead to infeasible solutions [2].
The Trajectory Bundle Method (TBM) [2] generalizes MPPI by using a sequence of sample trajectories, referred to as trajectory bundles. This allows constraint satisfaction at every knot point, making it suitable for long-horizon problems with more complex constraints.
However, it is still a local method, requiring a good initial guess to converge to local minima.

1. Graphs of Trajectory Bundles: We propose a novel formulation of the problem in Eq. 1 as a graph-planning problem over sampled trajectory bundles.

2. Sequential Convex Solution Approach: We solve the Graphs-of-Trajectory-Bundles problem with a sequential convex programming approach on a graph of sampled trajectories.

title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
authors: Tianyi Jiang,Tianyao Tong,Zhenshan Bing
abstract:
Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen.
Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question.
We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly.
We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model’s earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses.
Measured with the benchmark’s motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw.
With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
introduction:
Many everyday manipulation tasks cannot be solved from the current camera image alone.
A robot asked to place a cube on a target five times must know how many placements it has already made.
A robot asked to lift the container that hides the green cube must have followed the containers while they were shuffled, and one asked to move a cube “in the same manner as before” must have noticed whether the demonstrator pushed or carried it.
RoboMME [1] collects sixteen such tasks, and its evaluation shows that memory is the bottleneck for today’s robot policies: the best learned memory reaches about half the success of a π0.5\pi_{0.5} [2] executor driven by oracle subgoals.

Frontier vision-language models now perceive and reason well enough to act as robot planners without task-specific training [3, 4, 5, 6], and on RoboMME such a planner already succeeds more often than learned memory policies (Table 5).
How the planner should remember an episode, however, is still open.
The usual choices trade reliability against cost: a note that the model rewrites at every step, the scratchpad memory of language agents [7], is cheap but has to carry everything the planner will need later, while showing the model every frame keeps all the evidence and makes each decision more expensive as the episode goes on.
The question we ask is what a frontier planner needs to remember, and who should keep it.

We argue that this memory has to meet two requirements.
First, it must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, so that a placement that has just been completed is counted and a colour seen before the containers covered the cubes is still known later; a note that is rewritten at every step can lose either in a single rewrite (Figure 1a), and continuously rewritten memories are known to degrade [8].
Second, it must let the planner choose what to look at: frames recorded during an action rarely change but cost tokens, while some facts, such as a container swap or whether a demonstrator pushed or carried a cube, are visible only for a moment.

Both requirements suggest a division of labour in which the system keeps the record and the model decides where to look, and our execution-grounded memory (Section 3, Figure 2) is built this way.
The system writes a log of every executed action with the gripper state measured right after it, and keeps every note the model has written.
The model, in turn, names the image regions where it expects something to change during an action, and only frames that change there are returned; it skims each demonstration and inspects the parts it chooses.
The design is the same for every task and involves no training.

Measuring what the memory contributes turned out to need an executor whose own failures are rare and can be told apart from the planner’s.
With the learned π0.5\pi_{0.5} executor, swapping only the memory leaves the success rate unchanged, because empty grasps, stalls and late button presses decide almost all episodes in which the two memories disagree.
With the benchmark’s motion planner, whose execution fails far less often, our memory reaches the success of a note-only memory while sending the model 43% fewer tokens and less than half as many images. Separating the failures shows why the success rates end up close: the note-only memory fails three times as many episodes for reasons other than motion planning (12 against 4), and at least 11 of its 12, against one of our 4, come from what the planner remembered or saw; motion-planning failures, which the benchmark counts as failed episodes, strike both memories at random and decide most of the remaining episodes.
With direct control our planner solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set, and over the learned executor it comes close to oracle subgoals while using a quarter of the tokens of a planner that re-plans after every action chunk.
In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We identify two requirements for the memory of a frontier-model robot planner, keeping track of what was done and learned and choosing what to look at, and show in a per-episode analysis that a rewritten note fails on both.

We propose an execution-grounded memory in which the system keeps a record of what was executed and measured while the model decides which frames and which parts of a demonstration to look at.

We show that a learned executor hides differences between memories, and that with the benchmark’s motion planner our memory matches the success of a note-only memory at well under half the image cost, with far fewer failures caused by memory and observation.

1. We identify two requirements for the memory of a frontier-model robot planner, keeping track of what was done and learned and choosing what to look at, and show in a per-episode analysis that a rewritten note fails on both.

2. We propose an execution-grounded memory in which the system keeps a record of what was executed and measured while the model decides which frames and which parts of a demonstration to look at.

3. We show that a learned executor hides differences between memories, and that with the benchmark’s motion planner our memory matches the success of a note-only memory at well under half the image cost, with far fewer failures caused by memory and observation.

title: DynaSlots: Slot-Centric 3D Dynamics Pretraining for Robot Manipulation
authors: Meng Li,Lijiang Chen,Qi Zhao,Jun Jiang,Longhao Zou,Shuchang Lyu,Guangliang Cheng
abstract:
Robot manipulation involves localized changes: picking up a cup moves the cup while leaving the surrounding scene largely unchanged.
Yet existing 3D visual pretraining methods, including recent dynamics-aware variants, model state transitions at the scene level, compressing the motion of everything in a scene into a single global latent action.
This conflates semantically distinct transitions in scenes with multiple moving parts, obscures dependencies between changing regions, and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to task-irrelevant scene content.
We introduce DynaSlots, an action-free, label-free pretraining framework that decomposes each point cloud frame into a small set of temporally consistent slots and models dynamics at this per-slot level rather than the scene level.
A temporal slot propagation module promotes consistent slot assignments across frames; an inverse dynamics model then extracts one latent action per slot from feature differences, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model, paired with a self-supervised interaction head, predicts each slot’s future state while learning pairwise proximity-and-motion relations.
Experiments on Meta-World, Adroit, and a RealMan RM65-B robot demonstrate that DynaSlots outperforms prior scene-level baselines. It achieves superior success rates in simulation and exhibits strong robustness to scene clutter and unseen objects in real-world manipulation.
Code is available at https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/.
introduction:
Large-scale self-supervised pretraining has become a primary lever for scalable robot learning. In manipulation, 3D representations are attractive: point clouds expose object geometry in metric space, and policies built on them [42, 35] outperform 2D counterparts with less data. This has motivated a growing line of 3D visual pretraining methods [28, 41, 43, 46, 18] adapting masked autoencoding [14] and cross-modal objectives [1] to point clouds, initializing policies from representations learned on large unlabeled datasets such as RH20T [11] and Open X-Embodiment [26].

However, these methods largely overlook what matters most for control: dynamics. Pretraining objectives based on static appearance capture scene structure but not how it changes, and such representations underperform on manipulation benchmarks that demand understanding state transitions. Recent dynamics-aware pretraining closes this gap [23]: an inverse dynamics model (IDM) extracts a compact latent action from feature differences across frames, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model (FDM) predicts the next state conditioned on it, yielding substantial gains over static pretraining.

We identify a limitation of this scene-level formulation: it summarizes an entire point cloud into one global feature and one global latent action, yet manipulation induces localized changes: when a robot picks up a milk carton, the carton moves while the table does not. This formulation presents three potential limitations (Fig. 1a): semantic aliasing, since similar motions in different regions can yield similar global feature differences despite representing distinct transitions; implicit interaction dependencies, since a single global vector does not explicitly represent how changes in one region relate to changes in another during manipulation; and distractor sensitivity, since task-irrelevant scene changes can perturb the global representation.

To overcome these limitations, we propose DynaSlots (Fig. 1b), a label-free framework for slot-level dynamics-aware 3D pretraining: the latent action of a transition should be defined per slot, not per scene. DynaSlots decomposes each frame into KK slots via three components: temporal slot propagation, promoting cross-frame slot consistency rather than letting independent per-frame slot attention [24] reorder slots arbitrarily; an inverse dynamics model extracting one latent action per slot from feature differences; and a cross-slot diffusion forward dynamics model with a self-supervised interaction head, in the spirit of neural relational inference [21], that recovers a contact and co-motion relation between slots. The framework is trained end-to-end with variance-invariance-covariance regularization [4] against an EMA target encoder [7]. In summary, the primary contributions of this paper are threefold:

We introduce the first slot-based dynamics-aware 3D visual pretraining framework, requiring neither action labels, segmentation ground truth, nor reconstruction supervision.

We propose temporal slot propagation and a cross-slot diffusion forward dynamics model with a self-supervised interaction head to maintain cross-frame slot correspondence and capture cross-slot interactions.

Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DynaSlots for robotic manipulation.

1. We introduce the first slot-based dynamics-aware 3D visual pretraining framework, requiring neither action labels, segmentation ground truth, nor reconstruction supervision.

2. We propose temporal slot propagation and a cross-slot diffusion forward dynamics model with a self-supervised interaction head to maintain cross-frame slot correspondence and capture cross-slot interactions.

3. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of DynaSlots for robotic manipulation.

title: MAST-VLA: Skill-Conditioned Adaptation with Trajectory-Affordance Priors for Multi-Skill Robot Manipulation
authors: Jiachi Yang,Zhiyi Xu,Hongquan Zhang,Xin Tan,Zhizhong Zhang,Jingyu Gong,Yuan Xie
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026
abstract:
Generalist robot manipulation requires a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy to execute diverse skills across scenes and instructions.
However, current multi-skill VLA policies often leave two aspects of an instruction insufficiently modeled: which primitive skill to execute and where/how to contact and move objects.
We propose MAST-VLA (Multi-skill Adaptation with Skill-conditioned experts and Trajectory-affordance priors), a dual-conditioning framework for robot manipulation.
MAST-VLA introduces skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts (LoRA-MoE) adapters in the LLM backbone, where skill-query tokens and routing biases guide low-rank expert specialization, and converts a predicted affordance heatmap into a patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial prior for the action head.
On the CALVIN ABC→\rightarrowD long-horizon multi-skill cross-scene generalization setting, MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an Avg. Len of 4.65 over five-subtask evaluation sequences.
Real-robot multi-skill sequence experiments further validate its deployability under real perception and control noise.
introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) provide a unified interface for language-conditioned robot manipulation by connecting visual perception, language understanding, and action generation [51, 17, 3, 2].
Recent VLA policies show that pretrained multimodal models can be adapted to robot control across diverse objects, scenes, tasks, and embodiments [20, 28, 16, 27].
This capability makes VLAs a promising foundation for generalist robot manipulation, where a single policy is expected to reuse visual-language knowledge while executing and composing multiple manipulation skills [5, 29, 14].

Despite this progress, multi-skill long-horizon manipulation remains challenging because language-conditioned policies must maintain stable execution across sequential subtasks and skill transitions [24, 23, 22, 50].
A manipulation instruction requires the policy to infer the intended primitive operation, such as grasping, pushing, rotating, or stacking, while also grounding the contact regions, motion paths, and object interactions required for execution [34, 35, 10, 25, 39].
These two factors are referred to in this work as primitive-skill semantics and object-interaction semantics.
When either factor is insufficiently modeled, errors may accumulate across consecutive subtasks, leading to unstable execution under long-horizon skill transitions [24, 22, 26].

Existing VLA policies often leave these two forms of grounding implicit in language instructions,
visual observations, and low-dimensional action supervision [17, 16, 38, 48].
For skill-level grounding, shared adaptation parameters or task-level lightweight modules may not explicitly align expert capacity with primitive manipulation skills, making it difficult to separate skill-specific action patterns and control preferences within a shared policy [12, 40, 38, 21].
For interaction-level grounding, low-dimensional action supervision provides only indirect cues about contact regions, motion trends, and task-relevant geometry, whereas prior manipulation methods have shown the importance of explicit spatial, geometric, or affordance-level signals [44, 34, 35, 10, 1, 42].
Thus, multi-skill VLA policies require mechanisms that preserve shared visual-language knowledge while explicitly conditioning adaptation on primitive skills and strengthening action-relevant spatial supervision.

To address these limitations, we propose MAST-VLA, a dual-conditioning framework for multi-skill robot manipulation.
MAST-VLA combines skill-conditioned LoRA-MoE specialization in the LLM backbone with a trajectory-affordance spatial prior in the action head.
In the LLM backbone, skill-query tokens and routing biases condition low-rank expert specialization; in the action head, trajectory-derived affordance heatmaps are converted into patch-level attention biases for action decoding.
Together, these two paths reduce cross-skill interference and strengthen interaction-aware action generation.

The contributions are summarized as follows:

1) A dual-conditioning VLA framework is proposed for multi-skill robot manipulation, jointly modeling primitive-skill structure and interaction-relevant spatial grounding within a shared policy;

2) Skill-conditioned LoRA-MoE specialization and trajectory-affordance action guidance are introduced. The former uses skill-query tokens and routing biases to condition low-rank expert specialization in the LLM backbone, while the latter converts future gripper motion and scene geometry into heatmap supervision and patch-level spatial bias in the action head;

3) MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on CALVIN ABC→\rightarrowD with an Avg. Len of 4.65 and improves Success@5 from 80.0% to 84.7%. Real-robot experiments, ablations, and visualizations further validate sequential robustness and the complementarity of the two paths.

title: Delay Randomization Widens the Delay Margin of Learned Humanoid Motion Trackers
authors: Shaoqin Li,Yi Sun
abstract:
Learned humanoid controllers are usually trained in one simulator and then checked in a second one before they go near hardware.
We ask what that check says about command delay.
We train motion-tracking policies for a 24-joint humanoid on five motions taken from monocular video and test them in an independent CPU MuJoCo harness, which we first verify against the training model.
Every policy completes its motion in at least 26 of 30 episodes under the training randomization.
With 40 ms of constant command delay, however, survival drops to 15% on average (0–45%), and the delay margin is only 20–30 ms.
Randomizing the delay during training (0–50 ms) lifts survival at 40 ms to 95% on average (75–100%) and moves the margin to 50–70 ms.
A control arm trained for the same number of extra iterations without delay does not improve, so the gain comes from the randomization itself.
This holds for all five motions with three training seeds each, and a policy trained in PhysX behaves the same way.
The price is slightly looser tracking (0.02–0.06 rad on four motions) and, for the most dynamic motion, less robustness to other perturbations.
We also show that the first sim-to-sim gap we saw came from the harness, a missing floor and a wrong timestep, and not from the physics engines.
The 0–20 ms delay ranges common in locomotion training lie inside the margin an unrandomized tracker already has.
The benefit comes from randomizing beyond it, so the range should be set from the robot’s measured latency, and delay margin belongs next to other sim-to-sim metrics.
introduction:
Reinforcement-learned motion trackers can reproduce highly dynamic human motions on humanoid robots (Liao et al., 2025; He et al., 2025).
They are trained in a GPU simulator with randomized dynamics (Tobin et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018) and, before hardware, commonly checked in a second simulator (Gu et al., 2024; Lei et al., 2025).
The policy then runs on a robot whose control loop always has some latency between the policy output and the actuator response (Tan et al., 2018; Hwangbo et al., 2019).
In classical control, delay is a first-order concern: it erodes phase margin and can destabilize an otherwise stable loop (Richard, 2003).
For learned controllers it is usually handled by randomizing a small delay during training; humanoid locomotion frameworks report ranges such as 0–20 ms (Wang et al., 2025; Seo et al., 2025).
Few papers report how much delay a learned motion tracker actually tolerates, or what randomizing it in training buys.

This paper measures it.
The setting is a 24-joint humanoid tracking five motions recovered from ordinary video.
Each policy is trained in mjlab (MuJoCo-Warp) (Zakka et al., 2026) with the BeyondMimic tracking recipe (Liao et al., 2025) and evaluated in an independent, CPU-based MuJoCo harness (Todorov et al., 2012).
We make three contributions.

A verified evaluation protocol. The harness rebuilds the training model from the robot description and is validated to reproduce training-time observations and outcomes. A one-at-a-time ablation shows that the first sim-to-sim “gap” we observed came entirely from two settings (a missing floor and a 2.5×\times smaller timestep), not from the physics engine (Section 4.1).

Delay margins of learned trackers. Survival as a function of constant command delay, at 10 ms resolution, for policies trained with and without delay randomization, across five motions and three training seeds (Section 4.2).

A controlled attribution. A control arm with equal additional training but no delay isolates the effect of delay randomization from the effect of training longer (Section 4.3). A PhysX-trained policy shows the same failure and the same remedy (Section 4.5).

title: RoboCode: Learning Reusable Action Primitives for Robot Manipulation
authors: Xianyue Peng,Devi Amarsaikhan,Iman Soltani
abstract:
Recent robot manipulation policies commonly predict continuous action chunks
directly from observations, without explicitly modeling reusable structure in
the action space. However, manipulation demonstrations often contain recurring
short-horizon motion patterns that are shared across tasks. We introduce
RoboCode, which learns these patterns through a shared soft-gated
primitive action interface. Rather than assigning each action chunk to a single
discrete code, RoboCode represents it as a soft composition of
multiple learned primitives, providing a flexible intermediate representation
of short-horizon actions. The primitive interface is learned from action chunks
pooled across multiple tasks and then frozen while task-specific state encoders
are trained to map current state inputs into the shared latent space.
introduction:
Robot manipulation is often modeled as a sequence of continuous actions. Across tasks, demonstrations repeatedly contain short motion patterns such as reaching, lifting, placing, and pushing. This suggests that manipulation trajectories may be better understood through reusable primitive structure rather than as independent action chunks.

This raises a question of action representation. Recent token-based robot policies discretize each action dimension into bins [10], offering a simple interface but splitting coordinated actions into dimension-wise decisions. Task-level commands and planning operators [1] provide semantic structure, but often require a large vocabulary of task-specific actions, limiting generalization across tasks. Primitive-level representations offer a more compositional abstraction, capturing reusable motion units while preserving coordination across action dimensions and time.

Prior work has explored reusable units for robot manipulation [17, 25, 12], including behavior segments, semantic skill spaces, and discrete action modes. However, a single primitive may not be sufficiently expressive for a short action chunk, since the chunk can contain multiple motion factors. Inspired by memory-augmented models [4, 23], we learn primitive codes as entries in a shared primitive codebook and represent each chunk as a soft composition of multiple entries.

We propose RoboCode, a two-stage framework for learning soft-gated primitive codebooks from robot demonstrations. The first stage jointly learns an action encoder and a shared primitive action
interface from multi-task action chunks. The second stage trains task-specific observation-to-gate policies that use this frozen interface to generate continuous action chunks for execution.

Our aim is to study whether soft-gated primitive codebooks provide an effective intermediate action representation for robot manipulation. The method does not require manually designed primitives, task rewards, or task labels during primitive learning; it discovers reusable action components directly from demonstrations. Our contributions are:

We introduce a soft-gated primitive action representation that represents short-horizon manipulation actions as compositions of multiple learned primitives, rather than direct continuous predictions or single-code assignments.

We introduce a soft-gated primitive action representation that represents short-horizon manipulation actions as compositions of multiple learned primitives, rather than direct continuous predictions or single-code assignments.

The proposed two-stage framework learns a shared primitive action interface from pooled multi-task demonstrations and reuses the frozen interface for task-specific closed-loop control.

Experiments on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks demonstrate structured
cross-task primitive reuse. RoboCode achieves the highest or tied
success rate across all evaluated tasks, reaching an average success rate of
75.6%75.6\%, compared with 68.8%68.8\% for ACT and 41.6%41.6\% for DP-Large.
Controlled ablations and transfer experiments further examine the roles of
soft composition and cross-task primitive sharing.

1. We introduce a soft-gated primitive action representation that represents short-horizon manipulation actions as compositions of multiple learned primitives, rather than direct continuous predictions or single-code assignments.

2. The proposed two-stage framework learns a shared primitive action interface from pooled multi-task demonstrations and reuses the frozen interface for task-specific closed-loop control.

3. Experiments on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks demonstrate structured
cross-task primitive reuse. RoboCode achieves the highest or tied
success rate across all evaluated tasks, reaching an average success rate of

title: Do VLAs Know They Will Fail? Interpretable Success and Failure Patterns in Physical AI Systems
authors: Christian A. Rogers,Qian Lin,Daniel S. Brown
comment: (4 main pages + appendix), 4 figures. Accepted at the Science of Physical AI Safety Workshop at the 2026 Conference on Robotic Learning (CoRL 2026, non-archival)
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful general-purpose robot policies, but their successes and failures remain difficult to diagnose and understand. In this work, we show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations of OpenVLA activations contain outcome-predictive information and can be used to predict task failure before the robot reaches an unrecoverable state.
Moreover, to provide insights into what common behaviors may contribute to these outcomes, we identify individual SAE features whose strong activations are associated with specific stages of success or failure, and uncover recurring behavioral patterns by localizing temporal intervals where these features exhibit significant activation changes.
We further develop a VLM-based interpretation pipeline to generate behavioral descriptions of these patterns and validate their correspondence to feature activations on held-out intervals.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong generalist performance by scaling model capacity and training data [15, 9], but their internal representations make it difficult to diagnose why a rollout succeeds or fails.
Recent work shows that these representations anticipate failure. SAFE learns a multitask failure detector from internal VLA features and uses conformal prediction to trade detection accuracy against warning time [5]. Mahato and Ren show that near-term failure is linearly decodable from OpenVLA activations under visual distribution shift [11]. FPC-VLA instead predicts failures with an external VLM supervisor [14].
These works report warning time relative to the end of the episode. The problem is that every action an agent takes changes how easy the remaining task is to complete; thus, these approaches may trigger an alarm after the task has become unrecoverable. We therefore build on this line of research by measuring lead time against a point of no return, a timestep after which the only reachable states by branched policies are failures.

More importantly, we aim to move beyond predicting outcomes toward identifying the behavioral patterns strongly associated with success or failure. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising approach by decomposing dense, polysemantic activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features [3, 4].
Recent work has applied this technique to VLAs. Haon et al. [7] identify interpretable, steerable directions in OpenVLA. Swann et al. [13] find SAE features for motion and semantics, some of which causally steer behavior. Event-Grounded SAEs tie features to behaviorally salient events in closed-loop rollouts [8].
These works characterize features by what they represent or control. We ask a complementary question: which sparse features track whether a rollout will succeed, and what behavior do they correspond to?

We show that SAE features preserve the outcome-predictive information in OpenVLA activations, and that, evaluated against the point of no return, the predictor separates eventual failures from successes while the failures are still recoverable. We then select individual features by their association with trajectory outcomes and automatically localize the critical intervals where they emerge. Finally, we describe these intervals with a VLM and validate the descriptions on held-out clips via detection scoring [1, 12].
Together, these steps connect early failure warning to interpretable, failure-relevant behavior in VLA policies. An extended discussion of related work is in Appendix A.

title: Geometry-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Close-Fitting Wearable Insertion
authors: Takuma Tsukakoshi,Elle Miller,Tamon Miyake,Namiko Saito,Yushi Wang,Shigeki Sugano,Tetsuya Ogata,Sethu Vijayakumar
abstract:
Robot-assisted dressing is particularly challenging due to narrow openings and articulated body parts. Even small errors in the relative pose between the body part and garment opening can cause snagging, missed insertion, or incomplete dressing. To address these challenges, we formulate dressing as a geometry-aware insertion problem that represents task-relevant spatial relationships between the body part and object opening, rather than relying on the full deformable-object state. Based on this formulation, we propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework combining a staged curriculum, which progressively guides the policy from coarse alignment to insertion and final placement, with a finger-wise insertion soft gate that provides continuous feedback on individual finger insertion progress and helps suppress premature insertion.
We evaluate the framework on rigid and deformable bracelet dressing tasks through component ablations, systematic variations in the initial hand pose, and closed-loop execution of the learned policies on a real robotic system. On the post-training deformable evaluation, the full method reaches 84.7±1.2%84.7\pm 1.2\% success. The insertion gate accounts for the largest gain, and adding the curriculum on top of that gate reaches the top score. On a mannequin hand the same full policy succeeds on 15/2015/20 real-robot trials.
introduction:
Assistive dressing requires a robot to pass the opening of a wearable over a human limb while ensuring safety and precision [1].
For loose garments, such as sleeves or jackets, dressing mainly involves reaching and guidance problems. In contrast, for close-fitting wearables, dressing is fundamentally a precise insertion problem: a body part must pass through a narrow, deformable opening, where small misalignments can collapse the opening, cause snagging, or result in incomplete insertion [2].

For loose garments, existing dressing systems already solve several related tasks in both simulation and real-robot deployment.
Policies trained via real-world demonstrations can pull sleeves or jackets onto an arm when the opening is wide and the initial placement is constrained [3, 4].
Those policies, however, inherit the demonstrator’s skill and coverage, and the collected motions assume a wide opening.
In simulation, caregiving environments such as Assistive Gym and RCareWorld dress gowns and sleeves, typically on simplified body geometry [5, 6].
Reinforcement learning (RL) policies can dress hospital-gown sleeves onto a human model with spherical hands [5], later extended to collaborative human–robot dressing [7].
DexGarmentLab constructed a simulated glove-dressing task in which both hands insert the index fingers, open the cuffs, and pull the gloves onto the hands; the sequence was completed with an attachment-block workaround [8]. However, the small opening, the required index-finger insertion, and the subsequent thumb pinch were difficult under their FEM cloth model and dexterous-hand control.
Separately, learning-based cloth methods have achieved unfolding and related garment skills, including successful sim-to-real transfer [9, 10].

While these methods have advanced loose-garment dressing and general
cloth manipulation, their results do not directly address the constraints of close-fitting wearables.
Close-fitting placement introduces three distinct challenges.
First, geometric tolerance is tight: unlike loose garments with openings
substantially larger than the target body part [3],
close-fitting wearables leave little clearance for relative pose error
during insertion.
Second, insertion is sequential and contact-rich: successful dressing requires a sequence of coordinated interactions between the wearable opening and the body part, where local snagging or misalignment can prevent subsequent progress.
Third, deformable-object state is difficult to represent consistently across simulation and the real world: a full garment mesh is difficult to reconstruct from camera observations, while simulated cloth states depend on imperfect models of thin-contact dynamics [9].

We address these difficulties with three corresponding approaches.
To meet the tight geometric tolerances of close-fitting wearable dressing, we formulate the RL problem as geometry-conditioned insertion,
using bracelet dressing as a representative instance.
The policy conditions on proprioception and the relative pose between
the hand and the wearable opening.
To mitigate snagging and incomplete enclosure, we train an RL policy
with a staged curriculum that progresses from little-finger insertion
to thumb insertion and finally wrist enclosure, together with a soft
finger-wise insertion gate that modulates the wrist-stage reward based
on insertion progress.
To avoid both mesh reconstruction and mesh-dependent simulation, these geometric features are keypoints that can be measured from cameras, not a cloth mesh.

We evaluate the framework primarily on a deformable bracelet dressing task, using a rigid bracelet as a diagnostic baseline.
Ablations isolate the staged curriculum and the soft gate.
We also test robustness to moderate in-domain hand-pose variation and demonstrate the learned policy on a real robotic system (Fig. 1).
The contributions of this work are as follows:

Geometric formulation of close-fitting dressing to aid transfer:
We represent the task using task-relevant relative geometry between the articulated body part and the wearable opening, rather than relying on the full deformable garment state, thereby maintaining consistency between simulation and real-world execution.

Close-fitting curriculum and finger-wise insertion soft gate:
We guide learning from little-side alignment to thumb-side alignment and wrist insertion, and introduce a finger-wise soft insertion gate that modulates the wrist reward by containment within the object opening. This reduces premature failures such as finger snagging, opening collapse, and incomplete enclosure.

Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of close-fitting dressing with deformable openings:
We reconstruct the simulation geometric observation from real-world cameras and deploy the learned policies in closed loop without additional real-world training, demonstrating transfer to deformable bracelet insertion.

1. Geometric formulation of close-fitting dressing to aid transfer:
We represent the task using task-relevant relative geometry between the articulated body part and the wearable opening, rather than relying on the full deformable garment state, thereby maintaining consistency between simulation and real-world execution.

2. Close-fitting curriculum and finger-wise insertion soft gate:
We guide learning from little-side alignment to thumb-side alignment and wrist insertion, and introduce a finger-wise soft insertion gate that modulates the wrist reward by containment within the object opening. This reduces premature failures such as finger snagging, opening collapse, and incomplete enclosure.

3. Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of close-fitting dressing with deformable openings:
We reconstruct the simulation geometric observation from real-world cameras and deploy the learned policies in closed loop without additional real-world training, demonstrating transfer to deformable bracelet insertion.
