title: TravSUITE: Traversability via Self-Supervised, Uncertainty-Aware IRL and Terrain Estimation
authors: Samuel Triest,Amirreza Shaban,David D. Fan,Wenshan Wang,Sebastian Scherer
abstract: Traversability analysis in off-road settings remains a fundamental challenge for mobile robots. Key difficulties include constructing an accurate and expressive local map from multi-modal sensor data, and using the map to design traversability rules that yield desirable navigation behavior. Importantly, this system must be resilient to the limited sensing regime brought about by complex environments and high speeds. In this paper, we present TravSUITE, a traversability system suitable for high-speed navigation in off-road environments. TravSUITE consists of two major components: 1) an efficient voxel mapper that leverages visual foundation models (VFMs) to build a rich geometric-semantic local map from streams of on-board sensor data, and 2) a unified neural network that jointly predicts traversability-relevant quantities in bird’s eye view (BEV), including geometry, semantics, speed and cost. Our training strategy is entirely annotation-free and self-supervised, leveraging tasks such as map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn both map representations and traversability. We perform a thorough ablation study and comparison to state-of-the-art approaches, and the results indicate that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting each contribute significantly to planning quality, and their combination is critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance in off-road path planning. We also design a simple risk adaptation mechanism to leverage our method’s uncertainty estimates at deploy-time, and demonstrate that a combination of inpainting and risk estimation can result in 80%80\% fewer navigation errors and 5%5\% faster autonomous traversal speeds in real-world hardware experiments.
introduction:
Many important application domains such as construction [3, 8], disaster response [54, 62, 4], forestry [11, 9], and defense [66, 6, 73], require robots to be able to navigate in off-road environments reliably and autonomously. Most practical approaches see a mobile robot 1) use its on-board sensors to build a local map of its surroundings, 2) perform traversability analysis on the local map to determine where it can and cannot traverse, and 3) use the results of its traversability analysis to plan safe paths to a desired goal. This approach is preferred in safety-critical applications due to its modularity, interpretability, and ease of incorporating additional safety constraints, and has thus been the dominant framework for performing navigation across legged [24, 26, 62, 10] and wheeled platforms [61, 6, 40, 38], for both learning [15, 27, 63, 74, 71, 62] and non-learning based [18, 24, 16, 36] methods.

While this approach may seem simple at first glance, both the local mapping and traversability problems become very challenging in complex environments such as off-road settings. The quality of the robot’s local map can be significantly degraded due to factors such as observation noise and occlusion. Cost function design is a complex function of robot capability, operator preference and the environment’s geometry and semantics. Effective robot navigation systems must be able to produce reliable and nuanced traversability estimates even in complex environments where the presence of observational uncertainty may render the local map erroneous or incomplete.

There exist several recent works that aim to improve the resilience of off-road mapping pipelines to observational noise and uncertainty [57, 40, 64, 27]. These approaches typically rely on using a large neural network to predict some form of ground-truth map representation (derived from privileged data such as hindsight, hand-labeling, simulation, etc.) from the current observations. These approaches have been demonstrated to produce reliable local maps that are robust to occlusions and measurement sparsity at high speeds and long ranges [40, 27]. However, these methods often rely on robot-specific traversability data [27], or environment-specific semantics and hand-annotations [57, 40], making it challenging to generalize these approaches to novel robots or environments.

To address the challenge and tedium of hand-designing traversability rules, there has been significant prior work in learning cost functions directly from robot traversal data [6, 26, 63, 15, 33, 65, 74]. While these approaches have demonstrated promising results across many environments and robot morphologies, there lacks a common consensus on the choice of input representation (e.g. geometric, semantic, visual foundation model (VFM) features, etc.) [15, 33, 26, 65], and its effect on the downstream traversability are not well-explored. Additionally, these approaches may not account for perceptual uncertainty [51, 15, 33], and often lack large-scale datasets and dense supervision signals [26, 64, 59, 15].

TravSUITE (Fig. 1) synthesizes insights from both families of work to produce reliable and expressive traversability estimates in the presence of observational uncertainty. TravSUITE consists of three major components, 1) a flexible and efficient mapping module that produces real-time geometric-semantic map representations, 2) a framework for generating large, self-supervised, annotation-free perception and behavior datasets from robot experience, and 3) a unified neural network trained to jointly predict inpainted map representations and traversability estimates from this dataset with uncertainty. We leverage the flexibility of our mapping module and learning framework to compare against state-of-the-art approaches [40, 65, 74] and systematically evaluate what design decisions (such as mapping representation and training tasks) are important for improving path planning performance. We find that across all of our experiments, the existence of an inpainting task significantly improves traversability estimation performance, regardless of mapping representation. We also demonstrate that learning distributions of cost is important to enabling safer traversal at deploy time.

title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
authors: Jiabing Yang,Yuan Xu,Yixiang Chen,Qisen Ma,Peiyan Li,Kai Wang,Chenhang Cui,Tao Yu,Zichen Wen,Wen Ye,Bowen Fang,Ziheng He,Xiangnan Wu,Yingda Li,Yan Huang,Liang Wang
abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute–execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including π0\pi_{0}, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon-Depth-VLA/.
introduction:
Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] generate continuous action trajectories [6, 7] by numerically integrating learned velocity fields from prior Gaussian noise [8]. Deployment typically fixes two operational parameters, namely the execution horizon ss, the open-loop action prefix executed before re-querying the policy, and the sampling depth NN, the numerical integration steps allocated per chunk (equaling the number of function evaluations under forward Euler). For example, standard benchmark protocols for π0\pi_{0} on LIBERO conventionally default to (s,N)=(5,10)(s,N)=(5,10).

Prevailing deployment practices treat ss and NN as independent choices. Receding-horizon frameworks [4, 9] sweep execution horizons to amortize perception latency while holding solver depth fixed. Conversely, policy acceleration methods [10, 11, 5] distill or truncate numerical ODE solvers primarily under standard, short horizons. However, these two parameters are intrinsically linked. Solver depth NN dictates the dispersion of the generated action chunk, while execution horizon ss determines how long that dispersion compounds open-loop before sensory feedback intervenes.

In this work, we systematically investigate this interaction across frozen VLA checkpoints. On LIBERO-Long with π0\pi_{0}, the paired performance contrast between shallow (N=2N{=}2) and deep (N=10N{=}10) sampling exhibits a systematic sign reversal (Fig. 1). The reversal is consistent. While coarse solvers degrade task success under rapid replanning (s=5s{=}5), they outperform deep solvers under extended open-loop execution (s=20s{=}20). Multi-seed matched evaluations show that the contrast crosses zero between s=5s{=}5 and s=10s{=}10, shifting toward shallow sampling as the horizon lengthens. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 replicate this behavior on π0.5\pi_{0.5} across bimanual tasks, while also highlighting boundary conditions governed by predictive horizons and baseline task capacity.

To understand this mechanism, we examine generated action distributions under matched initial noise. Forward Euler truncation contracts trajectory dispersion around an invariant centroid. Under rapid replanning, wider dispersion aids task progress as feedback quickly catches deviations; under extended open-loop execution, however, that dispersion compounds into drift. Here, the contracted distribution of a shallow solver acts as an effective implicit regularizer. The mechanism is geometric. Diagnostic interventions corroborate this account. Scalar noise rescaling fails to recover the effect and distorts mean trajectories, while freezing sampling noise across replans eliminates the deep solver’s short-horizon advantage, which isolates redraw stochasticity as the primary driver.

This coupling provides practical and conceptual implications for robot learning. Practically, co-adjusting solver depth with execution horizon yields training-free Pareto improvements, improving task success while amortizing inference latency. Conceptually, it reframes numerical solver depth as an operational variance regulator that directly governs trajectory dispersion across the commitment window, offering a grounded perspective for compute–execution co-design (Figure 2).

In summary, our key contributions are:

We identify a sign-reversing coupling between execution horizon and sampling depth in flow-matching VLAs: coarse solvers degrade performance under rapid replanning yet improve success under extended open-loop execution.

We characterize the geometric mechanism: numerical Euler truncation contracts trajectory dispersion around an invariant centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer against compounding open-loop drift.

We evaluate this phenomenon across simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0) and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones, identifying operational boundaries for compute–execution co-design.

1. We identify a sign-reversing coupling between execution horizon and sampling depth in flow-matching VLAs: coarse solvers degrade performance under rapid replanning yet improve success under extended open-loop execution.

2. We characterize the geometric mechanism: numerical Euler truncation contracts trajectory dispersion around an invariant centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer against compounding open-loop drift.

3. We evaluate this phenomenon across simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0) and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones, identifying operational boundaries for compute–execution co-design.

title: TTT in VLA Models: Exploring Training with Human Demonstrations
authors: Qiangong Zhou,Jiafeng Liang,Yimin Dong,Yang He,Hongxiang Li

abstract: Long-horizon robot tasks require retaining and using past information. We integrate Test-Time Training (TTT), which stores context in fast weights, into InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5 to study action generation conditioned on human demonstrations through training on paired demonstrations and robot trajectories. We implement memory transfer between the two phases and truncated backpropagation, and examine training objectives, gradient coverage, and contrastive regularization across video, short-video, and single-frame cue tasks.
introduction:
Our overall goal is to explore the memory capabilities needed for long-horizon robot tasks. Later decisions may depend on information encountered much earlier, so models need to retain and use historical context. We therefore consider Test-Time Training (TTT)[1]. TTT writes past information into a fixed-size memory state by updating fast weights. Unlike caches that grow with history length, its memory-state storage remains constant during inference, offering a substantial advantage for long-horizon tasks. TTT also supports online updates and end-to-end learning of memory writes and reads. These properties motivate our exploration.

We focus on robot action generation conditioned on human demonstrations. Each training sample pairs a human demonstration with its corresponding robot trajectory. The model first reads the demonstration, then processes the robot trajectory using the resulting memory. TTT provides the memory mechanism, while task training teaches the model how demonstration conditions should affect action generation. We implement a standard TTT layer and integrate it into Pi0.5[2] and InternVLA-A1[3]. Following the TBPTT approach in RoboTTT[4], we organize state transfer and gradient propagation between human demonstrations and robot trajectories.

Our main contribution is to reproduce and clearly describe the TTT architecture and its training procedure for combining human demonstrations with robot trajectories in VLA models. Training infrastructure constraints have limited the scale of pretraining and training on memory-task data, leaving TTT’s memory capabilities insufficiently trained and evaluated. We also report observations across task settings and discuss training objectives, evaluation protocols, and contrastive regularization. We leave unresolved causes and incomplete validation explicitly open.

title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
authors: Minho Park,Kinam Kim,Donghu Kim,Byungkun Lee,Dongyoon Hwang,Yongjae Shin,Junha Hyung,Hojoon Lee,Jaegul Choo
abstract:
Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly.
We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning.
Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution.
We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success.
The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning.
Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world.
Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62%62\% from 40%40\% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78%78\% from 39%39\% on the real robot, respectively.
These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection.
Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo/
introduction:
Modern visuomotor policies are commonly trained from robot trajectories using behavior cloning (BC) (Pomerleau, 1988).
Scaling this paradigm, however, is constrained by the cost of physical data collection.
Robot trajectories are typically collected through human teleoperation, requiring access to physical robot hardware and operator time for every episode.
Consequently, even large robot datasets contain only on the order of a million episodes (O’Neill et al., 2024; Khazatsky et al., 2024), far fewer than the billions of image–text pairs (Schuhmann et al., 2022) or trillions of tokens (Grattafiori et al., 2024) used to train foundation models in vision and language.

Simulation offers a scalable alternative.
Robot trajectories can be generated cheaply and in parallel without requiring human teleoperation for every episode, and advances in sim-to-real transfer have made simulated experience increasingly useful for training real-world policies (Torne et al., 2024; Bauza et al., 2025).
Scaling simulated data, however, raises two key questions: how should successful trajectories be generated, and what distribution of successful behavior should they cover?
Together, these choices determine the supervision available to downstream BC.

Existing simulation pipelines generate successful trajectories in several ways.
Motion-planning methods construct feasible motions between task-relevant poses (Chen et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025b; Tian et al., 2026), but rely on task-specific planning structure.
MimicGen-style methods reduce this burden by retargeting successful demonstration segments to new scene configurations (Mandlekar et al., 2023; Garrett et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025), but remain constrained by the behaviors contained in the source demonstrations and by where those behaviors can be successfully retargeted.
These limitations are particularly relevant in contact-rich manipulation, where geometric transformation alone may not preserve successful interactions as the scene changes.
Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a complementary approach by learning closed-loop behavior directly from task feedback, and recent methods bootstrap RL from demonstrations or pretrained behavior priors to make successful data generation practical under sparse rewards (Tao et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026).

However, an RL policy that reliably solves the task does not necessarily generate a training distribution well suited to downstream BC.
As illustrated in Figure 1, task reward alone can concentrate an RL policy around a narrow set of successful solutions, so collecting more rollouts need not substantially expand the states represented in the dataset (Kumar et al., 2020).
This limited coverage can make BC brittle when prediction errors move the learned policy beyond states supported by its training demonstrations (Ross et al., 2011).
Perturbation- and recovery-based methods broaden supervision around an existing demonstration or policy (Dai et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026), but their additional experience remains anchored to the supplied behavior.
This motivates a different question: can the generator itself discover multiple successful ways of solving the task?

We address this question with DiscoDemo, which trains an RL generator to combine task competence with solution diversity.
Starting from a few successful demonstrations, we use a parallel reverse curriculum to bootstrap task-solving behavior under sparse rewards, using demonstration states for curriculum resets rather than treating demonstration actions as the target solution.
At the same time, we condition the generator on a latent skill and optimize a success-gated diversity objective that encourages different skills to realize distinct state-space behaviors while preserving task completion (Kumar et al., 2020; Park et al., 2024).
The resulting generator discovers multiple successful solution modes whose union provides broader successful-state coverage for downstream BC.

We evaluate DiscoDemo on four real-world manipulation tasks reconstructed in simulation, spanning pick-and-place, stacking, and precision-sensitive peg insertion.
For each data source, we train the same π0.5\pi_{0.5} vision-language-action policy (Intelligence et al., 2025), pretrained on DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), and compare against human demonstrations and simulation data-generation methods based on planning (Fu et al., 2026), augmentation (Mandlekar et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2026), and RL (Xiao et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2024).
DiscoDemo produces the strongest downstream policy across all four tasks in both simulation and the real world.
Averaged across tasks, it reaches 62%62\% success in simulation compared with 40%40\% for the strongest baseline, and 78%78\% compared with 39%39\% on the real robot.
The largest gains over the strongest baseline are 2323 percentage points on FMB-Round in simulation and 4545 on PnP-Banana in the real world.

title: Robotic Budding: From Homogeneous Cells to Diverse Morphologies in Physical Self-Reproduction
authors: Siyuan Zhang,Junyan Liu,Wanglin He,Hod Lipson
abstract:
Physical self-reproduction in modular robots remains difficult because a robot must not only move, but also collect, align, dock, and separate modules reliably in hardware.
Taking inspiration from how genetically identical cells form the varied tissues of an organism, we introduce a single standardized robotic module that combines a magnetic docking interface with two actuated joints and folds from a flat, two-dimensional configuration into three-dimensional structures.
Modules of this single design can be assembled into two morphologies: a three-module “trilobite” and a five-module “seal”.
Using a small set of discrete motion commands, a human operator steers an assembled parent robot to dock magnetically with a sequence of spare modules, which are assembled into a second, structurally identical individual that then separates from the parent.
Because the parent retains all of its original modules, this is a budding-style form of physical reproduction.
Here, we report preliminary hardware demonstrations of this full process on both morphologies.
We discuss the current scope of the system, including its present reliance on direct human teleoperation rather than autonomous control, and outline directions toward autonomous execution of this process and repeated validation across a larger number of independent trials.
introduction:
Modular robotic systems achieve versatility, robustness, and adaptability by composing a small set of standardized units into task-specific morphologies [1].
A particularly ambitious extension of this idea is physical self-reproduction: using the same modules that make up a robot to construct additional, independently functioning copies of it.
This goal’s theoretical foundations date back to von Neumann’s theory of self-reproducing automata [2].
Recent work has demonstrated kinematic self-replication in reconfigurable biological organisms [3], but achieving comparable physical reproduction in purely electromechanical systems has remained largely limited to simulation or to structured, partially scaffolded environments [4, 5, 6].

In this work, we investigate whether a single module design (Fig. 1) can support both (i) structurally distinct target morphologies, and (ii) physical reproduction via module collection and assembly, without redesigning the hardware between cases.
We report a system in which a human operator steers an assembled parent robot, through a small set of discrete motion commands relayed wirelessly to its modules, to dock with spare modules in sequence, culminating in the release of a structurally identical offspring.

To demonstrate reproduction across distinct morphologies, we implement two structurally and topologically distinct morphologies as proof of concept: a three-module “trilobite” featuring a segmented body with a short caudal extension, and a five-module “seal” equipped with a pair of rear flippers, as shown in Fig. 2.
Together, they show that one module design can produce morphologies that differ in module count and connection topology.
We demonstrate the full reproduction process on both morphologies.

The contribution of this work is a preliminary hardware demonstration and system description, rather than a comprehensive quantitative evaluation.

title: Input Bias Correction in Gaussian Process Regression
authors: Muzaffar Qureshi,Tochukwu E. Ogri,Trivikram Satharasi,Kyle Volle,Rushikesh Kamalapurkar
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L) (Oct, 2026)
abstract: In traditional Gaussian process (GP) regression, the inputs are typically assumed to be known, and uncertainty enters only through the measurements. When scalar fields are mapped using GP regression with measurements obtained from a mobile sensor, the inputs correspond to the estimated pose of the mobile sensor. The goal in this letter is to understand how a recorded GP, trained on erroneous inputs (e.g., pose estimates from dead-reckoning), can be corrected in a numerically efficient way when better estimates of the inputs become available. In the developed bias-aware GP (Ba-GP) framework, the recorded GP posterior-mean gradient is used to propagate estimated input bias and noise into mean and covariance corrections. The resulting additive covariance structure is then exploited to develop numerically efficient first-order correction algorithms. A simulation study and an indoor light-intensity mapping experiment show that Ba-GP improves predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration relative to noisy-input GP baselines with an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost relative to full GP retraining.
introduction:
Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a Bayesian framework for learning scalar fields from sparse measurements [1, 2], yielding predictive means and uncertainty estimates. Conventional GP regression assumes that the input locations are known accurately; however, this assumption may not hold in real-world applications. The motivating setting of this letter is mobile sensing in which measurements are incorporated into a GP model as they are collected, but accurate measurement locations are not available at a high frequency. High-frequency odometry data from sensors such as IMUs and wheel encoders provide location estimates in real-time but accumulate drift [3, 4], whereas lower-bias absolute-position measurements, such as GPS or motion-capture measurements, are available only intermittently. Consequently, waiting for the final refined trajectory before training would preclude the use of the GP map during the sensing episode. The GP is therefore trained using the available odometry-based locations whose errors can degrade the resulting map [5, 6, 7]. After the episode, filtering or smoothing techniques can be used to refine the recorded trajectory and reduce the accumulated localization drift [8]. The GP could then be retrained using the refined locations; however, doing so requires rebuilding the GP using the corrected input data.

Existing uncertain-input GP methods primarily address stochastic uncertainty in the inputs. For multi-step-ahead forecasting, Girard et al. [9, 10] approximated the non-Gaussian predictive distribution induced by uncertain regressors with a moment-matched Gaussian distribution. Dallaire et al. [11] showed that, for independent Gaussian input locations and a squared-exponential kernel, the covariance matrix can be computed analytically, yielding a modified GP kernel. McHutchon and Rasmussen [12] developed a first-order Taylor approximation, termed noisy-input GP (NIGP), in which measurement-location uncertainty is represented as an additional location-dependent noise term proportional to the squared gradient of the posterior mean. These methods account for the noise in the input locations, but they do not use an estimated input bias to correct a GP that has already been trained on recorded inputs.

In a recent study [13], input bias is corrected by treating the GP posterior mean and covariance as functions of the training inputs and applying Taylor expansions to compute Jacobians and Hessians offline. The resulting derivatives can then be used to correct the GP posterior when the bias estimate becomes available. However, the method does not account for the remaining input noise. In addition, the memory required to store the Jacobian and Hessian tensors increases with the dataset size, and the derivatives must be recomputed when predictions are required at new test inputs.

A straightforward way to address input bias is to retrain the GP with bias-corrected input locations. However, corrected input retraining requires reconstructing and factorizing the GP covariance matrix, whose computational cost scales cubically with the dataset size. When a GP has already been trained using recorded inputs, retraining also does not reuse the matrix computations already available from that GP.

These limitations motivate a GP correction framework that leverages an estimated input bias to update an already trained GP, explicitly accounts for the remaining input noise, and avoids complete retraining. To address this challenge, a bias-aware Gaussian process (Ba-GP) framework is developed. Ba-GP first uses the recorded-input GP to compute local gradients and propagates the estimated input bias through these gradients to obtain a first-order correction to the predictive mean. The residual input noise is then incorporated through an additive covariance correction. Conditioning on the corrected mean and covariance yields the Ba-GP posterior distribution. Furthermore, the additive covariance structure enables first- and second-order Neumann approximations that reuse the recorded GP matrix computations, thereby avoiding direct factorization of the full Ba-GP covariance matrix and reducing computational cost. The contributions of this letter are as follows:

A bias-aware GP framework, Ba-GP, is developed for regression with input bias and input noise. The Ba-GP posterior separates bias from noise through a first-order mean correction and an additive covariance correction to the recorded-input covariance matrix.

First- and second-order Neumann approximations of the Ba-GP posterior are derived by exploiting the additive covariance correction, reusing the recorded GP factorization to reduce computational cost while retaining accuracy.

The Ba-GP framework and its Neumann approximations are evaluated in simulation and mobile robot mapping experiments, demonstrating improved accuracy under localization drift and characterizing the accuracy–computation tradeoff.

title: Distributed Swarm Morphogenesis with Neural Cellular Automata
authors: Ray Verma,Eliseo Ferrante,Anthony Tzes
abstract: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site selection and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.
introduction:
Swarm morphogenesis aims to generate large-scale physical structures through local interactions among robots. Applications include coordinated aerial displays, distributed inspection, search, surveillance, and defence, where formations may need to scale or adapt across environments. Reliance on GPS, motion capture, or centralized estimation can limit applicability where signals or infrastructure are unavailable, including GNSS-denied environments; relative-sensing approaches instead use onboard vision [1], ranging and odometry [2], or distance-only measurements [3, 4]. Here, we consider local-relative sensing without globally referenced robot poses.

Distributed task-allocation methods assign tasks to robots [5], while assignment-based shape-formation methods allocate or dynamically select robot goals [6, 7]. Assignment-free methods guide robots to fill specified shapes without explicit robot-to-site assignments [8, 9]. These approaches differ in how robots occupy the shape, but both assume its geometry is supplied beforehand. We instead consider distributed attachment-site discovery.Essentially, we determine which physical attachment sites should exist as the morphology develops, so that a global structure can emerge from a local developmental rule trained offline, rather than a stored goal list. Existing assignment and control methods then coordinate robots to occupy these sites.

NCAs suit distributed attachment-site discovery because local computations generate global structure without a central coordinator. Each cell updates its state from neighbors, enabling pattern growth and regeneration [10], with extensions to graphs and higher-resolution generation [11, 12, 13]. We use these states to discover physical attachment sites, establishing a first step toward neural swarm morphogenesis.

The framework separates NCA attachment-site generation from assignment and control, allowing independent replacement. These methods can be replaced without altering NCA attachment-site generation. We use the artificial-light-field assignment and constrained controller of [7].

Standard Growing NCAs train on virtual grids without assembly constraints. During deployment, the NCA should instead evolve using local states of a gradually and asynchronously assembled formation. This mismatch can impair attachment-site predictions, motivating offline fine-tuning.

We propose an NCA-based framework for distributed swarm morphogenesis with three main contributions:

Modular lattice-morphogenesis framework. We couple developmental attachment-site generation, distributed assignment, and collision-aware control.

Distributed attachment-site discovery method. Robots in the formation exchange and update local NCA states to identify candidate attachment sites to occupy. This allows the formation to develop progressively without providing robots with a complete list of attachment sites.

Offline fine-tuning adapts a pretrained NCA to physical assembly using simulated partial attachment. An additional false-positive loss penalizes activation outside the desired morphology.

The attachment-site discovery layer is modular with respect to assignment and control; the reported implementation uses the artificial-light-field assignment and constrained controller in [7].

title: Silence Is Not Assurance: When Production Lane Keeping Assist Does Not Warn, and What It Costs
authors: Tianjia Yang,Yuxin Ding,Ke Li,Kaidi Liang,Ruwen Qin,Xianbiao Hu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Production lane keeping assist (LKA) systems tell the driver whether they detect the lane markings, but whether this displayed status reflects what the system perceives, and what happens when it does not, has not been examined in real-world driving. This study introduces CANDID-LKA, a CAN-based Diagnosis of the Indicated Detection status in LKA. It evaluates a proprietary driver-facing status using three signals: the displayed status and the driver’s steering torque, both recorded from the vehicle’s controller area network (CAN) bus, and the lane perception confidence of a third-party vision system observing the same road. The framework examines how the status responds to driving conditions and estimates how completely it reports degraded lane perception by comparing it with the other two signals in a latent-class model. We apply it to 39,800 seconds of real-world driving from 13 vehicle models of three manufacturers. The results show that the status does not respond consistently to the conditions that make markings harder to see, and that the three makes differ widely in how often they report not detected. The latent-class model shows that the displayed status is incomplete: it reports only 47% of degraded seconds as not detected, compared with 80% for the third-party low perception confidence, and in half of the low-confidence episodes it never reports not detected. In the silent seconds in which the status reads detected while the perception confidence is low and the driver is not in control, the standard deviation of lateral position over the next 3 s is about 60% larger than when the status and the perception confidence agree. A detected status thus does not guarantee reliable lane perception, and silence with the driver not in control is the case that most needs attention.
introduction:
Lane keeping assist (LKA) has become a standard function on most new passenger vehicles in the United States. Adoption rose from 1.4 percent of model year 2015 vehicles to 86.3 percent of model year 2023 vehicles [17], and the function is associated with measurable reductions in lane-departure crashes [3, 8]. Those benefits are not uniform. LKA relies on camera-based perception of the road ahead, so its performance can degrade where markings are worn, contrast is low, or weather obscures the lane [22, 20], and the benefit realized also depends on how drivers use the system [4]. A driver cannot directly observe the system’s internal perception. The lane-detection status on the dashboard is the vehicle’s primary explicit report of whether it currently recognizes the lane. This paper evaluates the trustworthiness of that report, the extent to which a driver can rely on it as an indication of the current condition of lane perception, and what it costs the driver when the report stays silent.

The displayed status can diverge from the underlying perception condition in two ways, with different consequences for the driver. In the first case, the status reports the lane as not detected while perception is adequate. The cost is a nuisance alert, and if such alerts repeat, the cue loses credibility and drivers may discount it or switch the function off [28, 29, 18]. In the second case, the status keeps showing detected after perception has degraded. The display continues to indicate normal operation, so the driver may keep relying on the system and respond too late to a developing lane departure. The latter is the more damaging of the two, because the driver is given no signal at the moment a lane departure is most likely.

Prior research has characterized when LKA perception succeeds and fails, but the trustworthiness of the displayed status has not itself been evaluated. Perception performance has been studied through controlled and instrumented-road testing, simulation of rare and severe conditions, and large-scale naturalistic evaluation of production vehicles [22, 30, 1]. A related line of work examines whether automated driving systems can recognize their own perception limits through runtime monitoring, out-of-distribution detection, and uncertainty estimation [23, 12, 11]. In parallel, human-factors research investigates how drivers calibrate their reliance on partial automation from system feedback and documents the mode confusion and miscalibrated trust that can arise when that feedback is misleading [28, 29, 18]. What is missing is an evaluation of the signal that connects them, the status the vehicle actually shows the driver.

Evaluating the trustworthiness of the displayed status faces two challenges. The first is access. The displayed status is a report produced by the system, not a direct view of what the system perceives. Production perception systems are proprietary, so what the system internally perceives cannot be observed, and only the detection state it reports on the vehicle bus is available. Any evaluation must therefore work from the report and from signals recorded alongside it, not from the perception itself. The second is the absence of a reference. Whether the lane markings are perceivable at a given moment is not a deterministic outcome, and no single agreed standard exists against which the displayed status could be checked directly. Marking perceivability depends on wear, contrast, lighting, weather, and the camera, and it varies continuously, so no ground-truth label of perceivable or not perceivable exists for each second of driving.

This paper addresses both challenges with CANDID-LKA, a CAN-based Diagnosis of the Indicated Detection status in Lane Keeping Assist. The name also states what the framework asks of the display: whether it is candid about what the system perceives. The report under evaluation is the lane-detection status shown to the driver by the production system. CANDID-LKA relates this status to two signals recorded from different sources during the same driving: the lane perception confidence of an independently implemented system observing the same road, and the driver’s control response from the vehicle’s Controller Area Network (CAN) bus. CANDID-LKA asks three questions of the displayed status. First, does it respond to the conditions that make lane markings harder to see? The internal test answers this question by examining whether the status changes coherently with those conditions. Second, does it agree with other signals recorded at the same moment about the same road? The external test answers this question by evaluating the status against the lane perception confidence and the driver’s control response, treating degraded marking perceivability as an unobserved state that all three signals indicate, and estimating how completely the status reports it. Third, when the status is silent about degraded perception, what does it cost the driver? The same test answers this question by examining the outcomes of these silent seconds, quantified by the standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP) and the lateral excursion that follow. Because CANDID-LKA analyzes what a system reports about its own perception, and not lane detection itself, the same design applies to other driver-facing indicators, including availability reporting for adaptive cruise control and automatic emergency braking.

This study makes three contributions.

1. Applying CANDID-LKA to 39,800 seconds of naturalistic driving from 13 production vehicle models in the OpenLKA dataset [25], we provide, to our knowledge, the first real-world evidence from production vehicles that the displayed lane-detection status is incomplete. Half of the sustained low-confidence episodes receive no not-detected report. In silent seconds when the driver is not steering, the 3 s SDLP is about 60% larger than after agreement seconds.

2. CANDID-LKA evaluates a proprietary driver-facing LKA report with a latent-class model that uses an independent vision system and the driver’s steering signal, without access to the manufacturer’s internal perception system or a ground-truth label. The framework could support consumer ratings, regulatory evaluation, and post-deployment audits, and extends to other driver-facing status indicators.

3. CANDID-LKA separates how often the status switches to not detected from how long it stays there. This shows that the share of not-detected time alone can hide long outages or frequent short ones, so evaluations should consider outage duration alongside how often outages start. Together with the large differences in how much each system reports, this suggests that the differences across manufacturers come partly from how each designs its status-reporting logic, and that more complete reporting is achievable.

The remainder of the paper reviews related work, formalizes the framework, describes the data and estimation, presents the two tests, and discusses their implications.

title: Move, don't think: sample-efficient collision avoidance with lossy proximity sensors
authors: Carson Kohlbrenner,Niraj Pudasaini,William Xie,Naren Sivagnanadasan,Nikolaus Correll,Alessandro Roncone
abstract: Data-driven robots must learn to avoid collisions with as few demonstrations as possible to avoid collecting large datasets of destructive collision examples. We explore whole-body proximity sensors as inductive biases for learning reflexive collision-dodging behavior and find that lossy sensors with low resolution were stronger biases than high-resolution coverage. We also found that, perhaps unintuitively, anticipating when and where contact happens on the body of a robot reduced its learning sample efficiency. We investigated eight candidate representations in a reinforcement learning environment, which included latent compression, future contact anticipation, lossy corruption, and privileged state estimation. The candidate representations were tested by training over 200 humanoid robots to play a simplified version of dodgeball end-to-end under an intentionally constrained sample and compute budget.
introduction:
Robots deployed in unstructured environments must avoid collisions that could damage themselves or others.
Data-driven models have enabled manipulation and locomotion tasks to be performed in unstructured environments (Kim et al., 2024b; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), but learning collision avoidance through data is challenging because collision data can be damaging and costly to collect. This expensive data constraint alone motivates the need for sample-efficient ways to learn safe, reflexive behavior in as few demonstrations as possible.

Forecasting future camera observations using generative world models
emerged as a strategy for safely experiencing potentially dangerous scenarios (Agarwal et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025), and forecasting has also been shown to dramatically improve task performance in dynamic tasks such as sports (Syed et al., 2026). However, occlusions and partial observability are a notorious problem for camera-based contact detection (Navarro et al., 2021), causing world models to rely on heuristic estimates of contact (Liu et al., 2025). We therefore look to alternative sensors than cameras that are designed to combat occlusions.

Egocentric proximity sensors exist as solutions to occlusion and partial observability due to their ability to sense directly from the surface of a robot (Scholz et al., 2024) and have been extensively used for safe collision avoidance (Navarro et al., 2021). A large variety of sensing methods power these whole-body proximity sensor constellations, such as light ranging, capacitive sensing, acoustic sensing, and more (Scholz et al., 2024). Despite the large variety of options, there is not a consensus on what properties of proximity sensors are ideal for sample-efficient learning, such as range or signal representation, and world models have yet to integrate such proximity sensors. Thus, we seek to answer the following questions for learning collision avoidance: How should a proximity sensor’s signal be shaped, and does anticipating contact help?

The goal of this paper is two-fold: 1) to investigate how whole-body proximity sensor observations can be best represented as inductive biases for sample-efficient collision avoidance, and 2) to investigate if predicting future contact observations can lead to improved sample efficiency for learning collision avoidance.
The contributions of this work are as follows:

We propose a design heuristic for using proximity sensors as sample-efficient inductive biases, which favors wide, overlapping coverage of low-resolution sensors and low signal dimensionality. We further show how a high-resolution proximity sensor can mimic a low-dimensional sensor using a simple lossy signal minimization to improve sample efficiency.

We propose that anticipating when and where contact will happen can create sample-efficiency deficits for learning collision avoidance, which we validate using a proximity world model (PWM) that forecasts future observations from whole-body proximity sensors to anticipate contact.

We rigorously ablate sensor observation representation, including signal processing, forecasting, and hardware properties, in a simulated collision avoidance task with a Unitree humanoid H1-2 robot equipped with 64 proximity sensors.

title: Emergent Cooperative Thermoregulation in Lunar Swarm Robotics
authors: Anais Jeger,Harry Holt,Lennart Puck
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters. Video in ancillary files
abstract:
Swarms of small robots are an attractive way to survey lunar caves and lava
tubes. Missions such as NASA’s CADRE will fly cooperating rovers for
distributed mapping, but only in daylight. The 354 h lunar night drops the
surface towards 95 K, and the radioisotope heaters that let single rovers
survive it cannot be supplied at swarm scale. In this study we investigate
whether a swarm can instead use its own members as thermal shielding.
We train one policy, shared by all twenty robots, by reinforcement learning
with an evolution-strategies estimator. The policy receives a single reward,
once, at the end of the night: the mean temperature of the five coldest
robots. Nothing in that reward refers to position, spacing, exposure or
motion. Two behaviors nonetheless emerge. The swarm aggregates, and robots
circulate between the sheltered core and the exposed rim, the same pair of
behaviors with which emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter.
We measure the survival threshold, the smallest stored energy per robot at
which every robot is still alive at sunrise. Across ten runs it is
155.6±1.3155.6\pm 1.3 pcm-h, where one pcm-h is 7.2 kJ of stored heat. That is
37%37\,\% below a motionless huddle and within 13%13\,\% of a physics-based
lower bound, and at a budget where the motionless huddle loses six robots,
every robot survives. The behavior needs no shared spatial reference and no
robot–robot contact, and transfers from twenty robots to forty without
retraining.
introduction:
Surviving the lunar night as a small rover remains a difficult problem due to temperatures falling towards 95 K95\text{\,}\mathrm{K} and its duration of approximately 354 h354\text{\,}\mathrm{h} [1, 2]. Recently, swarm robotics has become increasingly popular for mapping extraterrestrial environments [3, 4, 5]. This is especially useful for exploring underexplored environments such as lunar caves and lava pits, where the loss of one small robot would not necessarily compromise the entire mission [4, 5]. NASA’s CADRE mission, for example, will use three small cooperating rovers for distributed lunar mapping, but the rovers are only designed to operate during the daylight hours of a single lunar day and will therefore not survive the lunar night [3].

While some rovers have managed to withstand the extreme temperatures of the lunar night, the solutions used to achieve this are difficult to transfer to small swarm robots. Yutu-2, for example, uses radioisotope-assisted thermal control and has successfully resumed operation after lunar nights [6, 7]. Pragyan, in contrast, was designed for one lunar day and did not resume communication after the lunar night [8, 9]. Radioisotope Heating Units (RHUs) have allowed lunar systems to survive the night, but their fuel is scarce: holding a 2 W2\text{\,}\mathrm{W} heater needs about 5 g5\text{\,}\mathrm{g} of plutonium dioxide per robot, two standard units’ worth [10], and the US production target of roughly 1.5 kg1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{kg} per year [11] is sized for flagship radioisotope power systems rather than for expendable robots.

So before focus shifts towards sophisticated autonomy or science objectives such as mapping, a lunar robot swarm first needs to be capable of surviving the lunar night. In this study we investigate whether a swarm of robots can use each other as thermal shielding, and so reduce the stored energy each robot needs to survive the lunar night. We take the approach from emperor penguins, which huddle to reduce heat loss while continuously exchanging positions between the exposed outside and the sheltered core [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. We investigate whether a swarm of lunar robots can use this same principle to redistribute exposure between robots and reduce the thermal burden on each individual robot.

We propose a decentralized policy that commands each robot’s motion throughout the night from purely local observations, with one parameter set shared across the swarm, and train it by reinforcement learning.
Our contributions are: (i) we train a shared policy by reinforcement learning on a purely thermodynamic objective (ii) both aggregation and sustained core–rim circulation emerge from it, and together they keep every robot alive at a fixed energy budget where a motionless huddle does not (iii) the behavior requires no shared spatial reference and (iv) it generalizes beyond its training swarm size, controlling swarms from half to twice that number without retraining.

title: Full-Weight VLA Fine-Tuning Without an fp32 Master Copy Silently Erases Most Updates
authors: Shubham Singh
abstract:
When a vision-language-action (VLA) model is fine-tuned with its trainable weights in bfloat16 (bf16) and no fp32
master copy, AdamW writes each update straight into bf16, silently rounding away any update smaller than 1/512 of a
weight. In 9 of 12 open VLA codebases a default or documented recipe trains this way, 4 on full weight matrices,
including LeRobot’s SmolVLA default and its π0\pi_{0}/π0.5\pi_{0.5} guides. In our LIBERO runs without the copy, a probe
every 100 steps finds at least 79% of updates to bf16 weights erased. On the Hugging Face Hub, 99% of sampled
full-weight SmolVLA fine-tunes store the action expert in bf16, and 84% of recent π0.5\pi_{0.5} fine-tunes with a
training configuration set the bf16 flag. On LIBERO-Object, with rules fixed in advance, an fp32 copy raises success
over LeRobot’s storage from 4.3% to 49.3% for SmolVLA and from 5.1% to 80.9% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} at a ten-times lower
learning rate, where both models are undertrained, and from 89.0% to 97.7% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} at its default rate. For
SmolVLA at its default rate it adds 10.2 points with open-loop 50-action chunks but only 4.2 when re-planning every 10
actions. In these five comparisons and two more against SmolVLA with every trainable weight in bf16, every run with the
copy beats every run without it (p<0.05p<0.05); all gaps but the 8.7- and 4.2-point ones clear our 10-point threshold. The
fix is to keep the trainable weights in fp32 during training, a one-line change for SmolVLA in LeRobot.
introduction:
Fine-tuning a pretrained VLA on a new task is now routine, done with a few open codebases: LeRobot
[1, 2] for SmolVLA [3] and π0\pi_{0}/π0.5\pi_{0.5} [4, 5],
openpi [6], the OpenVLA family [7, 8, 9], and RL frameworks such as RLinf
[10]. To save memory, several cast the trainable weights to bfloat16 (bf16) before building the optimizer.
Compute in bf16 is intended, but PyTorch’s AdamW then also keeps its moments in bf16 and adds each update directly to
the bf16 weight, which mixed-precision training avoids by keeping an fp32 master copy of the weights and rounding
only the copy used for compute [11]. Without the copy, an update smaller than 0.2–0.4% of the weight is
rounded away [12]. Fine-tuning learning rates are 10−510^{-5} to 10−410^{-4} and most AdamW steps are smaller
still, so for weights of typical size a large share of updates is silently lost, with no error and a falling loss.

We first state when a statistic EE, computed from the weights alone [13, 14], is a lower bound on
the share of weights an AdamW step leaves unchanged, and check it with a per-step probe (Section II). We
then audit 12 open VLA codebases and sample fine-tunes on the Hugging Face Hub (Section III). Finally, on
LIBERO-Object [15], with rules fixed in advance, we compare three ways to store the trainable weights
(Section IV). Two keep no fp32 copy: all-bf16 stores them all in bf16, and LeRobot’s
recipe stores most of them in bf16 (SmolVLA’s default, or the bf16 flag of LeRobot’s π0.5\pi_{0.5} guide). The third,
the fp32 copy, stores them all in fp32.

title: Multimodal MPC via Bayesian Set Optimization for Dynamic Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects
authors: Youyuan Long,Gokhan Solak,Arash Ajoudani
abstract:
Dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects (DLOs) remains challenging due to underactuated, high-dimensional dynamics, delayed deformation responses, and the presence of multiple feasible motions under obstacle constraints. This paper presents BM2PC, a Bayesian Multimodal MPC framework for agile manipulation of DLOs. Building on the control-as-inference posterior, BM2PC formulates multimodal planning as a set optimization problem that balances control quality and behavioral diversity. An efficient incremental update maintains multiple promising control modes with low additional computational overhead. For real-world deployment, BM2PC incorporates an execution dynamics model that predicts actual end-effector motion and compensates for execution mismatch during fast manipulation.
We evaluate BM2PC on rope tracking and obstacle avoidance in simulation and hardware, and on simulated disturbance rejection. In trajectory tracking, BM2PC generalizes better to unseen trajectories than a learning-based baseline without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate long-horizon tracking, reducing RMSE by 44.0% on the longest task. In obstacle avoidance, BM2PC achieves comparable performance to existing multimodal MPC methods while reducing planning time by 29% to 66%.
These results demonstrate accurate dynamic control and efficient multimodal planning within a unified MPC framework.
The core implementation of BM2PC and supplementary videos are available at
https://github.com/Longyouyuan/BM2PC.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation of deformable linear objects (DLOs), such as ropes, cables, and hoses, is an important capability for service, industrial, and field robots [1, 2].
In applications such as automated cable routing, wire-harness assembly, and hose handling, robots must manipulate DLOs accurately and efficiently through structured workspaces containing fixtures and obstacles.
Compared with rigid-body manipulation, DLO manipulation is substantially more challenging due to its high-dimensional, underactuated, and highly nonlinear dynamics [1, 3, 4].
These challenges become more pronounced in dynamic manipulation, where fast motions induce large deformations and complex transient behaviors [5].
In environments involving obstacles, disturbances, and changing task conditions, multiple feasible motion strategies, referred to as control modes in this work, may coexist, with their relative desirability changing over time.
Consequently, practical control requires accurately handling complex deformable dynamics while preserving alternative motion strategies that can be rapidly selected when the current strategy becomes infeasible.

Previous advances in dynamic DLO manipulation can be broadly grouped into two categories: learning-based and optimization-based control approaches.
Learning-based methods shift the computational burden to an offline training phase by learning control policies [6, 7], enabling fast execution but typically requiring extensive training data and exhibiting limited generalization to unseen trajectories, object properties, and changing environments.
In contrast, optimization-based methods compute control actions online using predictive models [8, 9], naturally generalizing across tasks without retraining and readily accommodating changing objectives and constraints.
To handle environments with multiple feasible solutions, several multimodal optimization methods have been proposed [10, 11].
While these approaches improve planning robustness by maintaining diverse candidate solutions, they introduce additional computational overhead that limits their applicability to agile real-time manipulation.
Consequently, there remains a need for optimization-based methods that can efficiently maintain multiple feasible control strategies while preserving the computational efficiency required for real-time dynamic DLO manipulation.

To address this gap, we propose BM2PC, a sampling-based MPC framework for efficient multimodal planning without task-specific policy training. Building on the control-as-inference posterior, BM2PC formulates multimodal planning as a set optimization problem that jointly accounts for the posterior quality and behavioral diversity of control sequences. Rather than approximating the full posterior distribution, the method directly selects a compact set of promising control hypotheses through an efficient incremental update. The selected modes are propagated across MPC steps, allowing the controller to preserve alternative solutions and adapt to changing constraints with low computational overhead.

We evaluate BM2PC on dynamic rope manipulation, where the robot controls the grasped endpoint to track a desired rope-tip trajectory. Our evaluation focuses on two complementary capabilities. First, complex trajectory tracking and disturbance rejection demonstrate accurate predictive control of highly nonlinear rope dynamics with delayed responses. Compared with a learning-based method, BM2PC shows stronger generalization to unseen trajectories without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning. Second, obstacle avoidance evaluates multimodal planning under changing constraints. Compared with existing multimodal MPC methods, BM2PC achieves comparable control performance while reducing planning time by 29% to 66%. Further ablations demonstrate the benefits of maintaining diverse control modes when obstacles suddenly change, while comparison with exhaustive optimization confirms that the incremental update achieves high solution quality at substantially lower computational cost.

Real-world deployment introduces an additional source of prediction error, as commanded end-effector (EE) motions may deviate from their actual execution due to communication delays, actuator limits, and low-level tracking errors. To compensate for these effects, we incorporate an execution dynamics model that predicts the realized EE motion from commanded trajectories and recent execution history. This execution-aware prediction improves planning accuracy during fast dynamic manipulation and enables reliable real-world deployment of BM2PC.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We formulate multimodal MPC as Bayesian set optimization over finite-horizon control sequences and develop an efficient incremental approximation that maintains high-quality, behaviorally diverse control modes for real-time planning.

We enable reliable real-world deployment of BM2PC through an execution-aware predictive model that compensates for execution mismatch by incorporating predicted EE motion into the planning process.

We validate BM2PC through extensive simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating accurate dynamic manipulation of unseen trajectories without task-specific policy training and efficient multimodal planning under changing constraints.

1. We formulate multimodal MPC as Bayesian set optimization over finite-horizon control sequences and develop an efficient incremental approximation that maintains high-quality, behaviorally diverse control modes for real-time planning.

2. We enable reliable real-world deployment of BM2PC through an execution-aware predictive model that compensates for execution mismatch by incorporating predicted EE motion into the planning process.

3. We validate BM2PC through extensive simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating accurate dynamic manipulation of unseen trajectories without task-specific policy training and efficient multimodal planning under changing constraints.

title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
authors: Chubin Zhang,Changyuan Wang,Yirui Wang,Ao Li,Shilin Ma,Yue Su,Cai Zhou,Xiuwei Xu,Tianle Zhang,Yansong Tang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Project page:this https URL
abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source’s contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect broad visual and linguistic knowledge to robot control (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025b). We organize their supervision into an embodied data pyramid: vision–language data offer semantic coverage, egocentric demonstrations capture diverse interactions, and robot trajectories provide executable controls but require dedicated hardware and collection effort (Hoque et al., 2026; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024; Khazatsky et al., 2024). EgoMimic (Kareer et al., 2025) and EgoScale (Zheng et al., 2026b) demonstrate the value of egocentric data through human–robot co-training and large-scale policy pretraining.

However, recovering actions from egocentric videos introduces annotation noise. Camera tracking and hand-pose reconstruction can produce errors, particularly under occlusion and rapid motion (Zhang et al., 2025; Hoque et al., 2026). Retargeting adds a geometric mismatch: differences in palm size, finger proportions, and joint structure mean that accurately tracked human poses need not admit an equivalent robot configuration (Wang et al., 2024; Xin et al., 2026). Appearance and dynamics further complicate transfer. Effective learning from egocentric data therefore requires more than increasing its scale: policies must limit the influence of unreliable action labels while drawing on supervision beyond those labels, enabling additional ego-data to provide effective supervision.

To meet these requirements, we introduce EgoForesight, a VLA framework that reduces the influence of unreliable actions while learning from demonstrated outcomes. Inspired by prior unified video–action and dynamics–action models (Zhu et al., 2025; Lyu et al., 2026), our design couples experts for future visual representations and action chunks and trains them with modality-specific flow-matching paths. Separate corruption times control the information available in the vision and action streams, allowing us to regulate noisy action supervision and distill outcome-informed representations within the same model.

First, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability. Motivated by ADP’s finding that stronger diffusion noise can contract target and suboptimal distributions (Wei et al., 2026), our continuous source-reliability schedule shifts less reliable actions toward stronger corruption. Reliability-weighted action regression complements this schedule by controlling how strongly each source contributes to learning. Together, they enable learning from diverse egocentric data without assuming uniformly reliable labels.

Second, privileged-future representation distillation draws on demonstrated outcomes for action-relevant evidence beyond noisy annotations. An exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher receives the current observation and observed future at the clean endpoint, acting as a conditional inverse dynamics model (IDM). Initialized from higher-quality demonstrations, the teacher provides action representations informed by the observed scene change. Adapting Self-Flow’s cleaner, noise-shifted EMA teacher and cross-layer alignment (Chefer et al., 2026), we apply this mechanism to robot action tokens: a deeper teacher feature supervises an earlier student layer, which enriches early policy features with outcome-informed structure. In our setting, observed-future conditioning gives the teacher its inverse-dynamics role, and the student learns to anticipate the resulting outcome-informed representation while receiving a corrupted future.

For model training, we first establish visual–action correspondences on higher-quality robot demonstrations and curated egocentric trajectories. This checkpoint initializes the student and teacher before training expands to a larger action-annotated egocentric-data mixture with reliability-conditioned corruption and privileged-future distillation enabled. Our experiments examine scaling as a test of how effectively policies use noisy egocentric supervision. Under matched data and optimization budgets, EgoForesight translates added pretraining data into stronger gains in action prediction and closed-loop control. Ablations support complementary roles for reliability conditioning and future distillation, and show the value of establishing action correspondences on higher-quality data before expanding coverage.

title: FORCA: A Force-Aware Coding Agent for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
authors: Xiao Tan,Yixuan Wang,Zhexi Wang,Wenzhen Yuan
comment: Project website:this https URL
abstract: Coding agents can translate language instructions into robot programs. For contact-rich manipulation, a key challenge is to generate and refine control logic that responds to physical interaction. We present Forca, a coding agent that takes visual observations and wrist force/torque (F/T) measurements as input to write Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion. Between executions, the agent inspects force records alongside visual outcomes to diagnose failures and revise both motion and force-feedback control logic. Forca requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation. Across five real-robot tasks, we demonstrate its effectiveness in three forms of contact-rich manipulation: improving manipulation accuracy, adapting to changes in object or surface properties, and regulating contact under surface variation and object motion. Compared with a vision-only variant of the same agent, Forca improves grasp accuracy and task success and reduces contact loss in wiping and peeling.
introduction:
Coding agents based on foundation models turn open-ended instructions into executable robot programs that compose perception, grasping, and motion skills [1, 2, 3, 4]. They ground their decisions mainly in vision and proprioception, which is often insufficient for contact-rich manipulation: occluded or reflective surfaces yield uncertain geometry, mass and friction are not visible, and maintaining contact requires responding to surface variation and object motion.

Force and contact measurements complement vision by providing evidence about contact states and mechanical responses that are difficult to infer from visual observations alone. Learned policies exploit force and tactile signals for reactive control but require demonstrations or robot data [5, 6, 7, 8]. Foundation-model agents have used force through compliant or force-thresholded primitives [9, 10], inferred physical properties largely from priors [11, 12, 13], and revised force targets after failed attempts [14]. Supporting these diverse tasks requires agents to determine when contact information is needed, how it should guide ongoing motion, and how unexpected contact outcomes should inform subsequent attempts.

We present Forca, a training-free coding agent that uses wrist force/torque (F/T) sensing in both program execution and program revision (Fig. 1). It writes complete Python programs with access to the measured wrench. During a rollout, the program uses measurements from contact probes to guide subsequent actions and uses live force feedback to regulate its motion. Between rollouts, the agent relates the recorded force traces to visual outcomes, diagnoses failures, and revises the program.

Forca addresses three types of contact-rich manipulation: (i) precision manipulation, where force cues help refine grasp poses and improve manipulation accuracy; (ii) physical adaptation, where actions must be adjusted to changes in object or surface properties; and (iii) contact regulation, where motion must respond to surface variation and object movement. We evaluate Forca on five real-robot tasks spanning these categories: drawer opening, door-handle operation, cube-to-target knocking, vase wiping, and cucumber peeling. Compared with a vision-only variant of the same agent, Forca increases task success from 40% to 100% for drawer opening and from 10% to 100% for door-handle operation, while reducing contact-loss rates in wiping and peeling from 40.6–55.9% to at most 2.2%.

Our contributions are twofold. First, we introduce a coding-agent framework that generates task-specific motion and force-feedback control logic from language instructions. The resulting programs use measured contact to refine grasp poses and regulate motion during execution. Second, we extend program refinement to the force-feedback logic itself, enabling coding agents to revise how their programs respond to contact based on evidence from real-robot execution.
