title: WorldMirror: Agentic Real-to-Sim Generation of Interactive Worlds from In-the-Wild Robot Demonstrations
authors: Tianling Xu,Weijie Wan,Honghao Su,Kailun Su,Junyuan Tang,Huichi Zhou,Haozheng Zhang,Qi Xiong,Ping Luo,Wenbo Ding,Tianxing Chen,Yue Chen
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Existing approaches for robot learning in simulation often require substantial manual effort to construct scenes and specify tasks, limiting training scalability and data diversity. Meanwhile, in-the-wild robot demonstrations naturally provide diverse and realistic observations of real-world interactions. Leveraging these demonstrations for simulation requires both high-fidelity visual reconstruction and physically consistent interactions. General-purpose agents offer flexible adaptation to diverse scenarios and strong reasoning about 3D spatial relationships, while specialized generative models provide high-fidelity reconstruction of scene appearance and geometry. We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that constructs interactive digital twins from in-the-wild robot demonstrations. Our central idea is to formulate real-to-sim construction as the iterative refinement of an executable world program. A coding agent decomposes the observed scene, plans reconstruction steps, and orchestrates specialized image and 3D generation tools, refining the program through verification feedback. A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets while preserving spatial relationships among the scene, objects, and robot. The agent uses this representation to diagnose and correct reconstruction errors, enabling physically consistent interaction and trajectory replay.
Experiments on DROID demonstrate that WorldMirror can reconstruct visually faithful and geometrically consistent interactive worlds while preserving the physical validity of recorded robot trajectories.
introduction:
Scaling generalist robot policies requires diverse training data across a wide range of real-world scenarios (Physical Intelligence, 2025; Black et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026).
Yet collecting real-world demonstrations and testing policies across environments remain costly and labor-intensive.
Simulation offers a complementary route to scalable data generation and controlled, repeatable evaluation (Li et al., 2024; Jain et al., 2025).
Realizing this potential requires interactive environments that reproduce the appearance and physical interactions of real-world deployment settings.

For simulation to serve these purposes, scene geometry, object placement, camera viewpoints, and robot configuration must match the real setup.
Even small errors in scale or contact geometry can alter task outcomes.
Recent real-to-sim systems have advanced scene reconstruction and its use in robot learning and evaluation (Zhao et al., 2025; Ranawaka et al., 2026; Jain et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2024; Torne et al., 2024).
However, real-to-sim construction involves coupled visual, geometric, and physical constraints that an feed-forward reconstruction may not fully satisfy.
Meanwhile, general-purpose agents alone may not produce the fine-grained geometry and photorealistic appearance required for faithful scene reconstruction.
Different reconstruction errors require different forms of correction.
A misplaced object may require layout adjustment, whereas a missing object may require revisiting scene decomposition and asset reconstruction.
Unsuitable collision geometry may instead require revising an asset’s physical representation.
Addressing these errors calls for an adaptive and iterative correction process that selects and revisits reconstruction steps based on the current world state and verification feedback, rather than following a fixed sequence of tool calls.
These challenges motivate agentic world modeling, in which a coding agent coordinates specialized reconstruction tools and uses verification feedback to refine an executable world.

We introduce WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework that converts robot videos and their associated trajectories into interactive digital twins.
At its core, a coding agent decomposes the reconstruction objective into subtasks and coordinates specialized reconstruction tools to construct an executable world program.
Using the current world state and verification feedback, the agent determines which components to revise and which tools to invoke next, updating generated assets and assembly code accordingly.
A camera-pose-anchored scene representation organizes the reconstructed world into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets.
It places the scene, objects, and robot in a shared coordinate system, providing a consistent geometric reference for replaying recorded robot trajectories without modification.
Table 1 compares WorldMirror with representative real-to-sim and agentic world construction systems. We validate WorldMirror on DROID (DROID Team et al., 2024)
against existing baselines. Our contributions are:

We propose WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework constructing interactive digital twins via adaptive tool orchestration and verification-guided refinement of executable world programs.

We introduce a camera-pose-anchored scene representation that organizes reconstructed worlds into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets, preserving spatial relationships across the scene, objects, and robot while supporting replay of robot trajectories.

We evaluate WorldMirror on DROID robot manipulation demonstrations
across visual quality, layout fidelity, and motion and interaction fidelity,
demonstrating competitive reconstruction quality and improved replay fidelity
on the evaluated demonstrations.

1. We propose WorldMirror, an agentic real-to-sim framework constructing interactive digital twins via adaptive tool orchestration and verification-guided refinement of executable world programs.

2. We introduce a camera-pose-anchored scene representation that organizes reconstructed worlds into static visual context, support geometry, and editable interactive assets, preserving spatial relationships across the scene, objects, and robot while supporting replay of robot trajectories.

3. We evaluate WorldMirror on DROID robot manipulation demonstrations
across visual quality, layout fidelity, and motion and interaction fidelity,
demonstrating competitive reconstruction quality and improved replay fidelity
on the evaluated demonstrations.

title: SEVI: Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning
authors: Shaekh Mohammad Shithil,Lantao Liu
comment: . Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L), 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Real-world reinforcement learning has enabled contact-rich manipulation tasks to be trained directly on physical robots, but unsafe interactions during online learning remain a key barrier to practical deployment. We propose Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning (SEVI), a framework for reliability-aware safety intervention during real-world policy learning. SEVI introduces an Evidential Safety Critic that estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. During online learning, SEVI evaluates each task-policy action before execution; if the action is predicted to be unsafe or the prediction is insufficiently supported by evidence, SEVI overrides it with an offline-trained recovery policy that guides the robot toward a lower-risk region. We evaluate SEVI on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task under in-distribution and distribution-shifted conditions. Across task-learning and safety-critic baselines, SEVI achieves the strongest trajectory-level safety prediction, the highest final task success, and the lowest unsafe-event counts. SEVI also reduces unsafe events by 13.4–57.1% relative to recovery-based safe RL while preserving low-latency execution-time filtering. The project page is available at:
https://sevi-safe.github.io/.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of enabling robots to acquire complex manipulation skills through trial and error. Recent real-world RL systems have shown that contact-rich manipulation tasks can be trained directly on hardware within a practical time budget. These systems typically rely on demonstrations, sample-efficient off-policy learning, learned rewards, and carefully designed controllers [1, 2].
However, training RL on physical robots remains challenging because exploration can lead to unsafe interactions, such as excessive contact forces, object damage, workspace violations, or failures requiring human intervention. Therefore, as real-world RL becomes increasingly sample-efficient, a central remaining challenge is to reduce unsafe interactions during online training.

This challenge is particularly pronounced in complex tasks, where safety depends on perception, object geometry, contact dynamics, and the evolving task policy [3]. Existing real-world RL pipelines provide an effective foundation for online learning with prior data and off-policy updates. However, they do not explicitly address the autonomous intervention problem: determining when a proposed task action should be rejected and replaced by safe recovery behavior. One way to address this intervention problem is to augment the task policy with a recovery mechanism. Recovery-based safe RL methods instantiate this idea by switching to a recovery policy when a learned safety critic predicts future constraint violations [4]. A key limitation is that these intervention decisions rely on the reliability of the learned safety estimate, which may degrade under partial observations or in state-action regions poorly represented in prior data.

Existing approaches to uncertainty-aware safety attempt to detect unreliable predictions under distribution shift [5]. World-model-based safety filters use learned latent dynamics to imagine future outcomes and identify potential out-of-distribution (OOD) failures [6]. Although this is a promising direction, it relies on accurate long-horizon prediction and sufficient coverage of safety-critical interactions. In complex manipulation, limited unsafe data and partial observability can cause learned dynamics to produce optimistic predictions in unfamiliar regions, leading unsafe actions to be classified as safe. Although sampling-based uncertainty methods can improve reliability estimation, ensembles[7] and Monte Carlo dropout[8] require multiple models or repeated forward passes, which increases latency for real-time robot control [9].

To address this problem, we propose Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning (SEVI), a framework for uncertainty-aware autonomous intervention during online real-world RL. SEVI introduces an Evidential Safety Critic (ESC), which models safety prediction as evidence accumulation and estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. Unlike sampling-based uncertainty methods, the ESC does not require ensembles or repeated stochastic inference, making it suitable for low-latency safety decisions. During online training, SEVI evaluates each action proposed by the task policy using both predicted risk and prediction reliability. If the action is predicted to be unsafe or the prediction is insufficiently supported by evidence, SEVI overrides the task action with an offline-trained recovery policy that guides the robot toward a lower-risk region as illustrated in Fig. 1. This intervention mechanism reduces unsafe interactions without modifying the underlying off-policy RL objective.

We evaluate SEVI on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task with a Franka robot. The experiments show that SEVI improves safety prediction under distribution shift, provides better-calibrated uncertainty than dropout and ensemble baselines, and reduces unsafe events during online real-world RL while maintaining strong task performance. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

We introduce a modular real-world RL safety architecture that decouples task-policy learning from execution-time safety intervention while preserving the underlying task-learning objective.

We propose an Evidential Safety Critic that estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass, enabling low-latency reliability-aware safety assessment.

We integrate evidential safety prediction with an offline-trained recovery policy to enable autonomous intervention during online real-world RL with prior data, while remaining compatible with standard off-policy RL pipelines.

1. We introduce a modular real-world RL safety architecture that decouples task-policy learning from execution-time safety intervention while preserving the underlying task-learning objective.

2. We propose an Evidential Safety Critic that estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass, enabling low-latency reliability-aware safety assessment.

3. We integrate evidential safety prediction with an offline-trained recovery policy to enable autonomous intervention during online real-world RL with prior data, while remaining compatible with standard off-policy RL pipelines.

title: PrefO2O: Zero-Shot Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning via Offline-to-Online Latent Preference Transfer
authors: Ruiqi Wang,Dezhong Zhao,Xuesu Xiao,Erdem Biyik,Byung-Cheol Min,Guohua Chen
abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for learning robot behaviors aligned with human intent. However, its scalability is fundamentally limited by the need to collect expensive human preference labels for every new task. In this work, we present PrefO2O, an offline-to-online latent preference transfer framework that enables zero-shot PbRL on unseen target tasks without requiring any human feedback. The core idea is to learn a task-invariant latent preference space from a small amount of offline preference data on source tasks, where transferable preference structures are disentangled from task-specific variations. This learned manifold allows PrefO2O to transfer preference structures and reward priors to new tasks under distribution shift, while confidence-weighted optimal transport alignment generates reliable pseudo-preference supervision for online reward adaptation. Extensive experiments on robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrate that PrefO2O substantially outperforms existing preference-transfer baselines and matches or exceeds PbRL methods trained with real human feedback, while generalizing across multi-to-one and one-to-one transfer settings as well as across different robot embodiments. More information is available at our project website.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in robotics [1], yet its dependence on carefully engineered reward functions requires substantial domain expertise and remains vulnerable to reward hacking [2]. Preference-based RL (PbRL) offers a compelling alternative: instead of specifying rewards explicitly, it learns reward models from human comparative feedback, thereby aligning robot behaviors with human intent [3, 4, 5, 6].

However, PbRL introduces a fundamental scalability bottleneck. For each new task, high-quality human preference labels must typically be collected from scratch to train an effective reward model [3, 7, 8]. This per-task annotation overhead limits the practical deployment of PbRL in real-world robotic systems, where robots are expected to generalize rapidly across diverse tasks, embodiments, and operating conditions.

Several directions have been explored to reduce this scalability bottleneck. One line of work leverages foundation models to generate synthetic preference labels, enabling scalable feedback without direct human annotation [9, 10, 11, 12]. However, synthetic feedback might be inconsistent, diverge from genuine human intent, and often incurs substantial computational cost [13]. Another line of work applies meta-learning to PbRL, enabling faster adaptation to new tasks by meta-training reward models across task distributions [14, 15]. Yet these methods require extensive preference data during meta-training and still demand target-task feedback, which remains impractical in many real-world robotic settings.

More recent work has investigated zero-shot preference transfer by propagating pseudo-preference labels from source tasks to target tasks through trajectory alignment, for example using optimal transport [16]. While promising, existing methods typically operate directly on shallow trajectory-level similarity metrics. Such alignment can be brittle under distribution shifts, especially when tasks differ in dynamics, objectives, or state-action dimensionality. Moreover, treating preference transfer primarily as offline label propagation provides limited guidance for reward adaptation and policy improvement on the target task.

In this work, we explore how to enable PbRL to transfer across tasks without collecting human feedback on each new target task. Our key insight is that, although task objectives and dynamics may vary, human preferences often contain shared structures that are transferable across related tasks. For example, across manipulation tasks with distinct goals, humans may consistently favor efficient approaches, penalize unnecessary motion, and prefer stable object interactions. These recurring preference patterns suggest that reward learning need not start from scratch for every new task.

Motivated by this insight, we propose PrefO2O, an offline-to-online latent preference transfer framework for zero-shot PbRL across tasks. As illustrated in Fig. 1, PrefO2O learns a task-invariant latent preference space from offline preference data collected across multiple source tasks, abstracting away task-specific variations to expose shared, transferable preference structures. Upon deployment to an unseen target task, PrefO2O operates in this learned latent space to transfer preference priors and generate reliable pseudo-preference supervision, enabling online PbRL under distribution shift and heterogeneous state-action spaces. As overviewed in Fig. 2, PrefO2O consists of two stages:

Offline Phase. We jointly train a trajectory encoder, a preference encoder, and a meta reward model on source-task preference data. The trajectory encoder maps raw, potentially heterogeneous trajectories into compact behavioral representations. The preference encoder learns a structured latent preference manifold over pairwise trajectory differences, capturing shared preference structures across tasks. Concurrently, the meta reward model learns to map trajectory representations to preference-aligned scalar rewards, providing a transferable reward prior for target-task learning.

Online Phase. The pretrained trajectory encoder and reward model serve as a warm start for the target task. The preference encoder remains frozen to preserve the learned manifold, which serves as a stable reference for OOD-aware preference alignment via optimal transport. This alignment generates confidence-weighted pseudo-preference labels that guide continued reward adaptation and policy optimization on the target task.

Our key contributions are as follows:

We propose PrefO2O, an offline-to-online latent preference transfer framework that enables zero-shot PbRL across tasks, eliminating the need for human preference feedback on new tasks.

We introduce a task-invariant latent preference space that abstracts away task-specific variation to capture shared, transferable preference structures. PrefO2O leverages this learned space to transfer preference priors and generate reliable pseudo-preference supervision for unseen target tasks via OOD-aware optimal transport alignment.

We validate PrefO2O on two manipulation and one locomotion benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance over existing preference transfer baselines and PbRL methods trained with real human labels or synthetic feedback. Comprehensive ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component, and we show that PrefO2O generalizes across multi-to-one and one-to-one transfer settings, as well as both intra- and cross-embodiment scenarios.

1. We propose PrefO2O, an offline-to-online latent preference transfer framework that enables zero-shot PbRL across tasks, eliminating the need for human preference feedback on new tasks.

2. We introduce a task-invariant latent preference space that abstracts away task-specific variation to capture shared, transferable preference structures. PrefO2O leverages this learned space to transfer preference priors and generate reliable pseudo-preference supervision for unseen target tasks via OOD-aware optimal transport alignment.

3. We validate PrefO2O on two manipulation and one locomotion benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance over existing preference transfer baselines and PbRL methods trained with real human labels or synthetic feedback. Comprehensive ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component, and we show that PrefO2O generalizes across multi-to-one and one-to-one transfer settings, as well as both intra- and cross-embodiment scenarios.

title: KiRoSe: Using Kinematic Data for Efficient Segmentation of Robot Demonstrations
authors: Shuangyu Xie,Kaiyuan Chen,Muhammad Zubair Irshad,Richard Cheng,Sergey Zakharov,Ken Goldberg
abstract:
Segmenting robot demonstration data into disjoint temporal and semantic subsegments
is valuable for learning, cleaning, retrieval, and analysis.
Segmentation is often performed manually in a tedious and error-prone
process. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have the potential for
automating this process, but directly ingesting raw multi-camera video
streams into MLLMs can be costly and can quickly exhaust context windows.
In this paper, we introduce KiRoSe (Kinematics for Robot Segmentation), a novel framework that focuses on the companion stream of
robot kinematic data.
Inspired by the principle of classical entropy coding, such as Huffman coding, where frequently occurring symbols are represented more compactly, we propose Sparse Motion Tokens
(SMTs), a discrete kinematic vocabulary designed
to compactly represent recurring, temporally localized motion patterns, which we refer to as kinematic events.
SMTs are learned by encoding kinematic trajectories with
temporal-segment supervision and quantizing the resulting features.
We use increasingly available robot demonstration subtask annotations to supervise an open language model to interpret the resulting token sequences.
Evaluation against human-labeled segmentation shows that KiRoSe can substantially outperform baseline segmentation methods in F1 quality and transfers zero-shot to unseen robot embodiments and ego-centric human motion, while preserving the language model’s open-vocabulary knowledge. Beyond segmentation, KiRoSe tracks task progress on an unseen robot and detects when an action is being reversed. (website: https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/kirose/)
introduction:
Large-scale robot demonstration datasets, such as Open X-Embodiment (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2023), can grow to terabyte or even petabyte scale and span diverse robot embodiments and manipulation tasks. Beyond directly training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, understanding the structure within these trajectories is important for effectively using them. Robot demonstrations of “put the cup in the cabinet” and “put the book on the shelf,” for example, share stages such as reaching, grasping, transporting, and placing, potentially mixed with pauses or corrective motions. We refer to recurring, temporally localized motion patterns underlying these stages as kinematic events (Figure  1). Identifying meaningful kinematic events supports demonstration generation through subtask reuse (Mandlekar et al., 2023), learning and sequencing reusable skills (Garrett et al., 2024), and retrieving relevant behaviors for policy adaptation (Memmel et al., 2024). Such intervals also provide useful units for inspecting demonstration quality, complementing approaches that improve policy learning through data filtering (Chen et al., 2025) or progress-based weighting (Chen et al., 2026b).

Manually annotating this structure is tedious and error-prone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a promising route to automate subtask annotation, but processing long, synchronized multi-camera videos can incur substantial inference costs and quickly exhaust their context windows. We observe that proprioceptive kinematics provide a compact and information-dense alternative to video: for example, gripper closure may indicate grasping, while a subsequent increase in end-effector velocity may indicate the transition from grasping to object transport (Figure 1).
However, raw kinematic trajectories are high-frequency and high degree-of-freedom continuous time series without the discrete, semantically structured representation (e.g., directly convert a 1 minute bimanual robot trajectory at 30 Hz consumes approximately 500k text tokens).

In this paper, we introduce KiRoSe (Kinematics for Robot Segmentation), a framework that focuses on using compact kinematics representation to identify action and their boundaries. At its core are Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs), a low-rate kinematic tokenizer for pretrained VLMs.
Rather than asking a tokenizer to faithfully reconstruct every low-level state, we use the increasingly available subtask annotations in large-scale robot demonstration datasets as supervision for learning a sparse motion vocabulary that preserves information useful for language-model reasoning.
We first encode high-frequency kinematic trajectories into temporally contextual features and quantize them into a compact discrete vocabulary.
To make these tokens interpretable by a language model, we add the SMT vocabulary to a pretrained language model and supervise the reader with trajectory segment annotations containing segment boundaries and natural-language action descriptions.
The tokenizer remains fixed during this stage, so the language model learns to interpret the motion vocabulary rather than reshaping the underlying representation.

We evaluate KiRoSe on held-out trajectory segmentation, zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer, semantic description of unseen actions, and task-progress understanding.
Results show that KiRoSe achieves a boundary F1 within 1 second of 0.63 vs. 0.42 for the strongest alternative kinematic tokenizer on 200 held-out YAM episodes, and, transferred zero-shot to an unseen AgiBot embodiment, a boundary F1 within 0.5 seconds of 0.61 vs. 0.30 for GPT-6 Astra.
KiRoSe also retains the language model’s open-vocabulary knowledge, producing task-appropriate words absent from its training annotations on unseen human tasks; when a subtask is played backward, KiRoSe tracks the reversal with a progress correlation of ρ=−0.68\rho=-0.68 on AgiBot, compared with ρ=+0.88\rho=+0.88 for the video-based ReWiND baseline (Zhang et al., 2025).

To summarize, we make the following contributions:
(1) Sparse Motion Tokens (SMT), a boundary-supervised, low-rate kinematic tokenizer that compresses high-frequency robot motion into a compact discrete vocabulary with semantic and temporal motion structure;
(2) KiRoSe, an end-to-end framework that adapts an open language model to interpret SMT sequences with temporal markers, enabling trajectory segmentation, zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer, open-vocabulary action description, and task-progress understanding;
(3) Evaluation Data suggests substantial performance improvement in segmentation quality over baseline and frontier VLMs.

title: FLORA: An Open Model Suite for Scaling Robotics Data Engines
authors: Sicong Leng,Yunze Man,Zhiqi Li,Jing Wang,Yuhe Zhang,Ryan Punamiya,Siddharth Patki,Kaiyuan Zheng,Zi-ang Cao,Zhiding Yu,Sifei Liu,Danfei Xu,Ben Levin,Jan Kautz,Yuke Zhu,Johan Bjorck,Linxi "Jim" Fan
abstract: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly ∼125×\sim 125\times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Flora is battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.
introduction:
Robotics foundation models have evolved from single-embodiment policies [1] to generalist models trained on large, heterogeneous corpora [2, 3, 4, 5]. Across these large datasets, high-quality labels are imperative for performant models. Pretraining benefits from timestamped action instructions that enable language conditioning [6] and let practitioners rebalance the data mixture [7, 8]. RL post-training [9, 10] requires process rewards that measure progress within an episode, analogous to step-level supervision in language models [11, 12]. Deployment needs outcome rewards to monitor fleets, detect failures [13], and evaluate policies at scale [14].

Most existing systems cover only one annotation type. General-purpose frontier models can provide several types, but are expensive at the scale of modern robot datasets. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used to train GR00T models. It consists of three models—a captioning model, a segmentation model, and a reward model—that together produce timestamped captions, process rewards, and outcome rewards. User-defined rubrics additionally support flexible reward modeling at test time. The engine is battle tested at scale, labeling up to 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300 GPUs. By open-sourcing Flora, we enable researchers to scale custom robot datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research [15] and human-to-robot transfer [16].

title: See What I Need, Dream What I Want: A Navigation Foundation Model on a Self-Constructed Representation Space
authors: Jiawei Chen,Yinxi Wang,Zihan Yang,Meijun Gao,Yaowei Liu,Shuming Zhang,Zecheng Li,Xiangju Mi,Yuxuan Liu,Runzhong Huang,Tianlin Li,Xun Zhang,Zhengyang Wang,Xu Miao,Tong Yang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Project page:this https URL
abstract: What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? A central idea of representation learning is that the task’s own error should shape the representation. Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely set this idea aside: the encoders’ pretraining objectives decide much of what the vision-language backbone sees. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self-constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy’s own objectives out of the internal structure of vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three-layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain-of-thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end-to-end with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On the VLNVerse fine-grained benchmark, RepresentNav achieves a success rate of 83.80%, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT-Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). Analysis shows where they come from. With the same encoders, the self-constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot’s own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.
introduction:
Consider a robot asked to cross a cluttered hall to a point on its far side. What it needs to see is not every pixel but a representation: a description of the world that makes explicit what the next decision needs and leaves out the rest [8]. A person may name three things, how far the nearest surfaces are, what the objects around it are, and how those objects and the robot itself are moving; but what a representation should make explicit is a long-standing question in vision. One tradition answered that a general-purpose description of the scene should come first, built once for any task to read [38]. The other answered that perception is purposive: it exists for action and should pick out only what the behavior at hand needs [14]. Deep learning gave the second answer its mechanism: the task’s own error, back-propagated into the representation [26].

Vision foundation models have since made the general-purpose tradition practical; navigation, building on them, has largely set the purposive one aside. A vision foundation model is a general-purpose description at a scale no one could have built by hand, but it makes explicit what its own objective needs and by its final layer has left out the rest, including much of the spatial structure it built along the way [56, 42, 43]; most navigation policies built on vision-language models take that output through an interface fixed before the task exists [59, 58, 9]. Fine-tuning the encoder is only a partial remedy: it adapts one network behind the same output and can erode the general description [24]. They follow open-ended instructions and track a person described in words, yet still misjudge free space, collide with obstacles they could describe, and lose a target that turns a corner. The field has more general-purpose visual prior than ever, yet its policies have little say over what they see.

We argue that the two answers need no longer exclude each other in embodied navigation. With vision foundation models a general-purpose description now exists, so the purposive step can be taken on top of it rather than instead of it, and the action gradient is the instrument for taking it. We call the result a self-constructed representation space: a representation constructed by the policy’s own objectives out of the internal structure of vision foundation models. We present RepresentNav (RepNav), a navigation foundation model that sees and dreams in such a space. It builds the space with Representation Residuals (Fig. 2a), a compact three-layer transformer that attends over layers spanning the full depth of three complementary vision foundation models, semantic, geometric, and dynamic; what it makes explicit is found in training and differs across regions of one view. This is how RepresentNav sees what it needs.

The same question arises in future prediction. Seeing tells the robot where the free space is; crossing the hall requires knowing where it will be a moment later, once the things around it have moved, and an agent that carries a model of the world can anticipate these changes before it acts [49, 17, 25]. Latent reasoning and navigation world models do this, but in spaces defined by someone else: text, hand-designed spatial tokens, the latent space of a pretrained generative model, or pixels [19, 28, 32, 64, 6]. A policy that builds its own space for acting has a space of its own to dream in. RepresentNav therefore precedes every action with a latent chain-of-thought (Fig. 2b), trained to predict the representation of the scene 0.4 to 1.6 s ahead in that same space. Its targets are the [CLS] tokens of the future observations, a learnable token that attends alongside the spatial tokens through the three layers of Representation Residuals and gathers each view into one vector; the dream is learned jointly with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a VISReg regularizer [54] on the targets. This is how RepresentNav dreams what it wants: in the space through which it sees.

RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks (Figure 1), including 83.80% success on VLNVerse fine-grained (+20.05) and 85.5% tracking rate on EVT-Bench distracted tracking (+10.1) with a single camera, and the gains carry over to a physical robot (Section 4). Because our claims concern the representation, we then look inside (Section 5) and find:

The self-constructed space exploits the internal structure of the priors. Without a dream, it nearly doubles the gain of concatenating the same three models’ outputs, drawing on layers concatenation never sees, such as the dynamic model’s layer before its last, and differently across regions of a view (Section 5.1).

The dream pays off in the self-constructed space. Dreaming in the space the policy sees through removes a quarter of the collisions (Section 5.2).

One dreamed latent holds a compact world state. Decoded after the fact, it gives the scene’s depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, though occupancy was never a training target, and the rollout gives how the robot and the target move up to 1.2 s ahead (Section 5.3).

In summary, we build a purposive representation on top of a general-purpose one and realize it in RepresentNav with Representation Residuals, a latent chain-of-thought trained as a JEPA in the constructed space, and a two-stage curriculum that first makes the policy act through its dream and then lets it act on what it sees and dreams together.

2. The dream pays off in the self-constructed space. Dreaming in the space the policy sees through removes a quarter of the collisions (Section 5.2).

title: RobustRLlib: A Unified Library and Benchmark for Robust Reinforcement Learning Algorithms
authors: Xi Chen,Fengqi Hu,Zeyu Shen,Jiaying Xu,Shangding Gu,Pan Xu,Anqi Liu,Laixi Shi
comment: Project page, code, and tutorial:this https URL
abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms. The code and tutorial are available at https://robustrl-lib.github.io.
introduction:
Despite remarkable advances in reinforcement learning (RL), its real-world deployment remains limited by robustness and safety concerns, particularly in high-stakes domains such as autonomous driving (Ding et al., 2023b), clinical trials (Liu et al., 2015), robotics (Li et al., 2021), and semiconductor manufacturing (Kozak et al., 2023). Policies trained in idealized environments can easily fail under distribution shifts or disruptions affecting various stages of the interaction, such as observations (Zhang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2021; Xiong et al., 2022), actions (Huang et al., 2017), or environment dynamics (Iyengar, 2005; Pinto et al., 2017), induced by diverse factors such as sim-to-real gaps (Pinto et al., 2017), model uncertainty (Bertsimas et al., 2019), noise, or adversarial attacks (Zhang et al., 2020; Klopp et al., 2017; Mahmood et al., 2018).

Robust RL therefore aims to develop policies that remain reliable under diverse types of disruptions and shifts, or their combinations in real-world scenarios (Bertsimas et al., 2019; Tversky and Kahneman, 1974; Arthur, 1991). A broad range of robust RL algorithms has shown strong performance in their specific type of disrupted application scenarios. More importantly, existing methods provide a rich set of robustness mechanisms and principles, including adversarial training (Pinto et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021; Rigter et al., 2022), dynamics randomization (Peng et al., 2018), robust value updates (Yang et al., 2022; Panaganti et al., 2022), and data augmentation (Yu et al., 2020b; Lu et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2024), offering substantial promise across a far broader range of applications and shift scenarios.

However, realizing this broader potential faces two fundamental barriers: algorithm reusability and systematic characterization of the capability boundary.
First, existing robust RL algorithms are fragmented across separate implementations and training pipelines, lacking a unified library or interface through which practitioners can readily try and compare a broad collection of robust RL methods on a new application. Second, the empirical capability boundary of current robust RL remains unclear: for a given application and distribution shift, we lack a systematic understanding of how well existing methods perform, when they remain effective, and where they fail. This is largely because the methods are typically evaluated in distinct environments and shift scenarios, making cross-method comparison difficult and performance beyond their original settings poorly understood.

To address these two gaps, we introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric robust RL benchmark that brings together (1) a robust RL method library with reusable implementations to substantially lower the barrier to applying existing methods to new problems, and (2) a comprehensive evaluation pipeline across tasks and diverse real-world shift scenarios. Complementing existing robust RL benchmarks that primarily focus on developing evaluation tasks and shift scenarios (Dulac-Arnold et al., 2020; Zouitine et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2025), RobustRLlib focuses on making robust RL algorithms systematically accessible, comparable, and extensible, while providing a broader evaluation framework (Comparison in Appendix A.1). Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

A robust RL algorithm library.
We integrate existing 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms, understanding and systematically organizing them by their learning methods, intended target shifts, and base algorithms for applicators’ easy reference. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and
developing new robust RL algorithms.

A robust RL algorithm library.
We integrate existing 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms, understanding and systematically organizing them by their learning methods, intended target shifts, and base algorithms for applicators’ easy reference. It provides a reusable foundation for applying existing methods to new applications and
developing new robust RL algorithms.

An enhanced evaluation platform.
Our extensible disruptor toolbox covers a broad range of distribution shifts, including MDP-element shifts in observations, actions, dynamics, and reward/cost, as well as control-loop latency and task-semantic shifts. It supports diverse shift modes, including stochastic, adversarial, and parametric perturbations with non-stationary schedules, enabling both isolated and compound-shift evaluation. The same disruptor interface further extends to massively parallel training in Isaac Lab (Mittal et al., 2025) and advanced vision–language–action (VLA) robotic tasks (Intelligence et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026).

An up-to-date capability map of robust RL algorithms. Evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations reveals that
robust methods outperform standard references on
average, but both groups deteriorate markedly as shifts intensify. A method’s
claimed target shift does not reliably predict its empirical strengths, gains vary
across tasks and shift sources, with online methods showing larger incremental effects than offline ones. By connecting
diverse algorithm features to their measured strengths, this map provides
guidance for designing robust RL methods for deployment shifts.

title: Regularised RL improves sim-to-real transfer
authors: Danilo Vucetic,Mohamad H. Danesh,Florence Clerc,Hsiu-Chin Lin,Jonathan Tremblay
comment: of main-body content, with supporting details in the appendices. Under submission
abstract:
Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) has provable robustness guarantees that should ease the transfer of policies from simulation to robots, known as sim-to-real.
Yet, weakly regularised algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) remain the de facto choice in sim-to-real pipelines, while the practical benefits of regularisation for transfer remain poorly characterised.
In this work, we study the sim-to-real performance of commonly used RL algorithms, with the aim of characterising the effects of regularisation on robotic performance.
To that end, we derive Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a novel regularised RL algorithm based on the soft mellowmax value function, which carries strong robustness guarantees.
On MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks, SMM-AC is competitive with baselines like Soft Actor-Critic (SAC).
On real robots, SMM-AC achieves higher return, while exhibiting greater robustness to perturbations in observations, the environment, and dynamics than baselines.
Together, these results demonstrate that regularised RL improves real-world policy deployment through better robustness to the sim-to-real gap, and changing real-world conditions.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard tool for robotic control, with on-policy, weakly regularised algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) serving as the de facto choice in most sim-to-real pipelines.
Recent work has shown that carefully stabilised off-policy RL algorithms can match or outperform PPO in massively parallel simulators while also transferring to real legged robots, including humanoids and quadrupeds (Gallici et al., 2025; Seo et al., 2025a; Seo et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2026; Sabatini et al., 2026).
However, these evaluations primarily focus on task performance: whether a policy can complete a task under the conditions for which it was trained. In real-world deployment, policies must contend with changes in observations, environment properties, and system dynamics that are difficult to model exhaustively in simulation a priori. Robustness to such perturbations is therefore an important aspect of reliable sim-to-real transfer.

Regularisation provides a principled way to induce robustness. Regularised RL has long dominated benchmarks in continuous control and arcade games, demonstrating superior sample efficiency and stable optimisation (Dam et al., 2024; Haarnoja et al., 2018a; Ahmed et al., 2019).
Beyond these practical benefits, the theoretical duality between regularised and robust RL suggests that regularisation can also provide implicit robustness to dynamics and task perturbations (Derman et al., 2021; Eysenbach and Levine, 2022; Husain et al., 2021; Brekelmans et al., 2022).
This mechanism is complementary to Domain Randomisation (DR), which explicitly trains policies over a user-specified distribution of environment variations, such as changes to initial conditions or physical parameters (Eysenbach and Levine, 2022; Mittal et al., 2025).
Whereas DR requires the practitioner to anticipate and specify the perturbations of interest, regularisation can induce robustness without explicitly enumerating them.
This raises a natural empirical question: does the robustness induced by regularisation translate into more reliable real-world policy deployment?

Robotics is a natural testbed to evaluate the robustness of policies because the sim-to-real gap is precisely an unmodeled change in the dynamics under which the policy must achieve high return.
We hypothesize that policies robust to a larger set of perturbations achieve 1) higher real-world return under sim-to-real transfer, and 2) higher retention of their performance under deployment-time dynamics perturbations.
Jiralerspong et al. (2025) show that RL with the Soft MellowMax (SMM) value function is robust to a larger set of perturbations than entropy-regularised RL, making it a natural target for our investigation.
However, SMM has only been defined for discrete state-action spaces, usually in Q-learning algorithms (Asadi and Littman, 2017; Gan et al., 2021).
Extending SMM to continuous continuous control is non-trivial, as the value function requires integrating over an intractable reference policy. To overcome this, we propose Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), which approximates the SMM reference policy using a dedicated, slowly updated reference network, ensuring stable actor-critic optimisation in continuous domains.

To test our hypotheses, we evaluate SMM-AC alongside PPO, SAC, and TD3 in simulation and on real-world robots, including a Franka arm and an ANYmal-D quadruped.
In addition to real-world task performance, we evaluate policies under deployment-time perturbations to observations, environment properties, and system dynamics. Across these experiments, regularised methods maintain higher performance in sim-to-real transfer and under real-world perturbations, while SMM-AC achieves the strongest performance and robustness across tasks.
We also show that regularised methods are more likely to be deployable than standard RL policies, even under large sim-to-real gaps.
Figure 1 illustrates this sim-to-real robustness in the Franka cube-lifting task and in ANYmal-D rough-terrain locomotion, showing that under real-world perturbations, regularised methods deploy successfully.
Together, our results provide empirical evidence that the robustness induced by regularisation can translate into improved reliability during real-world deployment.
In this work we

extend soft mellowmax to continuous state-action spaces and derive Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a practical off-policy actor-critic algorithm based on SAC (Sec. 3);

validate SMM-AC’s performance in simulation on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, showing that it achieves similar average returns to SAC and other baselines (Sec. 4);

characterise the sim-to-real performance and real-world perturbation robustness of RL policies on manipulation and locomotion tasks, showing that SMM-AC achieves higher real-world returns and maintains stronger performance under perturbations than the baselines (Sec. 5).

1. extend soft mellowmax to continuous state-action spaces and derive Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a practical off-policy actor-critic algorithm based on SAC (Sec. 3);

2. validate SMM-AC’s performance in simulation on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, showing that it achieves similar average returns to SAC and other baselines (Sec. 4);

3. characterise the sim-to-real performance and real-world perturbation robustness of RL policies on manipulation and locomotion tasks, showing that SMM-AC achieves higher real-world returns and maintains stronger performance under perturbations than the baselines (Sec. 5).

title: Retiming Robot Demonstrations with a Learned Speed Prior
authors: Seungyong Moon,Deokjae Lee,Hansang Lee,Munkhtselmeg Battsengel,Youngin Kim,Seonghyeon Yun,Sungjin Jeon,SongEun Kim,Jeongmin Park,Hyun Oh Song
abstract:
The pace of a robot demonstration is often determined by the teleoperator rather than by the task itself. As a result, the same motion can appear at widely different speeds across demonstrations, and policies trained on such data may inherit operator-specific timing along with task behavior. We propose to learn a speed prior directly from large-scale demonstration data. Given a task instruction, a motion path and the images along it, it predicts a distribution over execution speed along the path, from which a chosen quantile defines a consistent clock for retiming each demonstration. Existing methods derive the acceleration signal from the very data they accelerate, so each new task costs another fit, annotation, or pair of predefined rates. A single trained speed prior instead covers every task in a corpus. We fit a speed prior on both robot teleoperation data and handheld demonstrations in which a human arm, rather than a robot arm, moves the gripper, and use it to retime robot demonstrations to the handheld pace before fine-tuning a vision-language-action policy. For execution, we pair the policy with a real-time optimal-control layer that tracks predicted action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace. On 120 RoboLab tasks, policies fine-tuned on our learned clocks succeed more often and move with up to half the jerk compared with policies fine-tuned on the original demonstration timing and uniformly accelerated to the same speed. On a real robot, our policy stacks cups in 3.50 s3.50\text{\,}\mathrm{s}, 1.72×\times faster than the default policy’s 6.02 s6.02\text{\,}\mathrm{s} while succeeding as often, in 29 of 30 trials. Videos and further material are available at
https://mllab.snu.ac.kr/projects/learned_speed_prior.
introduction:
The pace of robot demonstrations depends on both the collection setup and the operator. Moving a robot through a teleoperation interface is slower than moving a handheld gripper directly (Chi et al., 2024), and novice operators often hesitate or pause where experienced operators do not. Policies trained to imitate these demonstrations inherit the operators’ pace along with the task behavior, often executing more slowly than necessary (Guo et al., 2025; Arachchige et al., 2025).

Prior work speeds up such policies by retiming their demonstrations before or during training, or by accelerating their execution (Guo et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026a; Sanchez et al., 2026; Nam et al., 2025; Jing et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Arachchige et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026c). These methods shorten motion segments that require less precision, train the policy at a range of speeds, or execute the motion as fast as the robot’s limits allow. They typically adjust the original demonstration timing based on task requirements, external speed commands, or robot limits. Few instead learn the pace from demonstrators who perform similar motions faster.

We instead draw the pace from such demonstrators, for example those using a handheld gripper or experienced with the task, and give it to the demonstrations that the policy learns from. Their demonstrations need not follow the same paths, so we do not copy their timing but learn a speed prior, a model of how fast they move along a given path. Given the local shape of an end-effector path, the wrist-camera images along it and the task instruction, the prior predicts a distribution over the speed at which demonstrators traverse each part of the path. It is trained once on both kinds of demonstrations across all their tasks, with a label that marks the kind of each demonstration, so reading a path with the label of the faster demonstrators predicts how fast they would traverse it. A quantile of this distribution defines a clock that keeps the path of a demonstration but replaces its timing. We then fine-tune a policy on demonstrations retimed with the median clock and let it also predict tempo channels, the pace of higher quantiles, so that it can be sped up at deployment.

The predicted pace reflects human motion and may therefore exceed the velocity, acceleration or torque limits of the robot. Joint PD control, commonly used to execute such policies, does not plan within these limits, so fast targets can cause tracking lag or safety reflexes (Khazatsky et al., 2024; Physical Intelligence, 2025). Consecutive action chunks may also disagree at their boundaries, and each new chunk must accommodate the pace of the ongoing motion. We therefore introduce a controller that treats the predicted pace as an upper bound and executes each chunk as fast as the robot’s limits permit, slowing down only where a limit becomes active. When a new chunk arrives, the controller smoothly connects it to the ongoing motion, preserving continuity in position, velocity, and acceleration while carrying the execution clock forward.

We train the speed prior on teleoperated demonstrations from DROID and handheld demonstrations from FastUMI-100K, and use it to give DROID the handheld pace before fine-tuning the released π0.5\pi_{0.5} DROID policy (Khazatsky et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025; Physical Intelligence, 2025). On 120 tasks of the RoboLab simulation benchmark, this policy succeeds more often than a uniformly accelerated policy at the same speed-up, and at 2.4×2.4\times it does so with 52% less jerk (Yang et al., 2026c). Training only on fast demonstrations does not achieve this. A policy trained on the fastest DROID episodes alone, although their pace is 1.5×1.5\times that of all episodes, runs just 1.07×1.07\times faster than the policy trained on all of them. We observe the same on a real robot, where we adapt the prior to handheld demonstrations collected with a YUBI gripper and retime them to the pace of the shortest quarter of the episodes (Ohkawa et al., 2026). Our policy stacks cups in 3.50 s3.50\text{\,}\mathrm{s} instead of 6.02 s6.02\text{\,}\mathrm{s} and succeeds in 29 of 30 trials, whereas a policy trained only on this quarter succeeds in 9 of 30 trials. On the same three-cup pyramid, SAIL reports 14.71 s14.71\text{\,}\mathrm{s} at a success rate of 0.40 for a diffusion policy trained on teleoperated demonstrations and accelerated by 1.76×1.76\times (Arachchige et al., 2025), so our policy stacks them 4.2×4.2\times faster and succeeds more than twice as often. Finally, executing a human pace requires a controller that respects the robot’s limits. With our controller in place of joint PD control, even the policy trained on the recorded timing folds the towel in 97% of trials instead of 13%.

title: Not an Accident: Exploiting Safety Filter Inadequacy in Humanoid Robots
authors: Tiffany Bao,Shangtao Li,Yifan Sun,Mengwen He,Bowei Li,Alden Wang,Changliu Liu,Ruoyu Wang,David Brumley
abstract:
As humanoid robots move from research laboratories toward deployment in human-centered environments such as homes, hospitals, and warehouses, safe operation around nearby people and objects becomes a fundamental requirement.
Safety filters have emerged as a promising technique to address this challenge by providing mathematical guarantees that generated control actions do not result in collisions.
introduction:
As humanoid robots move into human-centered environments such as homes and hospitals, ensuring safe operation around people and objects becomes a fundamental requirement that one must meet, because even a single collision can cause physical injury, property damage, or disruption of critical tasks [49].

Safety filters have emerged as a promising approach to this challenge.
They monitor the control generated by a robot’s nominal controller and intervene whenever the nominal control violates safety constraints.
Optimization-based safety filters compute an alternative control by solving a constrained optimization problem based on formulations such as safety indices [28, 60], safe sets [28, 15], and control barrier functions (CBFs) [4, 3].
By construction, the resulting control satisfies the specified safety constraints whenever the optimization problem is feasible.
Thanks to these guarantees, safety filters have attracted significant industrial interest and have entered pilot deployments in large industrial sectors.

However, existing safety filters can still fail to prevent collisions.
One well-known limitation is safe control infeasibility [2, 16], where the underlying optimization problem admits no feasible solution and therefore no safe control exists.

We identify a second limitation that has received little attention.
Existing safety filters rely on safety-related parameters whose correct values depend on both the task and the environment.
Improper parameter configurations can cause the controller to generate controls that satisfy the optimization problem but nevertheless fail to maintain safety.
Humanoid robots exacerbate both limitations, as their high-dimensional articulated bodies and operation in cluttered, dynamic environments make optimization infeasibility more likely [22, 40] and accurate parameter configuration significantly more difficult [57].

Worse, we discover that existing optimization-based safety filters only optimize the current control step.
They neither predict future states nor account for future optimization feasibility.
As a result, a controller may successfully resolve the current safety violation while simultaneously steering the robot toward a future state where no feasible recovery exists.

In this paper, we show that these limitations expose a previously unrecognized attack surface.
An adversary can exploit them to steer a humanoid robot into a safety-inadequate state where the safety controller can no longer prevent collision.
Unlike prior attacks that compromise software, spoof sensors, or manipulate low-level control signals, our attack requires only legitimate task requests submitted through the robot’s normal user interface.
By carefully selecting intermediate goals or task locations, an attacker can intentionally drive the robot toward a safety-inadequate state that its safety filter cannot avoid.

We argue that this vulnerability has a real-world implication.
Consider a bedside assistant robot deployed in a hospital.
While the robot delivers medication to a patient, another patient or visitor requests that it also retrieve a glass of water or pick up medication from a nearby room.
Because the request appears legitimate and authorized, the task planner naturally inserts it into the execution schedule.
The synthesized intermediate goal then steers the robot toward a safety-inadequate state.
Depending on the robot’s fail-safe strategy, the robot may fail the original task, collide with nearby people or medical equipment, or even fall during recovery [18].
Since every interaction is legitimate, such attacks are difficult to detect or attribute.

To assess the practicality and impact of this attack, we develop Siren, short for Safe-control Inadequacy via Reachable-goal Exploitation Nexus.
Siren is an automated framework that identifies safety-inadequate states in a given scenario, which is a combination of an environment and a target task, and synthesizes adversarial task goals that steer the robot into those states.
We evaluate Siren against seven representative optimization-based safety filter algorithms, including Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) [4], Safe Set Algorithm (SSA) [28], Sublevel Safe Set (SSS) [52], and their variants [15].
The evaluation demonstrates successful attacks against every evaluated safety filter in both simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
Compared with a random-search baseline, the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) used by Siren discovers 1.86x times of attacks in 35 vulnerable scenarios from SPARK, a popular testbed that includes a benchmark for safety filter evaluation [48].

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

We identify safe-control inadequacy as a previously unrecognized security vulnerability in optimization-based humanoid safety filters and show that attackers can exploit the vulnerability to cause safety issues such as collisions.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first security attack that targets optimization-based safety filters in humanoid robots.

We identify safe-control inadequacy as a previously unrecognized security vulnerability in optimization-based humanoid safety filters and show that attackers can exploit the vulnerability to cause safety issues such as collisions.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first security attack that targets optimization-based safety filters in humanoid robots.

We present goal insertion attacks and develop Siren, an automated framework that discovers safety-inadequate robot states and synthesizes adversarial task goals through normal user interactions.

We evaluate Siren against seven representative safety filter algorithms in simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. The results show successful attacks against every evaluated safety filter, and that Siren discovers 1.86x times as many attacks as identified by the random-search baseline.

1. We identify safe-control inadequacy as a previously unrecognized security vulnerability in optimization-based humanoid safety filters and show that attackers can exploit the vulnerability to cause safety issues such as collisions.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first security attack that targets optimization-based safety filters in humanoid robots.

2. We present goal insertion attacks and develop Siren, an automated framework that discovers safety-inadequate robot states and synthesizes adversarial task goals through normal user interactions.

3. We evaluate Siren against seven representative safety filter algorithms in simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. The results show successful attacks against every evaluated safety filter, and that Siren discovers 1.86x times as many attacks as identified by the random-search baseline.

title: SAGE: A hybrid vision-language and geometry framework for work-zone pathway prediction under temporary traffic control
authors: Jiaxi Liu,Keshu Wu,Weizhe Tang,Bofeng Cao,Sikai Chen,Xiaopeng Li,Steven T. Parker,Bin Ran
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
