abstract: Temporary traffic control redirects vehicles through work zones, requiring automated vehicles to connect an interpretation of the visible devices to a continuous passing path. Geometric predictors can provide several plausible paths, yet selecting the one consistent with the temporary control remains difficult. We propose SAGE (Semantic-to-Action Grounded Execution), a read–decide–execute–check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a shared candidate space. The central idea is to use a vision–language model’s (VLM’s) trajectory as a preference over intact geometric candidates. A role-decoupled generator constructs the candidates, and rank fusion combines each candidate’s geometric score with its agreement with the VLM trajectory. Supervision structured around the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) trains SAGE-VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The predicted hazard side enters image-space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, which support a final intervention bounded in score and displacement. On 2,306 real-world ROADWork validation episodes, the candidates include a path within 10 px of the human demonstration in 87% of episodes, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker’s error. SAGE reduces average and final displacement errors by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to the ranker, mostly in the far field, and hard-constraint violations by 37%. The trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator–selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to state-of-the-art VLM modules in accuracy, with a faster-responding VLM, and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/SAGE-page/.
introduction:
Roadway work zones temporarily change where and how vehicles may travel. Under temporary traffic control (TTC), signs announce closures, tapers of channelizing devices redirect traffic, and barriers separate the traffic space from the work space. Where the temporary path departs from the permanent alignment, the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) calls for devices that emphasize the intended path (Federal Highway Administration, 2025, §6A.02, §6B.03–6B.07). An automated vehicle (AV) must therefore interpret the observed arrangement and translate it into a continuous passing path. The consequences of an incorrect passage can be severe: 850 people died in U.S. work-zone crashes in 2024, including nearly 170 pedestrians and pedalcyclists (Federal Highway Administration, 2026). Reliable pathway prediction in this setting requires both an understanding of the temporary control and sufficient spatial precision to pass the workers and devices that define it.

Transportation research has established how work-zone layouts affect capacity and merge management (Weng and Meng, 2013; Markakis et al., 2022), crash occurrence and severity (Theofilatos et al., 2017; Osman et al., 2018), merging risk and worker protection (Weng et al., 2015; Sabeti et al., 2024), and drivers’ speed, merge timing, and lateral positioning (Finley et al., 2015; Weng et al., 2016; Hess et al., 2020; Chitturi et al., 2025). For AVs, these findings motivate a complementary problem: inferring the passing path from the control arrangement visible on board. Work-zone perception methods recognize signs and scenes (Seo et al., 2015; Sundharam et al., 2023), but studies of partially automated driving identify difficulties at temporary markings and cone-delineated lane shifts (Naujoks et al., 2017; Cummings and Bauchwitz, 2022). The June 2026 Waymo recall likewise documents vehicles entering construction closures after passing closure signs or between channelizing cones (Waymo LLC, 2026). Infrastructure information can assist this interpretation. The Work Zone Data Exchange (WZDx), for example, communicates lane statuses such as closed and shift-left (U.S. Department of Transportation, 2023), and transportation research calls for coordinating such information with vehicle capabilities (Dehman and Farooq, 2021). The vehicle must still determine the continuous path through the layout that it encounters.

We study this problem as temporary-control-aware pathway prediction: an AV that takes front-view imagery and an observed path prefix as input should predict one future path. A coarse instruction such as shift left leaves the onset, extent, and shape of the shift unspecified. Conversely, a smooth continuation of recent motion can miss a redirection indicated by devices farther ahead. ROADWork provides real-world work-zone images, device annotations, scene descriptions, and demonstrated driver pathways from 16 U.S. cities for studying this problem (Ghosh et al., 2025). In more than 90% of its turning episodes, the demonstrated path crosses our departure threshold only in the far third of the prediction horizon (Section 4.2). Much of the relevant choice therefore concerns how the path develops beyond its observed prefix.

Geometry-based predictors offer a useful action space for this choice. Waypoint-conditioned models such as PECNet and Y-Net represent multiple plausible futures (Mangalam et al., 2020; Mangalam et al., 2021), while hierarchical planners generate alternatives and select among them using geometric, kinematic, or cost-based information (Yao and Sun, 2025; Chen et al., 2026). In a cone-delineated work-zone lane closure, polynomial trajectory planning similarly constructs alternatives and selects a collision-free path (Formosa et al., 2024). Device roles and spatial features can inform both generation and ranking, but their contribution depends on whether they help distinguish the passing options in a particular layout. Our candidate-pool analysis locates substantial room for improvement at this selection step: 87.4% of validation episodes contain a candidate with average displacement error (ADE) below 10 px, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker’s error. Geometric selection, however, lacks an interpretation of the temporary control, so in a work zone a smooth and kinematically plausible path can still head toward the coned-off side (Fig. 1(a)).

Vision–language models (VLMs) provide a complementary source of scene information. Driving-oriented models relate objects and decisions through graph-structured questions (Sima et al., 2024), produce planning decisions or trajectories from camera inputs (You et al., 2026; Xing et al., 2025; Qiao et al., 2025; Chi et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026a), and supply semantic rewards for driving policies (Huang et al., 2025). Work-zone studies develop retrieval, memory, latent trajectory reasoning, and causal supervision to improve this capability (Liao et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026b); complementary work predicts drivable boundaries from synthetic and real work-zone data (Sahu et al., 2026). Scene interpretation and coordinate prediction nevertheless remain distinct abilities. A model can identify the side to avoid while its path still ends on that side: SAGE-VLM names the described hazard side in 92.7% of the cases in which it names one, yet 2.25% of its paths, executed directly, end on that side (Sections 5.1 and 5.3). Such a path can take the vehicle into the closed side or across a channelizing line (Fig. 1(b)). Geometry thus provides precise candidates without an interpretation of the temporary control, and a VLM provides the interpretation without a path that reliably follows it; what is missing is a connection between the two.

To fill this gap, we propose SAGE (Semantic-to-Action Grounded Execution), a read–decide–execute–check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a common candidate space. Its central insight is that a VLM trajectory can inform path selection even when its endpoint is less accurate than that of the geometric prediction. The full trajectory expresses the spatial development of a passing option, preserving differences between candidates that share a coarse maneuver. A structured reading provides a complementary account of the temporary control against which the selected path can be checked. Compared with hybrid designs that pass VLM plans or controller parameters to a planner (Tian et al., 2025; Long et al., 2026) or score trajectory candidates with learned or VLM-enhanced scorers (Li et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026), SAGE keeps every output coordinate geometric, bounds the VLM’s influence in rank and path space, and checks the selection against MUTCD provisions.

SAGE implements this design with a role-decoupled generator, RD-YNet, whose free-space and TTC-conditioned branches construct alternative pathways. A learned geometric ranker supplies the default choice. The VLM trajectory induces an opinion ranking over the candidates, which is combined with the geometric ranking through trajectory-as-opinion (TAO) fusion. Every selected path retains its original geometric coordinates.

To support the checks, MUTCD-structured supervision trains SAGE-VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The hazard side enters image-space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, and a bounded intervention, Z0, can replace a flagged choice with a predicate-consistent candidate within fixed bounds on the score gap and the mean displacement. We evaluate the trajectory opinion and this intervention separately, using displacement errors, control-consistency measures, and a device-anchored metric frame that relates image-space predictions to lateral offsets in meters.

The main contributions are as follows:

We propose a shared-candidate framework for temporary-control-aware pathway prediction. SAGE combines a VLM trajectory’s preference information with geometric ranking while preserving every candidate’s coordinates, and separates this selection interface from the checks informed by the VLM’s reading.

We develop MUTCD-structured supervision for SAGE-VLM and connect its explicit control reading to a bounded intervention. The model reports the lane status and hazard side before completing its trajectory; the hazard side supplies the interpreted input to predicates on the candidate paths.

We establish the value of this division of labor on 2,306 ROADWork validation episodes. SAGE reduces ADE and final displacement error (FDE) by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to its geometric ranker, and hard-constraint violations by 37%, and the trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator–selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to OneVL in accuracy with a faster-responding VLM and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures.

We complement image-space displacement with a device-anchored metric frame, MUTCD-derived consistency measures, and a safety score on human-filtered episodes. These measures link the accuracy analysis to the spatial demands of work-zone passage, and recording-clustered confidence intervals quantify the uncertainty of the gains from the opinion and the intervention.

Section 2 formulates the problem, and Section 3 describes SAGE. Section 4 presents the experimental setup, followed by results in Section 5. Sections 6 and 7 discuss the implications and limitations and conclude the paper.

1. We propose a shared-candidate framework for temporary-control-aware pathway prediction. SAGE combines a VLM trajectory’s preference information with geometric ranking while preserving every candidate’s coordinates, and separates this selection interface from the checks informed by the VLM’s reading.

2. We develop MUTCD-structured supervision for SAGE-VLM and connect its explicit control reading to a bounded intervention. The model reports the lane status and hazard side before completing its trajectory; the hazard side supplies the interpreted input to predicates on the candidate paths.

3. We establish the value of this division of labor on 2,306 ROADWork validation episodes. SAGE reduces ADE and final displacement error (FDE) by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to its geometric ranker, and hard-constraint violations by 37%, and the trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator–selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to OneVL in accuracy with a faster-responding VLM and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures.

4. We complement image-space displacement with a device-anchored metric frame, MUTCD-derived consistency measures, and a safety score on human-filtered episodes. These measures link the accuracy analysis to the spatial demands of work-zone passage, and recording-clustered confidence intervals quantify the uncertainty of the gains from the opinion and the intervention.

title: StackGen3D: Stable 3D Block Stack Generation from Multiview Silhouettes
authors: Xiaopeng Zhang,Luzhe Sun,Yiqing Xu,Matthew R. Walter
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: A poster of this work is publicly available on the website of the Creativity in Assembly Workshop at IROS 2026 (non-archival)

introduction:
Creative assembly often begins from an incomplete specification rather than a fully defined 3D target: a user may provide a sketch, silhouette, or other abstract description of what the final structure should look like [1, 2]. We study a concrete instance of this problem: given a fixed set of primitive blocks and three orthographic silhouettes, generate a physically stable 3D structure that matches the specified views.

This setting presents two coupled challenges. First, silhouette-to-3D generation is inherently underdetermined. Many block-pose configurations can produce nearly identical projections, while only a subset avoid interpenetration and remain stable. The goal is therefore to model a multimodal distribution over physically feasible structures consistent with the visual specification. Second, learning such a distribution requires a diverse dataset of stable 3D structures paired with silhouettes. Obtaining this data is difficult: physical feasibility must be evaluated for each candidate structure, while repeatedly searching and validating configurations with a physics simulator is expensive and difficult to scale. Simple procedural stacking heuristics provide stable examples, but cover only a limited portion of the space of possible structures.

We propose StackGen3D to address these challenges. First, we construct a scalable dataset of physically stable structures. We train a physics-informed graph neural network (PI-GNN) over block support relations as a fast surrogate for stability evaluation, and use it to curate diverse stable structures that are paired with multiview silhouettes. Second, using this dataset, we train a conditional flow-matching model to capture the multimodal distribution of block poses conditioned on the block inventory and target silhouettes. At inference time, lightweight AABB-based Best-of-NN selection or Remove-then-Rerun refinement reduces residual inter-block collisions without physics simulation.

Our preliminary results support both stages of the approach. First, our data-generation pipeline provides a strong basis for scalable curation of physically stable structures. A PI-GNN trained only on simple structures transfers substantially better to complex structures than a parameter-matched MLP (92.66% vs. 46.86% accuracy), indicating that support-relation reasoning generalizes across structural complexity and can serve as an effective stability model. Second, the generative model trained on the resulting stable-structure dataset learns to produce structures that satisfy the target silhouettes while capturing useful physical regularities. A single flow-matching sample achieves 0.967 silhouette IoU, and simulator-free Best-of-10 selection increases post-hoc physical stability from 45.3% to 72.4% while preserving silhouette fidelity. Together, these results provide preliminary evidence that scalable stable-data generation can enable learned generative models for underdetermined creative structure.

title: PnP*: A certifiable solver for Perspective-n-Point
authors: Bang-Shien Chen,Caitrin E. Eaton,David M. Rosen
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: Estimating a camera pose from 3D-2D correspondences — Perspective-n-Point — is one of the most fundamental problems in computer vision. Existing methods either solve a minimal problem or replace the objective with an easier one. Surprisingly, no scalable certifiable solver for the actual Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) exists. We propose PnP*, the first practical solver that guarantees efficient computation and returns a certifiable globally optimal solution. We prove that the underlying convex relaxation is exact under moderate noise, which to our knowledge is the first stability guarantee for any relaxation for the MLE of PnP. Furthermore, we reduce the relaxation by exploiting chordal sparsity pattern and quotient ring reduction such that the relaxation is tractable and scalable. The stability and scalability results are verified numerically, as PnP* returns a provably correct camera pose at over 10 Hz.
introduction:
Perspective-n-Point (PnP) estimates a camera’s pose given NN correspondences between 3D points and 2D measurements. It is one of the most fundamental problems in computer vision, with various applications such as structure-from-motion, visual navigation, and augmented reality.

The Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) of PnP is non-convex because (i) the camera perspective projection is a rational function of the pose, and (ii) the feasible set of the pose is also non-convex. A natural approach is to minimize it locally through a nonlinear solver, e.g., Levenberg–Marquardt, but local methods require a good initialization. Common methods therefore solve an approximation of the problem in order to obtain an initial point.
Minimal solvers fix a small number of correspondences, which yields some equation system that can be solved efficiently. However, a minimal set is insufficient to average down the noise, and leaves open which correspondences to select. Non-minimal solvers, on the other hand, replace the MLE objective by an alternative error11
1
See Section 2.1 for examples of alternative errors. Some literature refers to such errors as algebraic errors, and to the MLE as geometric error (Hartley and Zisserman, 2003). that can be solved efficiently or even globally, but their solutions are for a wrong objective.
Finally, branch-and-bound optimizes the MLE objective directly, but its computation time can grow exponentially in the worst case (see Table 1).

We propose PnP*, the first scalable certifiable solver for the actual MLE, named after optimality and its star graph structure. We reformulate PnP as a quadratic program by introducing only the necessary auxiliary variables, and adding redundant constraints such that the problem’s sparsity pattern is preserved. We prove that the resulting semidefinite relaxation is exact under moderate noise by verifying the stability conditions (Cifuentes et al., 2022), which is to our knowledge the first stability guarantee for any relaxation of the MLE of PnP. We derive an equivalent tractable relaxation by exploiting the chordal star graph structure, and reduce the variable dimension by quotient ring reduction. In summary, PnP* is the first practical solver that guarantees efficient computation and returns a provably correct camera pose.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews prior work on PnP and certifiable solvers. Section 3 introduces the notation and preliminaries we use throughout. Section 4 derives the relaxation for the MLE of PnP, and Section 5 proves that the relaxation is stable. Section 6 reformulates the relaxation into a scalable one. Section 7 validates the stability and scalability results numerically, and finally, Section 8 concludes.

title: Does LeWorldModel Preserve Local Action Geometry?
authors: Vasil Vasilev,Siddharth Nayak
comment: . Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), Extended Abstract Track
abstract:
We examine how closely pretrained LeWorldModel (LeWM) reproduces the
effects of small action changes. Using matched simulator and model
responses, we measure action sensitivity with Gram matrices at three
perturbation scales. Across nearly a thousand states from Reacher and
OGBench Cube, the most sensitive action directions differ by median
angles of about 36∘36^{\circ} and 42∘42^{\circ}, respectively, at the smallest
scale. Increasing the perturbation tenfold reduces median normalized
Gram discrepancy by roughly 70% on Reacher and 47% on Cube.
Geometry measured in pixels and embeddings varies more across scales
than the chosen physical-state geometry. On held-out directions,
environment Grams achieve median embedding response errors of 17% and
28%, compared with 26% and 38% for an isotropic reference with the same
trace. LeWM’s errors are higher at this scale. These findings support
scale-specific evaluation of action sensitivity; its effect on control
remains an open question.
introduction:
World models support planning through learned predictive dynamics
(Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; Hafner et al., 2024). Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures learn in
representation space (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024), including action-conditioned systems
such as V-JEPA 2 and LeWorldModel (LeWM) (Assran et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026). Accurate prediction
at a sampled action does not establish that nearby action directions have
the correct relative effects. This motivates evaluating action sensitivity
alongside aggregate prediction and control scores.

We study pretrained LeWM on Reacher and OGBench Cube using simulator
counterfactuals and a shared frozen encoder. Related symmetry-aware and
geometric perspectives motivate this diagnostic (Lillemark et al., 2026; Cayco-Gajic and Pellegrino, 2026).
Our contributions
are a matched finite-scale comparison, calibration against simple references,
and validation on held-out action directions in three distinct output
metrics. We distinguish sensitivity in the encoder’s output space from
physical response and goal-directed action choice.

title: The effect of limb kinematics on the speed of a legged robot on granular media
authors: Chen Li,Paul B. Umbanhowar,Haldun Komsuoglu,Daniel I. Goldman
subjects: Biological Physics (physics.bio-ph); Soft Condensed Matter (cond-mat.soft); Robotics (cs.RO); Fluid Dynamics (physics.flu-dyn); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
To move effectively over a wide range of terrestrial terrain requires generation of propulsive forces through appropriate muscle function and limb kinematics [1, 2]. Most biological locomotion studies have focused on steady rhythmic locomotion on hard, flat, non-slip ground. On these surfaces kinematic (gait) parameters like limb frequency, stride length, stance and swing durations, and duty factor can change as organisms walk, run, hop and gallop [1]. There have been fewer biological studies of gait parameter modulation on non-rigid and non-flat ground, although it is clear that gait parameters are modulated as the substrate changes during challenges like climbing [3, 4], running on elastic/damped substrates [5], transitioning from running to swimming [6], and running on different preparations of granular media [7]. Even subtle kinematic changes in gait can lead to major differences in limb function [8]. A major challenge is to develop models of limb interaction with complex substrates and to develop hypotheses for how organisms vary gait parameters in response to substrate changes.

The RHex class of model locomotors (robots) has proved useful to test hypotheses of limb use in biological organisms on hard ground [9] and recently on more complex ground with few footholds [10] or the ability to flow [11]. These hexapedal devices model the dynamically stable locomotion of a cockroach and were the first legged machines to achieve autonomous locomotion at speeds exceeding one body length/s. In these devices, complexity in limb motion is pared down to a few biologically relevant parameters controlling intra-cycle “stance” and “swing” phases of 1-dof rotating limbs (referred to as“gait” parameters hereafter; see detailed description in Methods and Results). When these gait parameters are appropriately adjusted, RHex shows performance comparable in speed and stability to organisms on a diversity of terrain [12]. However, because of the scarcity of existing models of limb interaction with complex substrates, adjustment of the gait parameters is typically done empirically [13, 14].

Sand, a granular medium [15], is of particular interest for studies examining the effects of limb kinematics on locomotor performance on yielding terrain. In a previous study [11] we found that minor changes in the limb kinematics of a small RHex-class robot, SandBot (Fig. 1a), produced major changes in its locomotor mode and performance (speed) on a granular medium, poppy seeds (see Section 2.2). This sensitivity occurs, in part, because forced granular media remain solid below the yield stress, but can flow like a fluid when the yield stress is exceeded [16]. We tested SandBot on granular media of different yielding properties (set by granular volume fraction; see Section 2.1) at various limb frequencies but with the other gait parameters fixed. While there is no fundamental theory at the level of fluid mechanics that accounts for the physics of the solid-fluid transition of granular media or the dynamics of the fluidized regime, empirical models of granular penetration force have proved useful to predict SandBot’s speed [11]. SandBot’s propulsion is determined by factors that control this transition during limb-ground interaction (limb penetration depth, limb speed, body mass, grain friction, volume fraction, etc.). Using a simplified equation describing the granular penetration force, we developed a kinematic model to explain the locomotion of SandBot (see Section 2.2).

In this study, we advance our understanding of the effects of limb kinematics on locomotor performance by testing SandBot with varying gait parameters on sand of fixed yield strength and at fixed limb frequency. We find that robot speed depends sensitively on limb kinematics; while the original model qualitatively captures this sensitivity, the penetration force used in the model and other assumptions need to be modified to explain some important features. Our study not only reveals the specific optimal kinematics for SandBot on granular media, but also advances our understanding of how in general to achieve effective legged locomotion on complex terrain.
